reader_consequence: The Turkish reader is told the plot title is reordered, which is impossible, and misses the actual benefit of fct_reorder2(): the legend entries line up with the line order at the right-hand edge of the plot. The following paragraph then uses 'açıklama' (legend) for the same idea, so the two paragraphs contradict each other.

heading: Show all levels / Tüm seviyeleri gösterme
proposition: The English gives the motivating example as preparing many figures for MULTIPLE JURISDICTIONS; the Turkish replaces it with a tautology, 'many analyses (e.g. for more than one analysis)', so the jurisdictions example is absent.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader loses the concrete epidemiological reason for standardising levels: producing the same figure for several districts or regions whose data differ. The remaining parenthetical explains nothing.

heading: Show all levels / Tüm seviyeleri gösterme
proposition: The English says legends and tables should look identical even with varying levels of DATA COMPLETION or data composition; the Turkish keeps only data composition ('veri kompozisyonu') and drops data completion.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader misses one of the two situations that make fixed factor levels necessary: a dataset that is only partly reported, where a level exists but has no rows yet.

heading: Epiweeks in the data / Verilerde epiweeks
proposition: The English states the conversion of the epiweek column to the display format happens *within the data frame itself*, italicised as the contrast with the preceding 'in a plot' approach; the Turkish drops that clause entirely.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader loses the distinction this whole section rests on, that option 1 changes the stored column rather than only the plot display, and may assume the change is again plot-local.

heading: Convert to factor / Faktöre dönüştürme
proposition: The English says the level order is supplied AS a character vector TO the `levels = ` argument of factor(); the Turkish inverts the relation and says the order is set 'according to the `levels = ` argument in the character vector' ('karakter vektöründeki `levels =` argümanına göre').
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader is left without the actual calling syntax for base R factor(), and may look for a levels= argument inside a vector rather than passing a vector to levels=.

heading: Factors / Faktörler (intro)
proposition: The English says plot legends fluctuate when CERTAIN VALUES are temporarily absent from the data; the Turkish generalises this to the data itself being temporarily absent ('verilerin geçici olarak yok olması'), dropping the point that it is individual values that go missing.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader does not learn the specific failure this chapter exists to prevent, that a category with zero rows silently disappears from a legend, and may read it as a statement about missing data sets.

heading: Epiweeks in a plot
proposition: The English states that the date display formats use "%" placeholders and that those placeholders are documented in the Working with dates page; the Vietnamese drops that whole sentence and its cross-reference.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader who needs a format code other than %Y, %W or %U gets no pointer to the chapter that lists them, so they cannot build their own date_labels string.

heading: Reverse
proposition: The English limits guides() to reversing the plot LEGEND only; the Vietnamese says guides() reverses the order "in a plot" (trong mot bieu do) rather than the order of the variable, which the English does not support.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader may try guides() to reverse the order of categories on the x-axis of a plot. guides() changes the legend only, so the attempt fails with no obvious cause.

heading: By "end" value
proposition: The English states twice that fct_reorder2() aligns the level and legend order with the vertical order of the lines at the END (terminal right-hand side) of the plot; the Vietnamese says only "along the plot" (doc theo bieu do) and "the order of appearance of the lines in the plot", dropping the end-of-plot condition in both sentences.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader expects the legend order to match the line order anywhere in the plot. Where lines cross, the legend will not match at the left or middle, and the reader concludes the function is broken.

heading: Epiweeks in a plot
proposition: The English names the display format supplied to date_labels = as a "strptime" format; the Vietnamese omits the term strptime.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader loses the searchable keyword that identifies the format language, so they cannot look up the full set of codes in R help or online.

heading: Convert to factor
proposition: The English qualifies the alpha-numeric level order as the DEFAULT ("By default, the order of the levels will be alpha-numeric"); the Vietnamese states it without the qualifier, as though the order is always alphabetical.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader may believe factor levels are always sorted alphabetically and not realise the order is only a default that fct_relevel() and factor(levels = ) can set.

heading: YAML
proposition: The English says in-line R code in a YAML value is preceded by `r` WITHIN BACKTICKS; the Spanish says it is preceded by `r` 'entre comillas' (within quotes), then repeats 'pero tambien entre comillas' for the surrounding quotes.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader writes date: "'r Sys.Date()'" with quote marks instead of backticks, so the R code is never evaluated and the date renders as literal text.

heading: Narrative text
proposition: The English says in-line R code is inserted by surrounding the code with BACKTICKS; the Spanish says to surround it with 'puntos suspensivos' (an ellipsis, ...).
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader surrounds in-line code with dots instead of backticks, so no in-line R code in their narrative text ever executes.

heading: Code chunks
proposition: The English says a chunk is opened with three back-ticks plus CURLY brackets containing a lowercase r; the Spanish says 'corchetes' (square brackets), although the same translation uses 'llaves' for curly brackets at line 158.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader hand-typing a chunk writes ```[r] instead of ```{r}; knitr does not recognise it as an R chunk and the code is rendered as plain text.

heading: Section attributes
proposition: The Spanish bullet contains an extra attribute-looking token '{orientacion de los datos=}' that has no counterpart in the English, which lists only `{data-orientation=}`.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader may take '{orientacion de los datos=}' for a valid Spanish-language section attribute and write it after a page heading, where flexdashboard ignores it and the page keeps the default orientation.

heading: Interactive plots
proposition: The English says ggplotly() shows the value of every data point ON HOVER; the Spanish says it shows the value 'sobre el dashboard' (on the dashboard) and omits the hover trigger.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader does not learn that point values appear when the pointer rests on a point, so they may believe the interactive plot is broken when no values are displayed.

heading: Dashboards with R Markdown
proposition: The English says flexdashboard formats R Markdown output as a dashboard WITH PANELS and pages; the Spanish keeps only 'y paginas' and replaces 'with panels' with a parenthetical gloss of the word dashboard.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader misses that a dashboard is built from panels as well as pages, which is the structure the rest of the chapter builds on.

heading: Dashboards with R Markdown
proposition: The Resources section is located at the end of the page.
reader_consequence: The French reader is given a locative claim about where the Resources section sits that the English does not make; harmless if the layout matches, but it is unsourced content added by the translator.

heading: YAML
proposition: The YAML metadata example declares the document title with the key `title:`.
reader_consequence: The French example chunk writes `tite:` instead of `title:`, so a reader who copies the shown metadata block gets a document with no title and no error message pointing at the cause.

heading: YAML
proposition: Inline R code in a YAML value is written with the `r` preceded marker inside BACKTICKS.
reader_consequence: The French text says the `r` goes 'entre guillemets' (within quotes) rather than within backticks, so a reader writes date: "r Sys.Date()" with no backticks and the code is never evaluated; it prints as literal text.

heading: Code chunks
proposition: A code chunk is opened with three backticks followed by CURLY BRACKETS containing a lowercase r.
reader_consequence: The French text says 'parenthèses' (round brackets), so a reader writes ```(r) instead of ```{r}; the chunk is not recognised as R code and never runs.

heading: Narrative text
proposition: Inline R code is inserted into narrative text by surrounding the code with BACKTICKS.
reader_consequence: The French text says to surround the code with 'barres obliques inversées' (backslashes), so a reader writes \r 1+1\ and the inline code is never evaluated.

heading: Narrative text
proposition: The rendered page displays the literal inline-code syntax as an example, escaped so that it is not evaluated.
reader_consequence: The English escapes the example so the reader sees the syntax itself; the French writes it as live inline code, so the rendered page shows the evaluated result instead of the syntax, and the reader never sees the pattern being taught.

heading: Layout
proposition: The YAML parameter `orientation:` takes the literal value `rows` or `columns`.
reader_consequence: The French gives the accepted values as `rangees` or `colonnes`. flexdashboard accepts only the English literals, so a reader who follows this gets a dashboard that ignores the setting or fails to build.

heading: Orientation
proposition: Setting `orientation: columns` in YAML makes second-level headings create columns.
reader_consequence: The French instructs the reader to write `orientation: colonnes` (and gives `orientation: lignes` as the alternative). These are not valid flexdashboard values, so the layout will not change as described. The French code example at line 410 of the same file still uses `orientation: columns`, contradicting its own prose.

heading: Orientation
proposition: Setting `orientation: rows` in YAML makes second-level headings create rows instead of columns.
reader_consequence: The French instructs the reader to write `orientation: lignes`, which flexdashboard does not accept, so the rows layout the paragraph promises is never produced.

heading: Orientation
proposition: The per-page `{data-orientation=}` attribute takes the unquoted value `rows` or `columns`.
reader_consequence: The French tells the reader to specify `lignes` or `colonnes`, so a per-page orientation attribute written from this instruction is invalid. The same French file keeps `rows`/`columns` in the equivalent bullet at line 164, so the reader is given two contradictory value sets.

heading: Tables
proposition: The `options =` argument of `DT::datatable()` is supplied with the R function `list()`.
reader_consequence: The French example chunk writes `options = liste(...)`. `liste` is not an R function, so a reader who copies the block gets 'could not find function "liste"' and no table.

heading: HTML widgets
proposition: The HTML widget package for interactive time series display is named dygraphs.
reader_consequence: The French names it 'digraphs', which is not the package. A reader searching or running install.packages("digraphs") finds nothing.

heading: Settings
proposition: The example YAML header shown for enabling shiny is valid YAML that can be pasted into a flexdashboard script.
reader_consequence: The French example ends the title line with a full stop outside the closing quote (`title: "...".`), which is a YAML parse error. A reader who copies the block cannot render the document and the error points at the header, not at the typo.

heading: Tables
proposition: The English warns that flextable functions MAY PRODUCE tables that are shortened or cut off, a reason to prefer knitr::kable(). The Japanese instead states that using flextable functions you CAN CREATE summary tables and tables with a portion cut off, presenting the same behaviour as a capability rather than a drawback.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader reads the sentence as an endorsement of flextable and may use it for dashboard panels, then gets silently truncated tables in the panel with no warning that this was the documented failure mode.

heading: Section attributes
proposition: The English names the section attribute `{data-navbar=}` for nesting a page inside a navigation-bar drop-down menu; the Japanese names `{data-navmenu=}` for the same purpose.
reader_consequence: The two editions teach different attribute names for the same feature. A reader comparing the editions, or an editor syncing them, cannot tell which is authoritative. (The Japanese name is the one flexdashboard actually accepts, and it matches the English text at line 197, so the English bullet is the wrong one.)

heading: Interactive plots
proposition: The Japanese states the interactive functionality can be displayed even without an internet connection. The English only states it still works if the dashboard is emailed as a static file (not online on a server), and makes no claim about internet connectivity.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader takes an offline-rendering guarantee from the handbook that the English never gives, and may ship a dashboard to offline users without testing it, when the guarantee actually depends on whether the widget's JavaScript is self-contained.

heading: HTML widgets
proposition: The Japanese states that the htmlwidgets.org web page contains many samples of HTML widgets. The English only defines what HTML widgets are and where they can be embedded; it makes no claim about the content of the linked page.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader follows the link expecting a sample gallery. This is extra propositional content the English author did not write, so it is not maintained when the linked site changes.

heading: Tables
proposition: The English lists paging as a DT::datatable() capability: the user can click through the 'pages' of the data frame. The Japanese moves the word 'page' to mean the dashboard page ('within a page, the user can filter, sort and operate') and states no paging capability.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader does not learn that the DT table paginates the data frame, so the `pageLength = 5` setting described two paragraphs later has no stated purpose and may be read as a hard limit of 5 displayed records.

heading: YAML
proposition: The Japanese states that a value must be quoted if it contains a colon OR OTHER SYMBOLS SUCH AS BRACKETS. The English states only the colon case.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader learns a broader quoting rule than the handbook establishes and than YAML requires, and may quote values unnecessarily or, worse, generalise the rule wrongly to other punctuation.

heading: Code chunks
proposition: The English gives three ways to create a new code chunk: typing it out yourself, the keyboard shortcut, and the green insert icon. The Japanese gives only the keyboard shortcut and the green icon.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader is not told that the chunk delimiters can simply be typed by hand, so a reader without the RStudio toolbar (for example editing the .Rmd in a plain text editor) is left with no offered method.

heading: Layout
proposition: The English gives the heading markers as '#, ##, or ###'. The Japanese gives them as '#、##、##', repeating the second-level marker and never naming the third-level marker.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader taking the layout summary at face value does not learn from it that charts are added with a third-level (###) heading, and may write a second '##' where a '###' is required, producing an extra row or column instead of a chart panel.

heading: Tabs
proposition: The English says the same tabbing works with rows if your orientation is `rows`. The Japanese writes the YAML value as `row` (singular) in code formatting.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader copying the code-formatted value writes `orientation: row`, which flexdashboard does not accept as the row layout, and the dashboard falls back to the default orientation with no obvious error.

heading: Pages / Imagens
proposition: The English heading names this Layout subsection 'Pages'; the Portuguese heading names it 'Imagens' (Images), a subject the section never discusses and which its own first sentence ('Os titulos de primeiro nivel (#) ... representarao as "paginas" do painel') contradicts.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader scanning the table of contents or the Layout section for how to create dashboard pages skips this subsection, because it is labelled as being about images, and never finds that a first-level heading (#) creates a page.

heading: Section attributes / Atributos da secao
proposition: The English says {data-orientation=} must be set to the literal value `rows` or `columns`; the Portuguese instructs the reader to set it to `linhas` or `colunas`, values flexdashboard does not accept.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader writes {data-orientation=linhas} on a page heading, the attribute is silently ignored, and the page keeps the default orientation with no error to explain why. The same file uses `rows`/`columns` untranslated at lines 177 and 256, so the reader also gets contradictory instructions.

heading: Orientation / Orientacao
proposition: The English gives the two YAML settings as `orientation: columns` and `orientation: rows`; the Portuguese renders the second as `orientacao: rows`, a YAML key flexdashboard does not recognise.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader who wants row orientation copies `orientacao: rows` into the YAML header, flexdashboard ignores the unknown key and falls back to column orientation, and the reader cannot tell why the second-level headings still produce columns.

heading: Orientation / Orientacao
proposition: The English names the per-page attribute `{data-orientation=}`; the Portuguese names it `{data -idance =}`, an attribute that does not exist in flexdashboard.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader with a multi-page dashboard types {data-idance=rows} on a page heading, gets no orientation change and no error, and has no way to recover the correct attribute name from this sentence.

heading: Tables / Tabelas
proposition: The English tells the reader to see further DT arguments by entering `?datatable`; the Portuguese gives `?Datatable` with a capital D, which is not the function name.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader enters ?Datatable at the R console and gets 'No documentation for 'Datatable'' instead of the DT help page, so the pointer to the remaining datatable() arguments leads nowhere.

heading: Settings / Configuracoes
proposition: The English says the sidebar column can hold R chunks containing the shiny `input` commands; the Portuguese renders the object name as `entrada`, which is not a shiny object.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader looks for shiny commands named `entrada` in the sidebar chunk, finds none in the shiny documentation, and misses that the sidebar holds the input widgets whose values are later read as input$hospital_choice (still written in English at line 429).

heading: Load packages
proposition: The English says library() LOADS already-installed packages; the Russian says you can also INSTALL packages with library() from base R (Вы можете также установить пакеты с помощью `library()`).
reader_consequence: A Russian reader believes library() installs a missing package, so when a package is not installed they call library() and get an error they cannot explain, instead of installing it first.

heading: Worked example
proposition: The English step list states the worked example DOES create a sidebar ("Create a sidebar containing:"); the Russian states the reader should CONSIDER the possibility of creating one ("Рассмотрите возможность создания боковой панели").
reader_consequence: A Russian reader treats the sidebar as optional and skips it, then the selectInput() drop-down and the hospital vector have nowhere to live and the reactive epicurve in the screenshots cannot be reproduced.

heading: Dashboards with R Markdown
proposition: The English says flexdashboard formats R Markdown output as a dashboard with PANELS and pages; the Russian says with TABS and pages (со вкладками и страницами).
reader_consequence: A Russian reader forms the wrong mental model of the layout unit, expecting tabs as the default structure, when tabs are an optional {.tabset} feature described later and the default third-level unit is a panel.

heading: Text
proposition: The English says the summary panel's dynamic text shows the latest hospitalisation DATE; the Russian says it shows the latest hospitalisation DATA (последние данные по госпитализациям), dropping that the value is a date.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader does not learn that the demonstrated in-line code prints a maximum date, so they do not know what value the summary panel is supposed to compute.

heading: Load packages
proposition: The English says p_load() installs the PACKAGE if necessary; the Russian says it installs "the approach" (устанавливает подход), so the claim that p_load() installs a missing package is not stated.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader does not learn the main reason the handbook prefers p_load(), namely that it installs a missing package before loading it.

heading: Layout
proposition: The English instructs the reader to ADD pages, columns/rows and charts with R Markdown headings; the Russian bullet reads "Все страницы, столбцы/строки и графики с заголовками R Markdown" ("All pages...") and carries no instruction.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader reading the list of ways to adjust the layout does not get the first action, that headings are what add pages, columns/rows and charts.

heading: Dashboards with R Markdown
proposition: The English says dashboard content can be STATIC figures/tables; the Turkish says it can be 'istatistik' (statistical) figures/tables.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader loses the static-versus-interactive contrast that the sentence is built on, and may conclude flexdashboard content is restricted to statistical output rather than any non-interactive figure or table. The same file translates 'static' correctly as 'statik' at line 342, so the contrast is inconsistent within the chapter.

heading: Import data / Verileri ice aktarin
proposition: The Turkish adds a sentence instructing the reader to click in order to download the 'clean' linelist as an .rds file; the English has no such instruction and offers no click target.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader looks for a download link that does not exist on the page, and may stop before reaching the appliedepidata::get_data() call that is the actual supported route to the data.

heading: YAML
proposition: The English states that output: is a REQUIRED YAML parameter; the Turkish states only that a YAML parameter output specifies the type of file produced, with no requirement claim.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader does not learn that output: must be present, so may omit it from the YAML header and get a document that does not render as a flexdashboard.

heading: Tables / Tablo
proposition: The English says you can read more about customizing your TABLE with kable() and kableExtra; the Turkish says you can read more about customizing your PANEL/dashboard ('Panelinizi') with kable() and kableExtra.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader is told that kable() and kableExtra customise the dashboard panel, which they do not, and may follow the kableExtra link expecting layout or panel options instead of table formatting options.

heading: Other examples / Diger Ornekler
proposition: The English names the leaflet mapping widget (the R package leaflet); the Turkish renders it as 'brosur' (brochure/pamphlet), a common noun that names no R package.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader cannot identify which mapping widget the linked example uses, and cannot search for or install it; the chapter's own bullet list at line 356 keeps the name 'Leaflet', so the two references no longer refer to the same thing.

heading: Section attributes
proposition: The page-level drop-down-menu attribute is written with no space before the equals sign, as {data-navbar=}; the Vietnamese writes it {data-navbar =} with a space.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader copies {data-navbar =} into a page heading and the attribute silently does not apply, which is exactly the failure the same chapter warns about at line 196 ('do not include spaces around the equals sign otherwise it will not work'). The reader sees no error, only a page that never nests under the drop-down menu.

heading: Modify theme / Modificar el tema
proposition: The theme() reference table says plot.caption = element_text() adjusts the legend ("La leyenda"), whereas the English says it adjusts the caption.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader looking for the argument that styles the plot legend picks plot.caption and changes the caption text instead; the same reader also loses the table's only pointer to the caption argument, because everywhere else in this chapter 'leyenda' denotes the ggplot legend and 'pie del gráfico' denotes the caption.

heading: Free or fixed axes / Ejes libres o fijos
proposition: The translation names the argument as `scale = "free"`, while the English names `scales = "free"` and the code chunk beside it uses `facet_wrap(~District, scales = "free")`.
reader_consequence: A reader who copies `scale = "free"` into facet_grid() gets an ignored/unknown argument, the axes stay fixed, and `space = "free_y"` silently has no effect.

heading: Scaled to column values / Escalado a los valores de la columna
proposition: The translation says the alternative is to plot objects with sizes proportional to their column values, restricting the mechanism to the size aesthetic; the English says any plot aesthetic can be scaled by the values in a column.
reader_consequence: A reader concludes that only size can be driven by a column, which contradicts the section's own first example (color mapped to age) and discourages mapping color, shape or alpha to data.

heading: Plot aesthetics / Estética del gráfico
proposition: The translation says `color =` sets the colour of the point's perimeter ("el color del perimetro del punto") when using geom_point(); the English says it sets the point colour.
reader_consequence: A reader expects color= to draw only an outline on points and reaches for fill= to colour the dot, which does nothing for the default point shape, so the points come out unchanged.

heading: Import data / Importar datos
proposition: The translation states that ct_blood holds the cycle-threshold value of the PCR test ("cycle threshold, umbral de ciclo del test de PCR"); the English says only "CT values".
reader_consequence: The Spanish reader is given an interpretation of the variable that the English text never asserts, so the two editions disagree on what ct_blood measures and the claim is not verifiable from the handbook itself.

heading: Resources / Recursos
proposition: The translation adds that the listed pages carry material in English ("Consulta las siguietnes páginas con maerial en inglés"); the English text makes no claim about the language of the resources.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader who avoids English-language material skips the whole list, even though two of the listed links point to the Spanish edition of R for Data Science (es.r4ds.hadley.nz), so the added claim is contradicted by the list beneath it.

heading: Box plots / Diagrammes en boites
proposition: The French text says the fill aesthetic is set to the column `gender`, glossed as "issue finale de chaque cas" (each case's final outcome); the English says the fill is set to the column `outcome`, and the column `gender` holds sex, not outcome.
reader_consequence: A French reader is told that the column `gender` contains each case's final outcome, so they will look for death/recovery values in the sex column and misread the legend of plot B, which is coloured by sex.

heading: Facets / Small-multiples
proposition: With two variables in `facet_wrap()`, the panel headings show combined terms and carry no separate row-versus-column logic.
reader_consequence: A French reader who passes two variables to `facet_wrap()` is not warned that the strip labels merge both terms, so they will expect row and column headings like `facet_grid()` produces and misread the resulting panel labels.

heading: Mapping data to the plot / "Mappage"
proposition: The French text adds that the automatically generated y-axis of `geom_histogram()` represents the count of each "modalite" (each category/level of the variable); the English says only that the counts y-axis is generated automatically, and the histogram counts rows per bin of a continuous variable, not per category.
reader_consequence: A French reader learns that a histogram counts distinct values of a variable, which is the behaviour of `geom_bar()`, and so misses the bin-based nature of `geom_histogram()` that the chapter later insists on.

heading: Complete themes / Fonctions theme toute faites
proposition: The French note states that micro-adjustments made with `theme()` before a complete theme will not be taken into account ("sinon les ajustements ne seront pas pris en compte"); the English only says such adjustments should be made after the complete theme, without stating the consequence.
reader_consequence: A French reader receives an extra causal claim about override behaviour that the English original does not make, so the two editions teach a different rule about what happens when the order is reversed.

heading: ### General cleaning
proposition: The cross-reference for cleaning 'data friendly' underscore values into normal text or title case points to the Characters and strings chapter in English, but the translation points to the Cleaning data and core functions chapter (#cleaning).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader following the pointer lands on the data-cleaning chapter, which does not cover string case conversion, and never reaches the Characters and strings chapter where str_to_title() and friends are taught. The same #cleaning link is already given two paragraphs earlier, so the pointer is also a dead duplicate.

heading: ### Pivoting longer
proposition: English says the pivoted data has one ROW per possible symptom for each case; the translation says each case has 5 rows and then that there is one COLUMN per symptom.
reader_consequence: The whole point of pivot_longer() here is that symptoms stop being columns and become rows. A reader told there is one column per symptom in the long table misreads the output of the pivot, and cannot tell long format from the wide format shown just above.

heading: ### Plot aesthetics
proposition: The example of mapping an aesthetic to a data column is written color = hospital (bare column name) in English and color = "hospital" (quoted string) in the translation.
reader_consequence: A quoted value is a static assignment, the exact opposite of the mapping this bullet defines, and the chapter later states explicitly that the column name must not be in quotes. A reader copying aes(color = "hospital") gets every point drawn in one constant colour with a spurious one-item legend, not a grouping by hospital.

heading: ### Free or fixed axes
proposition: English states that faceted axis scales are by default the SAME (fixed) across all facets; the translation replaces that statement with a repeat of the following clause ('not always appropriate') and never says the default is fixed scales.
reader_consequence: The section exists to explain when to override the default with scales = "free". A reader who is never told the default is a shared fixed scale cannot see what scales = "free_y" changes, and may not realise that counts in different facets are directly comparable unless freed.

heading: ### `geom_col()`
proposition: The prose names the summary dataset built in the adjacent chunk as `outcomes` in English and as `outcome` in the translation.
reader_consequence: `outcome` is also the name of a real column in that table and in the linelist, so the reader cannot tell whether the text refers to the data frame or the column, and ggplot(outcome) fails because no such object exists.

heading: Rótulos / Labels
proposition: The translation says str_glue() was used in the TITLE assignment; the English says it was used in the CAPTION assignment, and the chunk beside it uses str_glue() only inside caption = .
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader looks for str_glue() in the title = argument of the labs() call above, where it does not appear, and may copy the dynamic-date pattern into title = instead of caption = .

heading: Modifique o tema / Modify theme
proposition: The translation attributes element_text(hjust = 0) to the plot TITLE; the English attributes it to the CAPTION, and the chunk beside it applies hjust = 0 to plot.caption, not to plot.title.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader believes hjust = 0 in the example controls the title and writes plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0) when trying to left-align a caption, producing the wrong element.

heading: `ggplot()`
proposition: The translation names the ggplot() dataset argument `dados = `; the English names it `data = `, and the chunk beside it writes ggplot(data = linelist).
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader who types ggplot(dados = linelist) gets an unused-argument error, because ggplot2 has no argument named dados.

heading: Modifique o tema / Modify theme

reader_consequence: The axis.text row and the axis.text.x row now carry the identical description in Portuguese, so a reader cannot tell the two arguments apart and may use axis.text.x when both axes need the change.

proposition: The translation adds a translator's note explaining that 'jitter' means agitated or nervous in English and that the points are spread so they do not overlap; the English has no such note.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader meets an in-text editorial aside in the bullet list of plot types that no other language edition carries; the content is correct but it is not part of the handbook text.

proposition: The Russian text states that `legend.position =` accepts the values "низ", "верх", "лево" and "право"; the English states it accepts "bottom", "top", "left" and "right", which are the only strings ggplot2 accepts.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader who types `legend.position = "низ"` gets an error, and cannot tell from the text what the accepted strings actually are; the adjacent chunk at line 679 uses "bottom".

reader_consequence: A Russian reader is told the formula names rows rather than data columns, which contradicts the very next clause of the same bullet ('only one column') and the `rows ~ columns` grid convention being explained.

reader_consequence: A Russian reader does not learn that box, jitter, violin and sina plots belong to the one-continuous-variable family, and may read them as an unrelated category alongside two- and three-variable plots.

proposition: The English lists four example geometries: bar graph, line plot, scatter plot, histogram. The Russian renders both 'bar graph' and 'histogram' as 'гистограмма', so the bar graph example is absent and 'гистограмма' appears twice.

proposition: The translation says the `c()` vector supplied to `breaks = ` contains the NUMBER of desired graduations ("le nombre de graduation souhaitées"); the English says it contains the desired break VALUES.
reader_consequence: A French reader may write `breaks = c(10)` expecting ten evenly spaced ticks and instead get a single break at the value 10, then conclude the argument does not work.

heading: Colorbrewer and Viridis

reader_consequence: A French reader looks for a two-value binary palette that does not exist, and misses that ggplot2 offers a binned viridis scale (`scale_fill_viridis_b`) for grouping a continuous variable into intervals.

heading: Contour lines
proposition: The translation adds the sentence "Elles permettent une différente visualisation de la répartition des points dans l'espace" (contour lines give a different visualisation of how the points are distributed in space); the English paragraph makes no such claim.
reader_consequence: A French reader is given an extra, unsourced rationale for contour plots that the English chapter does not state and that no figure in the section demonstrates.

heading: Combine legends
proposition: The translation says to remove one plot's legend "pour éviter la dé-duplication" (to AVOID de-duplication); the English says removing it IS the de-duplication.
reader_consequence: A French reader reads the stated purpose of the step as the opposite of what it is, and may leave both legends in place believing removal is what should be avoided.

heading: Point-and-click ggplot2 with esquisse
proposition: The translation opens with "**equisse** fournit une interface graphique pour la construction de graphiques avec **ggplot2**", a descriptive claim about the package that the English section does not make; the English gives only the quoted addin description.
reader_consequence: Low impact, but the French reader receives an editorial description presented alongside the quoted vendor text, blurring which words are the quotation.

heading: Resources
proposition: The English attributes the surveillance-data presentation guidelines to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control; the translation drops the ECDC attribution and gives the bare link.
reader_consequence: A French reader cannot tell who publishes the guidelines, so cannot judge their authority or cite them, and must open the PDF to find the issuing body.

reader_consequence: A Japanese reader sees the same function name in both bullets, cannot tell the two-colour function from the n-colour function, and will call `scale_fill_gradient()` with a colour vector, which errors or ignores the extra colours.

proposition: The English strategy is to merge the data AND convert it to 'long' format before plotting; the Japanese keeps only the merge plus adding a dataset-identifying column, and omits the conversion to long format.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader merges the datasets wide, has no single value column to map to an aesthetic, and cannot reproduce the recommended one-plot-from-several-datasets approach.

heading: Time axes / 時間スケール
proposition: The Japanese states that the Epidemic curves section sits inside the preceding ggplot basics chapter ('前章 ggplotの基礎 内 流行曲線 の章'); the English points to the separate Epidemic curves page and its ggplot section, and never places Epidemic curves inside ggplot basics.

reader_consequence: A Japanese reader attributes the label-collision limitation to base R graphics rather than to ggplot2 itself, and may assume plain ggplot2 geom_text()/geom_label() already handles overlap.

reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader never learns the `label_date_short()` technique and also loses its worked ggplot example, so they keep hand-specifying `date_breaks` and `date_labels` for every plot.

heading: Time axes / Eixos de tempo
proposition: The labels produced by `label_date_short()` adjust themselves automatically as the data extend over time, from days to weeks to months to years.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader does not know that this label approach survives a growing time series, so they do not consider it for a surveillance plot that is re-rendered as the outbreak lengthens.

heading: Time axes / Eixos de tempo
proposition: A complete example of multi-level date labels is available in the Epidemic curves page.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader loses the cross-reference and cannot find the full worked example of multi-level date labels elsewhere in the handbook.

heading: Gradient scales / Escalas em gradiente
proposition: The translation states that the code produces a "raster" FILE ("produzimos um arquivo 'raster' de um gráfico de densidade de calor"); the English states that the plot itself is a raster heat-tile density plot, and the chunk beside it only sets `geom = "raster"` inside `stat_density2d()` and writes nothing to disk.

proposition: The translation states that other CLASSES exist ("Existem outras classes"); the English states that other METHOD suffixes exist beyond `_discrete()`, `continuous()`, `_date()`, `_gradient()` and `_manual()`.

heading: Smart Labeling
proposition: English says to include `fill = ` WITHIN `aes()` to colour the label by value; the Russian says to use `fill = ` OUTSIDE of `aes()`.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader places `fill = outcome` outside `aes()` in `geom_label_repel()`, which errors on an unknown object or produces a single static fill, so labels are never coloured by outcome. The very next code chunk (line 611) puts `fill = outcome` inside `aes()`, contradicting the instruction.

proposition: English lists the literal allowed values of `type = ` as "histogram", "density", "boxplot", "violin", "densigram"; the Russian replaces those literal strings with Russian words ("гистограмма", "плотность", "коробчатая диаграмма", "скрипичная диаграмма", "денсиграмма").

proposition: English says `labels = ` controls HOW the values display; the Russian says `labels = ` controls the ORDER of display of the values ("порядок отображения значений").

proposition: English names the argument `size = `; the Russian capitalises it as `Size = `.

heading: ## Mutate on grouped data / ## Mutate con datos agrupados
proposition: The English says the code computes the difference between a row's delay-to-admission and the MEDIAN delay for its hospital; the Spanish says 'la demora media de su hospital', i.e. the MEAN delay.
reader_consequence: The two language versions describe the same chunk with different statistics. heading: Linelist cases into days / Grouper par jours (linelist)
proposition: The French says the first line of the chunk drops cases that have no 'date de rentrée' (date of entry/admission); the code drops rows missing date_onset, which the rest of the French chapter itself glosses as 'date de debut des symptomes' (date of symptom onset).

heading: Select on grouped data / select() sur les donnees groupees
proposition: The French instructs the reader to use ungroup() 'avant de degrouper' (before ungrouping); the English instructs the reader to use ungroup() before the select(), so that the grouping columns are not force-included.
reader_consequence: The French sentence is circular and names no operation to place ungroup() before, so a reader does not learn that ungroup() must precede select() and keeps getting grouping columns they did not ask for.

heading: Linelist cases into days / Grouper par jours (linelist)
proposition: The English notes that the first rows of the resulting table skip over dates on which no cases occurred; the French does not state this.
reader_consequence: The French reader loses the observation that motivates the whole section. Without seeing that empty days are absent from the output, the following complete() step reads as optional decoration rather than as the fix for a real gap in the time series.

heading: Slice rows per group / slice()
proposition: The English states that with_ties = TRUE keeps ties in slice_max(); the French entry for slice_max() omits the with_ties argument entirely (it keeps it for slice_min()).
reader_consequence: A French reader assumes ties are handled differently by slice_max() than by slice_min(), or does not learn the argument exists there, and silently drops tied records when taking the top n per group.

heading: Un-group / Degrouper les donnees
proposition: The English warns that forgetting to ungroup can lead to incorrect calculations; the French warns only to remember to ungroup before steps that need the complete ungrouped dataset, and never states that the results can be wrong.
reader_consequence: A French reader treats ungroup() as tidiness rather than as a correctness requirement, and has no reason to suspect a silently wrong denominator or total when they forget it.

heading: Add counts / Ajouter des colonnes contenant les decomptes
proposition: The French introduces add_tally() alongside add_count(); the English names only add_count().
reader_consequence: A French reader is pointed at a function the chapter never demonstrates and whose grouping requirement differs from add_count(): add_tally() needs a prior group_by(), so calling it the way the chunk calls add_count(hospital) fails or returns a single overall count.

heading: Slice rows per group / slice()
proposition: The French states that replace = TRUE gives sampling with replacement in slice_sample(); the English says only that slice_sample() randomly selects n rows.
reader_consequence: Content only French readers receive. It is correct, but the two editions no longer describe the same function surface, so a reviewer comparing them cannot tell whether the English is out of date or the French is unsourced.

heading: Linelist cases into weeks / Grouper par semaines (linelist)
proposition: The French states that floor_date(unit = "week") rounds each date to the first day of its week; the English makes this rounding claim only in the months section, not in the weeks section.
reader_consequence: Content only French readers receive. It is correct, but it is propositional content the English weeks section does not carry, so the two editions explain floor_date() at different depths.

heading: Import data
proposition: The translation says the data are imported with import() from the rio package, but the code chunk beside it loads the data with appliedepidata::get_data(name = "linelist_cleaned_rds").
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader looks for an rio::import() call that is not in the chunk, and does not learn that the handbook data now come from the appliedepidata package, so cannot reproduce the import in another chapter.

heading: Import data
proposition: The translation instructs the reader to click a GitHub link and download the cleaned linelist as a .rds file by hand; the English gives no manual-download instruction and points to the Download handbook and data page instead.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader follows a manual download route the English edition no longer uses, ends up with a local .rds file the chapter code never reads, and misses the pointer to the Download handbook and data page.

heading: Linelist cases into months
proposition: The translation says floor_date(unit = "months") rounds each date down OR up to the 1st of its month; the English says it rounds each date down only, and floor_date never rounds up.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader may believe a date late in a month is moved forward to the 1st of the next month, and so mis-assigns cases to the wrong month when reading the aggregated counts.

heading: Mutate on grouped data
proposition: The translation says the example computes the difference between a row's delay-to-admission and the MEAN delay for the hospital; the English says the MEDIAN delay.
reader_consequence: The two editions describe the same chunk differently, so a reader comparing them cannot tell which statistic the example uses; the Japanese wording matches the chunk's mean(days_onset_hosp) and the English does not, so the English is the side that is wrong.

heading: Unique groups
proposition: The translation limits the bolded principle to the case of grouping by MULTIPLE columns; the English states it unconditionally for the grouping columns, however many there are.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader may take the unique-combination rule as applying only to multi-column grouping, and so not expect a single-column group_by() to create one group per unique value, which is what the very next example shows.

heading: Casos Linelist em semanas / Linelist cases into weeks
proposition: The English instructs the reader to call floor_date() with unit = "week"; the Portuguese instructs unit = "semana", which is not the value used in the code chunk immediately below (unit = "week") and is not a unit lubridate accepts.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader who follows the prose instead of copying the chunk writes floor_date(date_onset, unit = "semana") and gets an error from lubridate, with no indication that the instruction, not their data, is wrong.

heading: Casos da Linelist em meses / Linelist cases into months
proposition: The English gives the floor_date() argument as unit = "months"; the Portuguese gives unit = "meses", which contradicts the code chunk below it (unit = "months") and is not a unit lubridate accepts.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader aggregating cases into months writes unit = "meses" and the call fails, so the monthly aggregation cannot be reproduced from the prose.

heading: Casos da Linelist em meses / Linelist cases into months
proposition: The English says the complete() step also uses by = "months"; the Portuguese says by = "meses", which contradicts the code chunk below it (by="month") and is not a value seq.Date() accepts.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader filling in missing months writes by = "meses" inside seq.Date() and the sequence call errors, so the gap-filling step described in the section cannot be run.

heading: Agrupoando por data / Grouping by date
proposition: The English tells the reader to supply fill = list(n = 0) to complete(); the Portuguese tells the reader to supply fill = lista(n = 0), translating the base R function list() into Portuguese, so the named argument no longer names an existing R function.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader who types fill = lista(n = 0) gets 'could not find function "lista"', and the stated purpose of the argument (setting filled-in rows to 0 instead of NA) is never achieved.

heading: Adicionar totais / Add totals
proposition: The English names the janitor function adorn_percentages(); the Portuguese names adorn_percentagens(), which is not a janitor function and contradicts the code chunk immediately below, which calls adorn_percentages().
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader searching help for adorn_percentagens() or typing it into a pipeline finds no such function, and may conclude the janitor percentage helper does not exist.

heading: Linelist cases into months
proposition: English opens a third-level section 'Linelist cases into months'; the Russian line has no space after '###', so it is not a heading and the monthly-aggregation material stays inside the preceding weeks section.
reader_consequence: The Russian reader sees the literal text '###Построчный список случаев по месяцам {.unnumbered}' in the body, gets no table-of-contents entry for the monthly section, and reads the monthly floor_date() instructions as if they were part of the weekly example.

heading: Arranging grouped data
proposition: English states that with .by_group = TRUE the rows are ordered first by the grouping columns and THEN by any other columns passed to arrange(); the Russian drops the second ordering stage entirely.
reader_consequence: The Russian reader believes .by_group = TRUE sorts only by the grouping columns, and does not learn that the columns they pass to arrange() still act as the secondary sort key.

heading: Arranging grouped data
proposition: The Russian says the rows are ordered by 'the grouping columns, which you specify in the arrange() argument'; in the English the grouping columns come from group_by() and only the ADDITIONAL columns are specified to arrange().
reader_consequence: The Russian reader may pass the grouping columns to arrange() expecting .by_group = TRUE to use them, and misunderstands where the grouping used by .by_group = TRUE actually comes from.

heading: Summarise
proposition: English links 'Descriptive tables' to the page tables_descriptive.qmd; the Russian keeps the bracketed label but supplies no link destination.
reader_consequence: The Russian reader sees literal '[Описательные таблицы]' with no link and cannot reach the detailed summarise() coverage the sentence sends them to.

heading: Grouping by date
proposition: English links 'Working with dates' to the page dates.qmd; the Russian keeps the bracketed label but supplies no link destination.
reader_consequence: The Russian reader sees literal '[Работа с датами]' with no link and cannot reach the dates chapter that explains how to build the date-unit column this section depends on.

heading: Slice rows per group
proposition: English links 'De-duplication' to the page deduplication.qmd; the Russian keeps the bracketed label but supplies no link destination.
reader_consequence: The Russian reader sees literal '[Дедупликация]' with no link and cannot reach the further slice() examples the sentence promises.

heading: Unique groups / Benzersiz gruplar
proposition: The English labels the second inline count as the number of recoveries ("... recoveries ..."); the Turkish gives that count with no label at all, so the sentence lists only 'deaths' and 'no outcome recorded'.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader sees a bare number between the death count and the missing-outcome count and cannot tell that it is the number of patients who recovered, so the three-way breakdown of the `outcome` column is incomplete.

heading: Unique groups / Benzersiz gruplar
proposition: The English inline expression is `nrow(linelist %>% filter(is.na(outcome)))`; the Turkish splits it into the invalid fragments `nrow(linelist %)` and `>% filter(is.na(outcome)))` with the backtick span broken across them.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader who copies the shown expression to count records with no recorded outcome gets an R syntax error, and the fragment `nrow(linelist %)` reads as a complete but wrong call.

heading: `count()`
proposition: The English says `count()` can be called multiple times with the functionality "rolling up" (successive aggregation); the Turkish says it can be called multiple times with the usefulness of "yuvarlama", which means rounding.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader is told the repeated `count()` idiom is about rounding rather than about aggregating one count into a coarser count, so they do not understand why the second `count(gender, ...)` returns hospitals per gender.

heading: Grouping by date / Tarihe göre gruplama
proposition: The English says the case count values in newly expanded rows will be `NA`; the Turkish renders 'case' as "büyük/küçük harf" (upper/lower letter case), so it states that the letter-case count values will be `NA`.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader does not learn that `complete()` leaves the epidemiological case counts as `NA` in the filled-in dates, which is the exact reason the following sentence tells them to pass `fill = list(n = 0)`.

heading: Linelist cases into weeks / Haftalara bölünmüş satır listesi vakaları
proposition: The prose names the argument as `unit = "hafta"`, but the chunk beside it uses `lubridate::floor_date(date_onset, unit = "week")`.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader who types `unit = "hafta"` as instructed gets a lubridate error, because the unit string must be the English "week".

heading: Linelist cases into months / Aylara ayrılmış satır listesi vakaları
proposition: The prose says the `complete()` step also uses `by = "aylar"`, but the chunk beside it uses `by="month"`.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader who writes `by = "aylar"` inside `seq.Date()` gets an error, because `seq.Date()` accepts only the English unit string "month".

heading: Mutate on grouped data / Gruplandırılmış verileri dönüştürün
proposition: The English says to use `mutate()` after `group_by()` instead of `summarise()`; the Turkish names the function to be avoided as `özet()`, which is not a dplyr function.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader cannot connect this instruction to the `summarise()` section they just read, and a reader who searches dplyr for `özet()` finds nothing.

heading: Filter on grouped data > filter()
proposition: The per-group filter threshold is the group's MEDIAN age. The Vietnamese states it twice and changes the statistic on the second statement: it first says 'độ tuổi trung vị' (median age), then says the filter keeps rows above 'độ tuổi trung bình của nhóm' (the group's MEAN age). The English says median in both places.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader is told the same operation uses two different statistics in one sentence, and will take the operative rule to be the second one. They will write filter(age > mean(age)) instead of filter(age > median(age)), which selects a different set of rows in any skewed age distribution.

heading: Grouping by date > Daily counts into months
proposition: This section is about aggregating daily counts into MONTHS. The Vietnamese heading reads 'Số lượng đếm hàng ngày theo tuần' (daily counts by WEEK), which is character-for-character identical to the preceding section heading at line 362, and contradicts its own body text at line 368 (which correctly says months and unit = "month").
reader_consequence: The Vietnamese table of contents shows two consecutive sections with identical names and no monthly section. A reader scanning for how to aggregate daily counts into months cannot find it, and a reader who lands on line 366 is told by the heading that the unit is weeks while the instruction below says unit = "month".

heading: Aggregate and summarize / Agregar y resumir
proposition: The English gives "Mondays" as the worked example of the week start day passed to floor_date(); the Spanish gives the non-word "onday" and names no day.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader gets no example of which day the week starts on, so the illustration of the week_start argument carries no concrete value and the later chunk setting week_start = 1 has no stated meaning at this point.

heading: Aggregate and summarize / Agregar y resumir
proposition: The English states the number of rows in expanded_weeks via the inline expression `r nrow(expanded_weeks)`; the Spanish sentence omits the row count entirely.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader cannot compare the size of expanded_weeks with the agg_weeks row counts quoted immediately before and after, which is the whole point of that running row-count commentary about how right_join() fills the gaps.

heading: Create heat plot / Créer un graphique de chaleur
proposition: The column mapped to the y-axis is named `location_name`.
reader_consequence: A French reader using this bullet list as the recipe for building the heat plot is not told which column to map to y, and must reverse-engineer it from the code chunk further down instead of from the instruction.

heading: Transmission matrix / 感染伝播マトリックス

reader_consequence: A Japanese reader follows the prose, writes an `rio::import()` call against a manually downloaded file path, and diverges from the chunk the rest of the chapter runs on. If the download link fails or the file is saved elsewhere, `linelist` is never created and every later chunk in the chapter errors.

heading: Transmission matrix / 感染伝播マトリックス
proposition: The Japanese text states that the cleaned linelist can be downloaded as an .rds file from the URL https://github.com/appliedepi/epirhandbook/raw/main/data/case_linelists/linelist_cleaned.rds; the English gives no download URL and instead says to load the data directly with `appliedepidata::get_data()`.
reader_consequence: The Japanese reader is sent to a hard-coded repository path that the English edition no longer relies on. If that path moves or is removed, the reader has no working route to the data, while the English reader does.

heading: Transmission matrix / 感染伝播マトリックス
proposition: The Japanese text adds that `import()` handles many file formats such as .xlsx, .rds and .csv, and cross-references the Import and export chapter (#importing); the English sentence contains neither claim and instead cross-references the Download handbook and data page.
reader_consequence: The Japanese reader is pointed at a different chapter for data access than the English reader, and takes away a claim about rio file-format support that this chapter never demonstrates, reinforcing the wrong loading route.

heading: Transmission matrix / 感染伝播マトリックス
proposition: The English explains WHY the Contact tracing page's dataset is simpler: the ages of cases and of their sources are already neatly aligned in the same row of the data frame. The Japanese keeps only the parenthetical "more simple" and drops the explanation.
reader_consequence: The Japanese reader cannot tell what makes the alternative dataset simpler, so cannot judge whether their own data resembles it and whether they can skip the long data-manipulation route this chapter takes.

heading: Carregar pacotes / Load packages
proposition: The English sends the reader to the R basics chapter (basics.qmd) for more on R packages; the Portuguese link target is #heatmaps, which is this chapter's own anchor (line 6 of the .pt.qmd), so it claims the R basics material is on this page.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader who follows the link stays on the heat plots page and never reaches the R basics chapter, so the pointer to package background is lost.

heading: Criar um data frame dos casos / Make cases data frame
proposition: The Portuguese prose says the data frame is called `idades_de_caso`; the chunk beside it creates `case_ages`, and every later chunk uses `case_ages`.
reader_consequence: The reader looks for an object named idades_de_caso that never exists, and cannot match the named data frame to the code they are told to run.

heading: Criar um data frame de infectantes / Make infectors data frame
proposition: The prose states that the first 50 rows of the joined infector records (with age added) are displayed below; the display chunk beside it shows `case_ages` instead of `infector_ages`.

heading: Criar um data frame de infectantes / Make infectors data frame
proposition: The prose states that the first rows of the combined case-and-infector-age data frame are displayed below; the display chunk beside it shows `case_ages` instead of `ages_complete`.

proposition: The prose states that the first rows of the long-format counts table are displayed below; the display chunk beside it shows `case_ages` instead of `long_counts`.

heading: Agregar e resumir / Aggregate and summarize
proposition: The English states the number of rows in expanded_weeks via inline R code (`r nrow(expanded_weeks)`); the Portuguese sentence drops the count entirely.

proposition: The English states the row count of agg_weeks before the join via working inline R code (`r nrow(agg_weeks)`); the Portuguese drops the leading r, so the sentence renders the literal text nrow(agg_weeks) and states no number.

heading: Eixo y ordenado / Ordered y-axis

heading: Aggregate and summarize / Toplama ve ozetleme
proposition: The English states the concrete pre-join row count of agg_weeks via an evaluated inline expression (`r nrow(agg_weeks)`); the Turkish drops the leading 'r', so no number is stated and the literal text 'nrow(agg_weeks)' is shown instead.

heading: Aggregate and summarize / Tổng hợp và tóm tắt

heading: Aggregate and summarize / Tổng hợp và tóm tắt

heading: The reprex package / El paquete reprex
proposition: The English says the arguments and possible variations are documented in the reprex documentation (a separate resource, given as a link labelled 'documentation'); the Spanish says they can be read 'en esta página' ('on this page'), locating that material inside the handbook page itself.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader looks for a fuller account of the reprex arguments on the current handbook page, where it does not exist, instead of going to the reprex package documentation. The reader may conclude the page is incomplete rather than consulting the external reference.

heading: The **reprex** package / Le package **reprex**
proposition: The English says the reprex HTML output contains any warnings produced by the code; the French replaces "warnings" with "messages", so the claim that warnings are captured is absent.
reader_consequence: A French reader may not expect warnings to appear in the reprex output, and may separately paste warning text into a forum post believing reprex did not capture it. In R, message() and warning() are distinct conditions, so the substituted term names a different output type.

heading: The **reprex** package / **reprex** パッケージとは？
proposition: The English says the `wd =` argument is where you SUPPLY a working directory to reprex; the Japanese says that using `wd =` lets you DISPLAY the working directory (作業ディレクトリを表示できます).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader believes `wd =` is a flag that prints the working directory into the reprex output, so they will not pass a directory path to it and will not know how to point reprex at a different project folder.

heading: The **reprex** package / **reprex** パッケージとは？
proposition: The English says that because **reprex** ships with **tidyverse** you may load EITHER package; the Japanese instructs the reader to load **tidyverse** only.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader does not learn that loading **reprex** alone is sufficient, so they load the whole tidyverse when only the one package is needed.

heading: Minimal data / 最小限のデータとは？
proposition: The English offers anonymising and subsetting as options to CONSIDER; the Japanese states they are NECESSARY (必要になります) to build a minimal dataset.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader treats anonymisation and subsetting as mandatory steps for every minimal dataset, rather than as suggestions to weigh against their own data.

heading: Posting to a forum / Postar em um fórum
proposition: The reproducible example posted to a forum should include your R session information.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese bullet reads 'com as informações do seu trabalho' (information about your work), so a reader omits R and package version output (sessionInfo / session_info) from the forum post, and answerers cannot reproduce version-dependent behaviour.

heading: The **reprex** package / O pacote **reprex**
proposition: Setting session_info = TRUE causes the output of sessioninfo::session_info() to be included in the reprex output.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese sentence only says session_info() output 'will include your R and package versions'; it never states that the argument adds that output to the reprex. A reader does not learn what the argument actually changes in the posted reprex.

proposition: English says the plot displays the PROPORTION of days per week that facilities reported data; the Turkish says the plot visualises "the data obtained from facilities on some days of the week" ("haftanin bazi gunlerinde tesislerden elde edilen veriler"), which is a different quantity and is contradicted by the chunk beside it (p_days_reported, title "Percent of days per week that facility reported data").
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader misreads the heat tile fill scale as counts or values collected on selected weekdays, rather than as a reporting-completeness percentage, and therefore misinterprets every tile in the figure.

heading: Heat tiles
proposition: English says the facilities report data TO THEIR PROVINCE; the Turkish instead states the facilities are ESTABLISHED IN certain provinces ("belirli illerde kurulmus olan malarya tesisleri").
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader loses the reporting relationship that the figure is about, and reads the province only as a location filter rather than as the recipient of the reports being counted.

heading: Plot with `ggplotly()`
proposition: English states the last toolbar control adjusts whether data show WHEN YOU ARE NOT HOVERING ON THE LINE; the Turkish drops that condition and says only "adjust settings about whether data are shown".
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader does not learn which hover state the button governs, so cannot tell what changes when the button is pressed and may confuse it with the spike-line toggle listed above it.

heading: Resources
proposition: English says plotly works with really ANY data science language BECAUSE it is built in JavaScript; the Turkish says it works with "any JavaScript-based data science coding language", turning the reason into a restriction on which languages qualify.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader concludes plotly is limited to JavaScript-based languages and may not look for the Python, Julia or MATLAB bindings that the English sentence points them toward.

heading: Start with a `ggplot()`
proposition: English calls `linelist` the case line list DATASET used in many pages of the handbook; the Turkish calls it the `linelist` METHOD ("`linelist` metodunu kullanarak").
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader may look for a function or method named linelist instead of recognising the imported data frame that the next section loads with appliedepidata::get_data().

heading: Plot with `ggplotly()`
proposition: The Turkish adds that the summary dataset contains the NUMBER of cases with a known outcome ("ciktilari bilinen vakalarin sayisi") as a listed element; the English names only the epidemiological week and the percent of known-outcome cases that died.
reader_consequence: None harmful: the added element matches the n_known_outcome column in the chunk below, but the Turkish inventory of the summary dataset no longer matches the English one.

heading: Heat tiles
proposition: The English hedges the claim as "almost any ggplot() plot" can be made interactive; the Vietnamese states "bất kỳ loại biểu đồ nào tạo bởi ggplot()" (any ggplot() plot at all), dropping the hedge.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader takes ggplotly() coverage of ggplot2 as universal, so when a geom does not convert (the chapter's own commented-out geom_sf map section is the stated counter-example) the reader assumes a mistake in their own code rather than a known plotly limitation.

heading: Plot with `ggplotly()`
proposition: The English defines the summarised percentage as the percent of cases WITH A KNOWN OUTCOME that died; the Vietnamese says only "phần trăm các trường hợp có outcome là tử vong" (percent of cases whose outcome is death), omitting the restriction of the denominator to cases with a known outcome.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader reads pct_death as a percentage of all cases in the epiweek and so misreads the n_known_outcome denominator in the adjacent chunk (lines 102-110), overstating or misinterpreting the case fatality figure the plot displays.

heading: Testing your for loop
proposition: The English carries '### Testing your for loop' as a rendered level-3 heading; the Spanish writes '###Probar tu bucle for  {.unnumbered}' with no space after the hashes, so it is not a heading at all.
reader_consequence: The Spanish reader sees the literal string '###Probar tu bucle for {.unnumbered}' as body text, gets no table-of-contents entry for testing a for loop, and the testing advice appears to belong to the preceding 'Impresion' section.

heading: Core components / Componentes basicos
proposition: The English gives the for-loop syntax skeleton as R code, `for (item in sequence) {do operations using item}`, keeping the R keyword `in`; the Spanish replaces the skeleton with Spanish prose inside the same code span, `for (para cada elemento de la secuencia) {hacer operaciones con el elemento}`, which contains no `in` keyword.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader learning the syntax from this line never sees the required R keyword `in`, and the next sentence tells them to note the parentheses and curly brackets of a template that is not valid R.

heading: Sequence / Secuencia
proposition: The English states the basic structure of a sequence statement is `item in vector`, using the R keyword `in`; the Spanish states it is `elemento en el vector`, replacing the keyword `in` with the Spanish preposition `en`.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader takes `en` to be the R keyword and writes `for (i en x)`, which is a syntax error.

heading: Sequence / Secuencia
proposition: The English shows the first and second iteration values as `hospital_names[[1]]` and `hospital_names[[2]]` with matched double brackets; the Spanish shows `hospital_names[1]]` and `hospital_names[2]]`, with one opening bracket and two closing brackets.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader copies a malformed subsetting expression that errors, and the chapter's own rule that double brackets `[[ ]]` are used for indexing is contradicted where it is first demonstrated.

heading: Sequence / Secuencia
proposition: The English example is `for (i in seq_along(hospital_names) {OPERATIONS CODE}`; the Spanish example is `for (i en seq_along(nombres_de_hospital) {Codigo_de_operaciones}`, replacing the R keyword `in` with `en` and naming an object `nombres_de_hospital` that is never created anywhere in the chapter.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader who runs this line gets a syntax error from `en` and then an object-not-found error, because the code chunks in the same section define `hospital_names`, not `nombres_de_hospital`.

heading: Looping plots / Bucles con graficos
proposition: The English says the loop produces a separate plot for each hospital's cases, that is one plot per hospital; the Spanish says 'un grafico separado para cada caso del hospital', that is one plot per case of the hospital.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader expects one epicurve per case and cannot reconcile that with the loop below, which iterates over `hospital_names` and prints one plot per hospital.

heading: map()
proposition: The English tilde example is `map(.x = my_list, .f = ~mean(., na.rm = T))`; the Spanish writes `map(.x = mi_lista, .f = \~mean(., na.rm = T))`, with a backslash before the tilde inside the code span.
reader_consequence: The rendered Spanish code shows a backslash before the tilde, so a reader copying the only tilde-syntax example in this bullet pastes a character R rejects, in the same sentence that tells them to use the tilde `~`.

heading: Example - import and combine Excel sheets / Ejemplo: importar y combinar hojas de Excel
proposition: The English names the first sheet "Central Hospital", the value actually held in `sheet_names`; the Spanish names it "Hospital Central", while leaving "Military Hospital" untranslated in the same sentence.
reader_consequence: The Spanish reader compares the sentence with the printed `sheet_names` output two chunks above, which lists "Central Hospital", and cannot tell which spelling to pass to `which = ` or to `linelist_split[[...]]`.

heading: Export as CSV files / Exportar como archivos CSV
proposition: The English bullet writes the indexing expression as `linelist_split[[.x]]`; the Spanish writes it as a broken span, `linelist`_split[.x]], splitting the object name and losing one opening bracket.
reader_consequence: The Spanish reader sees a mangled expression at the exact point the text explains how `.x` indexes the list, so the mechanism the bullet exists to teach is not legible.

heading: Mapping a function across columns / Mapear una funcion a traves de las columnas
proposition: The English says the element made of two or more sub-elements (`mean in group f` and `mean in group m`) is `estimate`; the Spanish attributes those two sub-elements to `conf.int` instead.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader looks for the group means under `conf.int`, and is then contradicted by the later section which correctly extracts them with `map(., "estimate")`.

heading: Convert list to data frame / Convertir una lista en un dataframe
proposition: The English names the two sub-elements of `estimate` as `mean in group f` and `mean in group m`, the literal names R returns; the Spanish renames them `media en el grupo f` and `media en el grupo m`.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader searching the printed `unnest_wider(means)` output, whose column names are the English strings, does not find the names the text told them to expect.

heading: Convert list to data frame / Convertir una lista en un dataframe
proposition: The English says `hoist()` acts like `unnest_wider()` but you specify which elements to unnest; the Spanish says you specify which elements are to be annulled ('se van a anular').
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader understands `hoist()` as a way to delete list elements rather than to un-nest selected ones, and will not reach for it when they need to lift specific elements out of a list-column.

heading: Core components
proposition: The basic for-loop syntax is written with the French words 'pour ... dans ...' instead of the R keywords 'for ... in ...'.
reader_consequence: A French reader copies `pour (element dans la sequence) {...}` into R and gets a syntax error, because `pour` and `dans` are not R keywords; the English shows the runnable form `for (item in sequence) {do operations using item}`.

heading: Core components
proposition: The third core part of a for loop is named 'le contenu des resultats' (the content of the results) rather than the container that holds the results.
reader_consequence: The reader does not learn that the third component is a pre-created storage object, so the later 'Conteneur' section and the `vector()`/`data.frame()` pre-allocation step read as unrelated material.

heading: Sequence
proposition: The heading carries the extra visible text '(sans numero)' after the attribute block.
reader_consequence: Because the attribute block is no longer at the end of the line, Pandoc does not parse it, so the section renders as the literal heading 'Sequence {.unnumbered} (sans numero)' and is numbered, unlike every sibling section.

heading: Sequence
proposition: The second iteration value is written as `noms_hospitaliers[[2]]`, an object that the chunk beside it never creates.
reader_consequence: The chunk above defines only `hospital_names`, and the same sentence uses `hospital_names[[1]]` for the first iteration; a reader who runs `noms_hospitaliers[[2]]` gets 'object not found' and cannot tell which name is correct.

heading: Container
proposition: The permitted values of the `mode = ` argument of `vector()` are given as "double", "caractere" and "logique".
reader_consequence: `vector(mode = "caractere")` and `vector(mode = "logique")` both fail with 'vector: cannot make a vector of mode', so a reader building an empty character or logical container from this sentence cannot proceed; R accepts only "character" and "logical".

heading: Printing
proposition: The character vector is described as being used to 'sous-titrer' (subtitle) the linelist by hospital, rather than to subset it.
reader_consequence: The reader is told the sequence adds a subtitle, when the chunk below actually uses `filter(hospital == hosp)` to take a subset, so the stated purpose of the loop does not match what the code does.

heading: Example - import and combine Excel sheets
proposition: The translation adds the parenthetical gloss '(`combine` en francais)' after naming the output list `combined`.
reader_consequence: The gloss is set in code formatting like a real object name, so a reader may believe the list can also be referred to as `combine`, which no chunk in the chapter creates.
