heading: Example - import and combine Excel sheets
proposition: The `map_at()` example chunk assigns to `sheet-names` and reads a workbook named "hospital_linelinest.xlsx", and it omits the `appliedepidata::save_data()` call that the English chunk runs first.
reader_consequence: The prose above says the sheet names are stored in a vector called `sheet_names` and that the workbook is "example_hospital_linelists.xlsx"; a reader copying this chunk hits a parse error on `sheet-names <-`, has no file of that name on disk, and the following `map_at()` call then uses a `sheet_names` object the chunk never defined.

heading: Mapping a function across columns
proposition: The sentence names the function applied to the numeric columns as `mappons()`.
reader_consequence: `mappons()` does not exist in purrr and does not appear in the chunk below, which calls `map()`; a reader searching the help for `mappons` finds nothing.

heading: Convert list to data frame
proposition: The prose says the element to extract is `estimate`, but the chunk immediately below plucks `"estimation"`.
reader_consequence: `map(., "estimation")` returns a column of NULLs because t.test results carry no element called 'estimation', so the reader's tibble has an empty `means` column and the `unnest_wider(means)` step in the next chunk produces different output from the one shown.

heading: Discard, keep, and compact lists
proposition: The discard-by-class example pipes an object named `combinws`, while the prose of the section works on the list `combined`.
reader_consequence: A reader running the chunk gets 'object combinws not found' and cannot reproduce the class-based discard, even though the surrounding text and every neighbouring chunk use `combined`.

heading: Mapping a function across columns
proposition: The English gives the t.test() formula template as `t.test(numeric column ~ binary column)`; the Japanese gives it as `t.test(文字列 ~ バイナリ変数の列)`, i.e. a character string on the left-hand side instead of a numeric column.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader is told the left-hand side of a t-test formula is a character/string column, which is impossible. The code chunk immediately below (select(age, wt_kg, ht_cm, ct_blood, temp) %>% map(.f = ~t.test(.x ~ linelist$gender))) and the surrounding bullets both use numeric columns, so the reader is left contradicting the example and may try to feed a character column to t.test().

heading: Convert list to data frame
proposition: The English says names() is used to CREATE A COLUMN WHOSE VALUES are the t-test variable names; the Japanese says names() is used when you want the COLUMN NAME (列名) to be the t-test variable name.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader believes names() sets the tibble's column heading rather than filling a column with the list-element names. In the code beside it the column is named `variables` and names(.) supplies its contents, so the reader misreads the tibble() call and cannot generalise it.

heading: Convert list to data frame
proposition: The English says map_dbl() is used to CREATE A COLUMN CONTAINING the p-values; the Japanese says it is used when you want the COLUMN NAME (列名) to be the p-value.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader thinks map_dbl(., "p.value") produces a column heading, not the numeric column contents. The code beside it names the column `p` and fills it with map_dbl(), so the reader misattributes which part of `p = map_dbl(., "p.value")` does what.

heading: Convert list to data frame
proposition: The Japanese states that the tibble passed to unnest_wider() is `t.test_results`; the English says only that 'the tibble' is passed, and `t.test_results` is the list, not the tibble.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader is told `t.test_results` is a tibble. It is the list of five t-test results; the tibble is the unnamed object built by the {tibble(...)} step in the pipe. The reader may try `unnest_wider(t.test_results, means)` directly, which fails because the list has no `means` column.

heading: Discard, keep, and compact lists
proposition: The English says the command removes all empty LIST ELEMENTS; the Japanese says it removes all empty COLUMNS (すべての空の列).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader thinks compact() drops empty columns from the data frames inside the list, when it drops empty elements of the list itself. This also contradicts the same page's own bullet at line 862, which correctly says compact() removes all empty 要素 (elements), so the reader gets two incompatible definitions of one function.

heading: map()
proposition: The English defines a list as an object class like a vector 'but whose elements can be of different classes'; the Japanese renders this only as 'a list is similar to a vector but its constituent elements are different' (構成要素が異なります), dropping the claim that the elements may be of different classes.
reader_consequence: At the point where map()'s return type is first defined, a Japanese reader does not learn the defining property of a list. The following sentence (a list may hold many data frames, vectors, single values or lists) then has no stated reason behind it, and the reader may assume a list, like a vector, must be homogeneous.

heading: Convert list to data frame
proposition: The English says the resulting data frame will have columns for the variable, its p-value, and the two group means; the Japanese lists only the p-value column and the group-mean columns, omitting the variable column.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader expects a two-part output and is not told in advance that a `variables` column is produced, although the code creates one. The reader has to infer the target shape from the code rather than from the stated goal.

heading: Sequence
proposition: The English warns that inside the loop `col` holds only the character column name, so the column itself must be referenced as `linelist[[col]]` and never as bare `col`; the Portuguese segment ends after the `is.na()`/`sum()` explanation and omits this warning entirely.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader writing their own column loop is never told the most common failure of this pattern, so they write `sum(is.na(col))` and silently get a result computed on a one-element character vector instead of on the column.

heading: Core components
proposition: The English tells the reader to note the parentheses and the CURLY brackets that delimit the loop body; the Portuguese says 'os parenteses e os colchetes', and 'colchetes' means square brackets [ ], not curly brackets { }.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader is told the loop body is delimited by square brackets, so writing `for (i in x) [ ... ]` looks correct to them and fails to parse; the same reader also cannot connect this sentence to the `{ }` shown in the syntax line just above it.

heading: Testing your for loop
proposition: The English identifies the code to run when testing a loop as 'the code within the curly brackets'; the Portuguese says 'o codigo entre colchetes', which names square brackets [ ] rather than the curly brackets { } that actually enclose the loop operations.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader following the test procedure looks for square brackets to decide which lines to run, and in a loop that also indexes with `[[ ]]` they may run the indexing expression instead of the loop body, so the test does not exercise the operations it was meant to check.

heading: map()
proposition: The English gives the runnable call `map(.x = my_list, .f = mean, na.rm=T)`; the Portuguese renders the same inline call as `map(.x = my_list, .f = media, na.rm=T)`, presenting `media` as the R function to supply to `.f`, which is not an R function.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader who copies this call gets 'object media not found'; the same sentence writes `.f = mean` correctly a few words earlier, so the reader cannot tell which of the two spellings is the real function name.

heading: map()
proposition: The English states that `map_dbl()` produces NUMERIC vectors; the Portuguese says only 'map_dbl() para produzir vetores', dropping the word numeric while keeping 'vetores de caracteres' for `map_chr()`.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader loses the contrast that distinguishes the two variants and cannot tell what class `map_dbl()` guarantees, so they do not know it is the function to reach for when a numeric vector is required.

heading: Convert list to data frame
proposition: The English says `map()` used inside `tibble()` creates a column whose CLASS IS LIST ('a column of class list within the tibble'); the Portuguese says it creates 'uma coluna da lista de classes dentro do tibble', that is, a column of the list of classes.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader does not learn that the new `means` column is a list-column, which is the exact property that makes the `unnest_wider()` step two paragraphs later necessary, so that step reads as unmotivated.

heading: Sequence
proposition: The inline example of the sequence statement is written `for (i в 1:nrow(linelist)) {КОД ОПЕРАЦИЙ}`, replacing the R keyword `in` with the Russian word `в`, whereas the English writes `for (i in 1:nrow(linelist)) {OPERATIONS CODE}` and the code chunk immediately below (ru:163-167) uses `in`.
reader_consequence: A reader who copies the inline sequence statement out of the prose gets a syntax error, because `в` is not an R keyword; the surrounding text presents it as the literal code form of the sequence, so the reader has no signal that only the placeholder words were translated.

heading: Operations
proposition: The translation says to check the parts of your code that CHANGE the "item" ("каждая часть вашего кода, которая меняет "элемент""), reversing the English claim that the parts to check are those that change BY the "item" (vary with it).
reader_consequence: A Russian reader is told the loop body is what changes the item, so they may write code that reassigns `i` or `hosp` inside the loop instead of checking that each item-dependent expression is correctly indexed; the English warning about `[[ ]]` indexing then has no stated cause.

heading: Mapping a function across columns
proposition: The translation says the example applies `as.character()` only to the single column "age" ("только к столбцу \"age\""), whereas the English says the "age" columns (plural) and the chunk beside it uses `across(.cols = contains("age"))`, which selects every column whose name contains "age".
reader_consequence: A Russian reader believes `contains("age")` targets one named column and may run the code expecting only `age` to change, while `age_unit`, `age_years` and `age_cat` are also converted to character; the chunk's own comment (ru:773) says the opposite, leaving the reader with two conflicting statements.

heading: *for loops* in R
proposition: The Turkish says for loops let you advance quickly to iterating with purrr-mapped functions ("*for donguleri* sayesinde hizla ilerleyebilirsiniz", i.e. "thanks to for loops"); the English instead tells the reader they MAY move quickly through the for-loops material on to purrr, that is, they may skip ahead.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader does not learn that the whole for-loops section is optional and can be skimmed on the way to purrr. They read it as a claim that for loops are a prerequisite that speeds up learning purrr, so they work through material the English explicitly lets them pass over.

heading: *for loops* in R
proposition: The English gives a third reason for loops help a beginner: they make it easier to grasp exactly what is happening at each iteration. The Turkish drops this as a property of for loops and turns it into an obligation on the reader ("her yinelemenin tam olarak ne oldugunu anlamalisiniz" = "you must understand exactly what happens in each iteration").
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader loses the stated pedagogical reason to learn for loops, and instead reads a requirement placed on them. The motivation for the section is weakened and the reader may treat per-iteration comprehension as a demand rather than as a benefit for loops provide.

heading: Core components
proposition: The English gives the basic for-loop syntax as `for (item in sequence) {do operations using item}`, which contains the R keyword `in`. The Turkish renders the same template as `for (siradaki oge) {ogeyi kullanarak islemler yapin}`, which has no `in` keyword and is not valid R.
reader_consequence: A beginner who copies the Turkish template writes a for statement with no `in` and gets a syntax error. The code chunk four lines below (both files, lines 91-96) uses `for (num in c(1,2,3,4,5))`, so the prose contradicts the example beside it and the reader cannot see where `in` came from.

heading: Sequence
proposition: The English states the basic structure of a sequence statement is `item in vector`. The Turkish gives it as `vektordeki ogedir` ("is the item in the vector"), a Turkish noun phrase in code formatting, so the R keyword `in` is absent from the stated structure.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader is shown a sequence statement with no `in` keyword, immediately before code chunks in the same section that all use `for (hosp in hospital_names)` and `for (col in names(linelist))`. They cannot map the stated structure onto the working code, and a copied statement will not parse.

heading: Container
proposition: The English says to set `mode = ` to one of the literal R values "double", "character" or "logical", and then to use "double" for the median delays. The Turkish translates these literals to "cift", "karakter" and "mantiksal", and then says to use "Cift".
reader_consequence: `vector(mode = "cift")` raises an error, because "cift" is not an R mode. The code chunk directly below (Turkish lines 219-223) uses `mode = "double"`, so the prose names a value the adjacent code does not use, and the reader has no way to know which of the two to type.

heading: `map()`
proposition: The English names the purrr function `map_dfr()` as the variant that produces a data frame. The Turkish writes it as `.map_dfr()`, with a leading dot, which is not a purrr function.
reader_consequence: A reader who types `.map_dfr()` gets "could not find function". The same function is written correctly as `map_dfr()` later in the Turkish text (line 526), so the reader also meets two spellings of one function and cannot tell which is right.

heading: Convert list to data frame
proposition: The English says `hoist()` acts like `unnest_wider()` but you specify which elements to UNNEST. The Turkish says you specify which elements will be NESTED ("hangi ogelerin yuvalanacagini siz belirlersiniz"), the opposite operation. The same Turkish segment uses "ic ice den cikarmak" for un-nesting four lines earlier, so the reversal is unambiguous.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader understands `hoist()` as a function that nests selected elements, when it extracts them out of a nested list-column into their own columns. They will not reach for `hoist()` when they want to pull two named elements out of a list-column, which is exactly the task this section is teaching.

heading: Mapping a function across columns
proposition: The English says the vector linelist$gender is supplied 'statically' (its value does not change across iterations); the Vietnamese says it is supplied 'co y nghia thong ke' (statistically significantly), a claim about a significance test that the English does not make and that the t.test() code beside it does not support.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader is told the gender vector is supplied 'with statistical significance', which is meaningless here, and loses the actual point: that linelist$gender is held constant across every iteration of map() while only .x changes. The reader may believe some significance criterion governs the right-hand side of the t-test formula.

heading: Container
proposition: The English lists the accepted values of vector(mode = ) as "double", "character" and "logical"; the Vietnamese lists them as "double", "ky tu" and "logic", which are not values vector() accepts.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader who copies the listed values writes vector(mode = "ky tu") or vector(mode = "logic") and gets an error from R, because only "character" and "logical" are valid modes. The inconsistency is compounded by "double" being left untranslated in the same list, which signals that these strings are literal code values.

heading: Container
proposition: The English example stores the MEDIAN delay-to-admission per hospital; the Vietnamese says 'trung binh' (mean/average) delay-to-admission.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader takes the worked example to be about a mean rather than a median. In a handbook that distinguishes the two elsewhere, this teaches the wrong summary statistic for the stated task and would produce a different number if the reader implements the example.

heading: Joining data
proposition: An epidemiological analysis or workflow rarely avoids multiple data sources and the linkage of multiple datasets, with examples such as laboratory data to clinical outcomes, Google mobility data to disease trends, or a dataset to a transformed version of itself.
reader_consequence: The Spanish reader gets no motivating rationale for why joining matters in epidemiology, and none of the three concrete linkage examples, so the chapter opens as a bare technique list with no use case.

heading: Joining data
proposition: The page demonstrates code for three specific tasks: joins matching rows on common identifier-column values, joins based on probabilistic (likely) matches between values, and expanding a data frame by binding (appending) rows or columns.
reader_consequence: The Spanish reader has no roadmap of the chapter's three topics, so cannot tell before reading that probabilistic matching and row/column binding are covered here, and may look elsewhere for them.

heading: Bind columns
proposition: The column to join on is named `hospital`; the translation names it `hospitals`, which does not exist in the `case_info` or `contact_fu` data frames created in the chunks immediately above (es.qmd:840, 855).
reader_consequence: A reader who copies the named column and writes left_join(case_info, contact_fu, by = "hospitals") gets an error that the join column is not found, and has no cue that the name in the prose is wrong.

heading: Probabilistic matching
proposition: The two `my_matches` columns are converted to character so that they can be joined to the CHARACTER rownames (the rowname column created in the previous step), not merely to the rows.
reader_consequence: The Spanish reader loses the stated reason for the conversion, which is that the join key on the other side is a character rowname column, and so may not see why the class conversion is required at all.

heading: Resources
proposition: The first resource link is the tidyverse reference page on joins (https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/join.html); the translation labels its link as being about joins but points it at the general dplyr function index (https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/index.html).
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader following the first resource link lands on the full dplyr function index instead of the join documentation, and must search for the join page themselves.

heading: Inner join / Jointure interne
proposition: The animation shown in this section is an example of an inner join; the French caption instead calls it a full join ("jointure complete").
reader_consequence: A French reader in the inner-join section reads the caption of inner-join.gif as describing a full join, so they may take the animated behaviour (rows kept only where both sides match) to be what a full join does, and conversely have no animated illustration labelled for the inner join they are reading about.

heading: Probabilistic matching / Appariement probabiliste
proposition: The second left_join matches the newly acquired "inds.b" values in cases to the rownames of results; the French says it matches them to the "noms de domaine" (domain names) in results.
reader_consequence: A French reader looking for a column of "domain names" in results finds none, and may not realise the join key on the results side is the rowname column created by rownames_to_column(), which is exactly what the code chunk below uses (by = c("inds.b" = "rowname")).

heading: Pre-cleaning / Nettoyage preliminaire
proposition: str_to_upper(), str_to_lower() and str_to_title() are functions supplied by stringr; the French describes them as "une des colonnes de stringr" (one of stringr's columns).
reader_consequence: A French reader is told to combine mutate() with a stringr *column* rather than a stringr *function*, which misstates what the package provides and gives no usable instruction on how to apply the case conversion inside mutate().

heading: General syntax
proposition: English names the third argument of the join functions as `by = `; the translation names it `y = `, which is not an argument of `left_join()` and does not appear in the adjacent code chunk (`left_join(df1, df2, by = c("ID" = "identifier"))`).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader looks for an argument called `y` in the join functions, does not find it in `?left_join`, and cannot connect the prose to the `by =` argument used in every join example on the page.

heading: Left and right joins
proposition: English says the two new columns `catchment_pop` and `level` were added on the LEFT side of `linelist_mini`; the translation says they were added on the RIGHT side (`linelist_mini` の右側に).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader is told the opposite of the English about where joined columns appear. The Japanese statement matches the actual `left_join()` output, so a reader comparing the two language versions cannot tell which is correct.

heading: Inner join
proposition: English introduces the example as the output of an `inner_join()` of `linelist_mini` with `hosp_info`; the translation says the output comes from `full_join()` (完全結合), while the code chunk immediately below runs `inner_join()`.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader in the inner-join section is told the demonstrated result is a full join, so the bullet points about dropped non-matching rows appear to contradict the named function, and the reader may believe `full_join()` removes non-matching rows.

heading: Probabilistic deduplication
proposition: English says the two rows ADDED to make `cases_dup` are the possible duplicates, i.e. "Tony" duplicates "Anthony" and "Maria Rodriguez" duplicates "Marialisa Rodrigues"; the translation reverses the first pair, saying the row "Anthony Smith" was added as a duplicate of "Tony Smith".
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader reading the `cases_dup` chunk (row 2 is "Anthony", added row 10 is "Tony") sees the prose contradict the data, and mis-identifies which record is the original and which is the suspected duplicate when interpreting the `dedupe.ids` output.

heading: Probabilistic deduplication
proposition: English says to run `fastLink()` comparing the `cases_dup` data frame TO ITSELF; the translation says to run `fastLink()` and compare its OUTPUT with the `cases_dup` data frame (出力結果を `cases_dup` データフレームと比較します).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader is told to compare a result object against the data frame, which is not what the adjacent chunk does (`dfA = cases_dup, dfB = cases_dup`), and misses the rule that deduplication is triggered by passing the same data frame twice.

heading: Pre-cleaning
proposition: English advises converting the VALUES of a column to all lowercase or all uppercase before a join; the translation advises converting the COLUMN NAMES (列名をすべて小文字または大文字に変換する).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader may rename columns instead of case-standardising the values that the join matches on, leaving the case-sensitivity problem the paragraph exists to prevent; the very next sentence then contradicts it by referring to all values in a column.

heading: Bind columns
proposition: English says `bind_cols()` combines two data frames SIDEWAYS (horizontally); the translation says it combines them 縦向きに (vertically/lengthwise).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader may understand `bind_cols()` as stacking data frames one below the other, the same as `bind_rows()`, and so misunderstand why row order and positional matching matter in this section.

heading: Hospital information data frame
proposition: English describes the extra hospital information as the catchment population and the level of care; the translation describes it as 患者数 (the number of patients) and the level of care.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader interprets `catchment_pop` (values such as 1950280) as a patient count rather than the population served, which changes the meaning of the column in every joined table on the page.

heading: Probabilistic matching
proposition: English states the purpose of the alternative approach: to obtain only the "original" 9 records of `cases` with the new column(s) from `results`. The translation states only that you may want to add specific columns, and omits the 9-record result.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader does not learn what distinguishes this second approach from the first (a 9-row result rather than one carrying all columns of both data frames), so cannot tell which approach to choose.

heading: Probabilistic matching
proposition: The translation names the columns to keep as `rowname` 列と `results` 列; the adjacent code chunk selects `select(rowname, result)`, and `results` is the name of the data frame, not of a column in it.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader who follows the prose writes `select(rowname, results)`, which errors because no column `results` exists.

heading: Anti join
proposition: English lists troubleshooting SPELLING in a join as a common use of an anti-join; the translation keeps only the parenthetical idea of reviewing records that should have matched, and drops the spelling motivation.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader loses the main diagnostic use of an anti-join for exact-match joins, namely finding values that failed to match because of spelling differences, which is the problem the Pre-cleaning section earlier set up.

heading: **dplyr** joins
proposition: English credits the gifs with a link to https://github.com/gadenbuie/tidyexplain/tree/master/images; the translation's link target is the malformed URL https://github.com/gadenbuieに感謝します。 (Japanese text merged into the address).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader who clicks the credit link reaches a non-existent page instead of the tidyexplain image repository, and cannot find the source of the join animations used throughout the chapter.

heading: Semi join
proposition: The translation adds a statement not present in the English segment: that `hosp_info` is the baseline data frame and `linelist_mini` is the secondary data frame, and names the join columns `hosp_name` and `hospital`.
reader_consequence: No factual harm: the added statement agrees with the code. A Japanese reader gets an explicit baseline/secondary framing that English readers must infer, so the two versions differ in what the reader is told at this point.

heading: ### Probabilistic matching
proposition: Step 1 of the join strategy matches the ROW NAMES of `cases` to "inds.a"; the Portuguese says it matches "os nomes das colunas" (the column names) of `cases` to "inds.a".
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader is told the first `left_join()` keys on column names rather than on the rowname column, which contradicts the code `left_join(cases_clean, matches_clean, by = c("rowname" = "inds.a"))` and the preceding `rownames_to_column()` step, so the reader cannot see why `rownames_to_column()` is needed and may key the join on the wrong thing when adapting it.

heading: ### Probabilistic matching
proposition: Both columns of `my_matches` are converted to character so they can be joined to the character ROW NAMES; the Portuguese says they are joined to "os nomes de coluna que são caracteres" (the character column names).
reader_consequence: The stated reason for the `as.character` conversion is wrong in Portuguese: the reader learns the conversion exists to align with column names, not with the `rowname` column produced by `rownames_to_column()`, so the cleaning step looks arbitrary and is likely to be dropped when reused.

heading: ### Probabilistic matching
proposition: The prose names the function and its help topic as `fastLink()` and `?fastLink`, and the package as **fastLink**; the Portuguese writes `fastlink()`, `?fastlink` and **fastlink**, all lower-case.
reader_consequence: R is case-sensitive, so a Portuguese reader who types `?fastlink` in the console gets no help page, and the name in the prose does not match `fastLink::fastLink(...)` in the code chunk immediately below.

heading: ### Probabilistic deduplication
proposition: The command is used to return the ROW NUMBERS of rows that are likely duplicates; the Portuguese says it returns "o número de linhas que são potenciais duplicidades" (the number of rows that are potential duplicates).
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader expects a count of duplicate rows from `count(dedupe.ids) %>% filter(n > 1)`, whereas the purpose is to identify WHICH duplicate-id groups (and hence which rows) to inspect with the next command.

heading: ### General syntax
proposition: The Russian says the `by` columns are the columns "you group by" ("по которым вы группируете"); the English says only that they are the `by` columns whose names must be exactly the same in both data frames, and nothing in the chapter or the `left_join()` code beside it involves grouping.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader is told the join key is a grouping variable, so may look for or add `group_by()` before the join, or confuse `by = ` with dplyr grouping, which changes what the pipeline computes.

heading: #### "Should I use a right join, or a left join?"
proposition: The English instructs the reader to use the data frame that must keep all its rows AS THE BASELINE ("use this one as the baseline"); the Russian drops "baseline" and says only "use it as the data frame" ("используйте его как датафрейм").
reader_consequence: The Russian sentence gives no instruction at all, so the reader learns the diagnostic question but not the rule it answers: which data frame to write first, and therefore whether to pick `left_join()` or `right_join()`.

heading: ### Pre-cleaning / ### Ön temizleme
proposition: The dplyr function used to re-code values by logical criteria is named case_when(); the Turkish prose names it case_while().
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader learns a function name that does not exist in dplyr, contradicting the case_when() call in the very next code chunk (tr lines 155-167), and gets 'could not find function "case_while"' if they type what the text says.

heading: ### Probabilistic matching / ### Olasılıksal eşleşme
proposition: The lubridate function that extracts the month is month(); the Turkish tip states that lubridate provides ay().
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader following the tip calls lubridate::ay() to split a date column and gets an error, because no such function exists; day() and year() are left in English so the reader has no cue that only this one name was altered.

heading: #### Use match() to align ordering / #### Sırasını hizalamak için match() kullanımı
proposition: The first argument of match() is a stand-alone vector or, in this case, a COLUMN in a data frame; the Turkish text says it is a stand-alone vector or, in this case, a data frame.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader may pass a whole data frame (contact_fu) as the first argument of match() instead of a column (case_info$hospital), which does not reproduce the ordering vector shown in the chunk at tr line 881.

heading: Hospital information data frame
proposition: The secondary-level 'Military Hospital' has a catchment population of 40500; the English text states 50280.
reader_consequence: The Vietnamese figure (40500) is the one actually in the identical hosp_info code chunk on both sides, where 50280 belongs to 'port'. A reader who cross-checks the Vietnamese chapter against the English original sees two different catchment populations for the same hospital and cannot tell which edition is authoritative; a reader who trusts the English number will look for 50280 in the printed table and not find it against 'military'.

heading: Full join
proposition: The Vietnamese bullet says all possible combinations are returned in the case of 'one-to-one or many-to-one' matches; the English says 'one-to-many or many-to-one'.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader is told that a one-to-one match lengthens the result, which is false, and is never told that a one-to-many match does. They will not expect a full_join() to duplicate a baseline row that matches two secondary rows, which is exactly what happens to 'Military Hospital' in the worked example printed immediately below.

heading: General syntax
proposition: The English CAUTION states that joins are case-specific (sensitive to upper/lower letter case); the Vietnamese renders this as joins being based on specific situations/instances ('Noi dua tren nhung truong hop cu the'), which is a different claim.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader loses the stated reason for the advice that follows and does not learn that a join fails when the same value differs only in letter case. The same chapter translates case-sensitivity correctly at line 113, so the reader gets two inconsistent accounts and may not apply case conversion before joining.

heading: Types of missing data
proposition: MCAR (Missing Completely at Random) is a rare situation.
reader_consequence: The Spanish reader is told the probability of missingness is equal across all cases and that MCAR permits complete-case analysis without bias, but is never told MCAR is rare. That reader is more likely to assume MCAR for their own data, skip imputation, and produce biased estimates.

heading: Load packages
proposition: The translation carries a stray editorial marker '##hastaqui' as body text after the p_load() chunk; the English has nothing there.
reader_consequence: Because '##hastaqui' has no space after the hashes it is not a Markdown heading, so it renders as literal text on the page. The Spanish reader sees an untranslated working note in the middle of the Preparation section and cannot tell whether it is instruction or debris.

heading: Shadow columns
proposition: The shadow technique visualizes missingness in one column against the values of a second, different column.
reader_consequence: The Spanish text says only that a second column acting as a 'shadow' of the first is used, dropping the stratification-by-another-variable purpose. The reader misses why the section exists and may not understand the following example, which plots missingness of days_onset_hosp against date_hospitalisation.

heading: `na.omit()`
proposition: Applied to a data frame, na.omit() removes rows that have ANY missing value; the French states it removes rows whose values are ALL missing ("les lignes dont *toutes* les valeurs sont manquantes").
reader_consequence: A French reader believes na.omit(linelist) keeps every partially incomplete row and only drops fully empty rows. They will run it expecting almost no rows to be lost, and silently lose the large majority of the linelist, or wrongly conclude the function is broken.

heading: `drop_na()`
proposition: drop_na() with no arguments removes rows with ANY missing value; the French states it removes rows whose values are ALL missing ("elle supprime également les lignes dont *toutes* les valeurs sont manquantes").
reader_consequence: A French reader mis-predicts the size of the filtered data set and cannot reconcile the row count printed by the very next chunk in the chapter (linelist %>% drop_na() %>% nrow()), which drops rows on ANY missingness.

heading: Types de donnees manquantes / Types of missing data
proposition: The English says imputing MCAR data is often fairly simple; the French says imputing MA (its abbreviation for MAR) data is relatively simple, and contrasts it only with MOP (MNAR).
reader_consequence: A French reader takes MAR data to be the easy case and loses the chapter's actual ranking of difficulty (MCAR easy, MAR intermediate and the assumption of most methods, MNAR hard). The same segment then says most common methods assume MA, which now reads as a tautology instead of the intended contrast.

heading: Imputation par la moyenne / Mean Imputation
proposition: The English justifies mean imputation by an assumption of MCAR (twice: for the general case and for the missing temperature measurements); the French substitutes MA, its abbreviation for MAR, in both places.
reader_consequence: A French reader applies mean imputation to data they believe are MAR, which the chapter elsewhere describes as systematically and predictably missing. Mean imputation under MAR is biased, and the reader has been told the opposite by the text that introduces it.

heading: `NA`
proposition: The French adds a gloss that NA stands for "Non available"; the English never expands the abbreviation.
reader_consequence: A French reader learns an expansion the English does not give, and the form given is not the R documentation's wording ("Not Available"), so a reader who repeats it is quoting something no R source says.

heading: Types de donnees manquantes / Types of missing data
proposition: The French MCAR definition adds that missingness is also unrelated to unmeasured variables ("ou avec des variables non mesurees"); the English restricts the statement to the other variables in your data.
reader_consequence: A French reader is given a stronger definition of MCAR than the English chapter states, so the two language versions disagree on what a reader must be able to assume before analysing non-missing data without imputation.

heading: Types de donnees manquantes / Types of missing data
proposition: The French calls the MNAR mechanism "non-ignorable" ("Ce mecanisme de non-reponse est _non-ignorable_"); the English introduces no such term.
reader_consequence: A French reader meets a technical term with no definition and no counterpart in the English chapter, and cannot look it up anywhere else in the handbook.

heading: Imputation par regression / Regression imputation
proposition: The English states that predictions are produced only for observations where temperature is missing but age and fever are NOT missing; the French drops the condition on the predictors.
reader_consequence: A French reader expects predictions_for_missing_temps to cover every row with a missing temperature, and is not warned that rows also missing age or fever get no imputed value.

heading: Versions of `NA`
proposition: The Japanese says `NA_real_` is the variant to use for DATE values (日付型や数字型の場合は `NA_real_`, and the bullet `NA_real_` - 日付型、数字値に用いる); the English says dates take plain `NA` and reserves `NA_real_` for numeric only.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader writing `case_when()` over a date column follows the text and puts `NA_real_` on the right-hand side, which is a double, so the call errors with a class mismatch. The reader also never learns that plain `NA` is the correct choice for dates.

heading: Versions of `NA`
proposition: The Japanese says these `NA` variants arise when using `case_when()` to create a new ROW (新しい行); the English says a new COLUMN.
reader_consequence: The reader is told `case_when()` creates rows, which it does not. Someone looking for where the variant-`NA` problem occurs will not connect it to the column-creation step shown in the chunk above.

heading: Examples
proposition: The English results table states an outcome for each of `5 / Inf`, `NA - 5`, `Inf / 5`, `class(NA)`, `class(NaN)`, `class(Inf)` and `class(NULL)`; in the Japanese grid table these seven commands are collapsed into one run-together cell whose single outcome column reads only "NULL", so no command keeps its own stated outcome.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader cannot read that `5 / Inf` is 0, that `Inf / 5` is `Inf`, or that `class(NA)` is "logical" while `class(NaN)` and `class(Inf)` are "numeric". The one visible outcome, "NULL", appears to belong to all seven commands.

heading: Filter out rows with missing values
proposition: The Japanese says you can DISPLAY ROWS in order (順番に行を表示することも出来ます); the English says you can LIST COLUMNS one after the other as arguments to `drop_na()`.
reader_consequence: The sentence introduces the chunk below, which passes column selections to `drop_na()`. A Japanese reader is told the sentence is about displaying rows and so misses that `drop_na()` accepts several column names in sequence, and that the tidyselect helper named next selects columns.

heading: Types of missing data
proposition: The Japanese states MAR is THE MOST COMMON type of missing data (欠損データの種類としては、最も多いタイプのものです); the English says only that it is A COMMON type.
reader_consequence: The reader takes an empirical ranking of missingness mechanisms from a text that does not make one, and may default to assuming MAR rather than reasoning about why their own data are missing.

heading: Multiple Imputation
proposition: The English states that each imputed dataset therefore has slightly different imputed values, while the non-missing data are identical across all of them; the Japanese paragraph has no counterpart to this sentence.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader is not told what actually differs between the imputed datasets. They may expect the observed values to vary too, and they lose the reason why the several datasets must be analysed separately and pooled.

heading: Multiple Imputation
proposition: The English states that multiple imputation is not always much more work than a complete case analysis; the Japanese replaces this with a claim that multiple imputation is preferable to a complete case analysis, and states no comparison of effort.
reader_consequence: The reader loses the practical argument the paragraph closes on, that the cost of multiple imputation is often small, and gets an unsupported preference claim in its place.

heading: Explore and visualize missingness relationships
proposition: The translation states that in a geom_miss_point() scatterplot one of the two columns is drawn without its missing values and the other is drawn with them ('uma delas e construida sem os valores em branco, e a outra com estes pontos'). The English makes no such asymmetric claim: it says records with one value missing and the other present are shown, with the missing value set 10 percent below the lowest value in the column.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader believes geom_miss_point() treats the x and y columns differently, and that records missing the other variable are dropped. They will misread the red points, which mark missingness in either column, and may swap the axes expecting a different plot.

heading: Multiple Imputation
proposition: The translation claims that pooling the imputed datasets often makes 'os resultados' (the results) more accurate. The English claims only that it often results in more accurate STANDARD ERROR estimates.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader expects multiple imputation to improve the point estimates themselves and misses that the stated benefit is correct uncertainty quantification. They may report imputed estimates as more accurate than a complete-case analysis without support.

heading: LOCF and BOCF
proposition: The translation says the year value is recorded 'apenas no ano final' (only in the final year). The English says it is recorded only at the END OF THE YEAR, and the chunk beside it records a year on the Q4 line of both 2000 (line 605) and 2001 (line 609).
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader expects a year value on the last row only and cannot reconcile that with the 2000 value in the middle of the tribble. The point of the example, that fill(.direction = 'up') carries each year backwards within its own year, is lost.

heading: LOCF and BOCF
proposition: The translation says the invented dataset holds case counts for each 'quadrimestre' (four-month period, three per year) of 2000 and 2001. The English says each QUARTER, and the chunk beside it holds four rows per year labelled Q1 to Q4.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader is told the time unit is a four-month period, of which there are three per year, while the data shows four periods per year. They mis-describe the worked example and may carry the wrong time unit into their own fill() code.

heading: ### Versions of `NA`
proposition: The English bullet states that the plain `NA` form is the one to use for DATE values ("use for dates or logical TRUE/FALSE"); the Russian bullet says "используется для данных" (used for DATA), so the guidance about dates is absent.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader choosing an `NA` variant inside `case_when()` for a date column gets no rule for dates, and reads a vacuous instruction ("for data") that applies equally to the two other bullets, so they may pick `NA_character_` or `NA_real_` for a date column and hit a class error.

heading: ### Types of missing data
proposition: The English MAR example gives the reason the value is missing: every patient with chills and aches was ASSUMED TO HAVE A FEVER, so their temperature was never taken. The Russian says only that "it was assumed that for every patient with chills and aches the temperature simply was not measured", which drops the clinical assumption and states the missingness as its own cause.
reader_consequence: The worked example of Missing at Random loses its mechanism. A Russian reader is given a circular statement (the value is missing because it was assumed not to be measured) and cannot see WHY the other recorded variables predict missingness, which is the whole point that separates MAR from MCAR.

heading: ### Types of missing data
proposition: The English says the observations in the MAR example have a missing value FOR FEVER; the Russian says they have a missing value for TEMPERATURE ("с отсутствующим значением температуры"). The linelist carries `fever` and `temp` as separate columns.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader mapping the example onto the dataset used elsewhere in the chapter attributes the missingness to the `temp` column rather than the `fever` column, and the second half of the same paragraph (predicting that the observation had a fever) then reads as predicting the variable that was said to be missing.

heading: ### Multiple Imputation
proposition: The English names the comparator method as "a complete case analysis", a defined technique (analysing only records with no missing values). The Russian renders it "полного анализа случая" (a full analysis of a case), which does not name that technique.
reader_consequence: The closing recommendation compares multiple imputation against an unnamed alternative, so a Russian reader does not learn that the baseline being improved on is complete-case analysis, which is the approach described at the top of the Imputation section.

heading: Versions of `NA`
proposition: English names the dplyr function as `case_when()`, which is what the code chunk below uses; the Turkish names it `case_while()` (and links to anchor `#clean_case_while`).
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader searching for or typing `case_while()` finds no such dplyr function and gets an 'object not found' error; the cross-reference link also points at a non-existent anchor.

heading: Versions of `NA`
proposition: English says the NA variants are unlikely to be met unless you use `case_when()` to create a new column; the Turkish says `case_while()`.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader is told the rule applies to a function that does not exist, so cannot connect the NA_real_/NA_character_ guidance to the real `case_when()` they will actually write.

heading: Shadow columns
proposition: English says the shadow columns are used to STRATIFY a statistical summary; the Turkish says only that they can be used to CREATE a statistical summary.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader loses the point of the example: that `group_by(date_outcome_NA)` splits the summary by missingness. They may read the chunk as an ordinary summary and miss the missingness comparison it is making.

heading: Types of missing data
proposition: English says the chills-and-aches information could be used to IMPUTE the missing data; the Turkish says it could be used to ASSESS ('degerlendirmek') the missing data.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader is given an assessment example where the English gives the worked motivation for imputation under MAR, weakening the link between MAR and why imputation is possible.

heading: Types of missing data
proposition: English advises collecting more data about why data are missing RATHER THAN ATTEMPTING TO IMPUTE under MNAR; the Turkish drops the 'rather than attempt to impute it' clause.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader facing MNAR data does not receive the explicit warning against imputing it, and may go on to apply the mice methods taught later in the chapter to data where the chapter says they should not.

heading: Imputation
proposition: English says it is probably unreasonable to drop every variable that has A LOT OF MISSING DATA; the Turkish says every variable that has 'too much data' ('cok fazla verisi olan'), dropping the word missing.
reader_consequence: The Turkish sentence states a rule about variables with plenty of data, which is the opposite population, so the reader gets no guidance about the variables the paragraph is actually about.

heading: Useful packages
proposition: English introduces the chunk as loading the `mice` package; the Turkish calls it the 'Fare' package (Turkish for the animal mouse), while the chunk runs `pacman::p_load(mice)`.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader who takes 'Fare' as the package name will try to install a package that does not exist, and cannot match the prose to the `mice` in the chunk beside it.

heading: Regression imputation
proposition: English says that even with a very good model the variability of imputed data may be UNDERESTIMATED; the Turkish says only that the variability may not be well estimated, dropping the direction of the error.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader loses the specific, actionable warning that single regression imputation biases variance downward, so will not know that standard errors and confidence intervals from such data are too narrow.

heading: LOCF and BOCF
proposition: English defines LOCF and BOCF as IMPUTATION methods for time series/longitudinal data; the Turkish calls them assessment/evaluation methods ('degerlendirme yontemleri').
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader may file LOCF and BOCF under missingness assessment rather than imputation, and not recognise them as alternatives to the mean, regression and multiple imputation methods in the surrounding sections.

heading: LOCF and BOCF
proposition: English says the missing year values for quarters after Q1 will need to be IMPUTED; the Turkish says they will need to be COUNTED ('saymamiz gerekecek').
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader is told the demonstration is about counting missing years, so does not see that the `fill(year)` chunk that follows is performing the imputation the sentence set up.

heading: Multiple Imputation
proposition: English says the mice package CAN TAKE CARE OF many of the modelling details for you; the Turkish says you MUST PAY ATTENTION TO the modelling details of the mice package.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader is told the opposite of the English reassurance, and may conclude that multiple imputation with mice demands manual specification of the modelling details that mice in fact handles by default.

heading: Multiple Imputation
proposition: English says there are many details it has GLOSSED OVER; the Turkish says there are many details it has DWELT ON ('Uzerinde durdugumuz birçok ayrinti').
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader does not learn that the section is a simplified summary, so may treat what they have read as complete coverage of multiple imputation and not consult the referenced book for the omitted detail.

heading: Multiple Imputation
proposition: English recommends multiple imputation because it ISN'T ALWAYS MUCH MORE WORK than a complete case analysis; the Turkish says it is NEVER MORE USEFUL than a complete case analysis ('her zaman tam bir vaka analizi yapmaktan daha fazla ise yaramaz').
reader_consequence: The Turkish sentence ends the chapter by telling the reader multiple imputation gains them nothing over complete case analysis, which reverses the chapter's recommendation and would lead them to skip imputation entirely.

heading: Examples / Các ví dụ
proposition: The English reference table gives a separate outcome for each of `5 / Inf` (`0`), `NA - 5` (`NA`), `Inf / 5` (`Inf`), `class(NA)` ("logical"), `class(NaN)` ("numeric"), `class(Inf)` ("numeric") and `class(NULL)` ("NULL"); the Vietnamese table collapses all seven of these commands into a single unparsed cell whose only stated outcome is "NULL".
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader cannot learn the result of `5 / Inf`, `NA - 5`, `Inf / 5`, or the class of `NA`, `NaN` and `Inf`. The rendered table appears to say that all seven expressions evaluate to "NULL", so a reader could conclude that `class(NA)` is "NULL" rather than "logical".

heading: Multiple Imputation / Gán số liệu nhiều lần
proposition: The English states that multiple imputation is not always much more WORK than a complete case analysis (an effort claim recommending it); the Vietnamese states that multiple imputation is not always more EFFECTIVE than a complete case analysis (an efficacy claim undercutting it).
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader reads the chapter's closing recommendation as a warning that multiple imputation may be no better than complete case analysis, and may therefore skip multiple imputation, which is the opposite of the advice the English gives.

heading: Filter out rows with missing values / Lọc bỏ các hàng có giá trị bị thiếu
proposition: The English says you can drop rows with missingness in certain COLUMNS, matching the chunk `drop_na(date_onset)` which names a column; the Vietnamese says "trong một số hàng nhất định" (in certain ROWS).
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader is told the argument to `drop_na()` selects rows, so they may try to pass row identifiers or an index to `drop_na()` instead of column names, and the call will fail.

heading: Handling `NA` in `ggplot()` / Xử lý `NA` trong hàm `ggplot()`
proposition: The English says that where several columns contribute to values NOT being plotted, you must also filter on those columns to count the omitted records correctly; the Vietnamese clause boundary is misplaced so it states that if several columns contribute to the values, then the plot cannot be drawn.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader takes away a false limitation of `ggplot()` (that multi-column contributions prevent plotting) and misses the actual instruction, so the caption count of excluded records will be wrong.

heading: Types of missing data / Các loại số liệu bị thiếu
proposition: The English says that in practice MAR is more of a SPECTRUM ("In practice, this is more of a spectrum"); the Vietnamese renders this as "Trong thực tế, đây là loại nhiều hơn", which drops the spectrum concept entirely.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader does not learn that MAR is a matter of degree rather than a binary property, so they may treat predictability of missingness as all-or-nothing when choosing an imputation method.

heading: Multiple Imputation / Gán số liệu nhiều lần
proposition: The English limits the bias-reduction claim to MCAR and MANY MAR settings ("both MCAR and many MAR settings"); the Vietnamese drops the qualifier and claims it works for MCAR and MAR without restriction.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader may assume multiple imputation removes bias under every MAR mechanism and skip checking whether their particular missingness mechanism is one the method handles.

heading: Indexed data / Datos indexados
proposition: The English names the objective a rolling 7-day incidence; the Spanish names it 'incidencia acumulada de 7 dias' (cumulative 7-day incidence), which is the measure this same chapter defines as an expanding window set with '.before = Inf'.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader may equate the 7-day rolling sum with cumulative incidence and apply the expanding-window recipe ('.before = Inf') from the 'Ventana expansiva' subsection instead of '.before = days(6)', producing a running total rather than a 7-day window.

heading: Rolling by group / Rouler par groupe
proposition: The French page displays as visible body text the draft paragraph beginning "Vous pouvez regrouper les donnees avant d'utiliser une fonction slider... ci-dessus le delai moyen glissant entre l'apparition des symptomes et l'admission a l'hopital (colonne days_onset_hosp)"; in English the same paragraph is inside an HTML comment and is not rendered at all.
reader_consequence:
The French reader sees a stray, incomplete instruction about a rolling mean delay from symptom onset to admission on column days_onset_hosp, followed by literal markup (a leading

and a trailing -->). No code chunk or dataset in the chapter supports that calculation, so the reader tries to follow an instruction the chapter never carries out, and may believe the page is broken or that a step is missing.

heading: Calculate with **slider**
proposition: The translation glosses "rolling regressions" as 移動平均 (moving average). The English gives no gloss, and a rolling regression is not a moving average.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader learns a false definition: they will believe slider's regression functions compute moving averages, and will not understand that slider can fit a regression repeatedly over a sliding window.

heading: Calculate with **slider**
proposition: The translation glosses "rolling averages" as データの時期をずらして回帰する手法 (a method of regressing by shifting the data's time period). The English gives no gloss, and a rolling average is an average, not a regression.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader is told that the rolling average, which is the entire subject of this chapter, is a regression technique. That contradicts every subsequent example, all of which call sum() or mean().

heading: Calculate with **slider**
proposition: The translation glosses a "complete window" as 範囲を指定する必要のない場合 (the case where you do not need to specify a range). The English defines a complete window only as one where the full window of rows exists.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader misunderstands .complete = TRUE as being about whether the window extent must be given, rather than about suppressing calculations on partial windows at the start of the series. They may set it expecting the range arguments to become optional.

heading: Calculate with **slider**
proposition: The translation renders the English "centered" window as 中央値を基準としたウィンドウ, a window based on the median. The English says the window is centred on the current value, and says nothing about a median.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader believes setting .before and .after to the same number produces a median-based statistic, when it only positions the window symmetrically around the current row. They may expect median output from a mean or sum calculation.

heading: Rolling by group
proposition: The translation states that the error means something is masking **tsibble**'s slide(). The English states the opposite direction: **tsibble**'s slide() is masking **slider**'s slide().
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader troubleshooting the deprecation error is told the wrong package is being masked, so the recommended fix slider::slide_dbl() looks unrelated to the stated cause. They may instead try to namespace or detach tsibble and stay stuck.

heading: Calculate with **tidyquant** within `ggplot()`
proposition: The inline comment beside theme_minimal() in the translated chunk reads 移動平均の表示 (display the moving average). In the English the same comment reads "simple background", and theme_minimal() sets the plot theme, not the moving average.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader reading the annotated chunk attributes the moving-average line to theme_minimal() rather than to tidyquant::geom_ma(), and may drop theme_minimal() believing it removes the average, or keep it believing it draws one.

heading: Rolling by date / Скольжение по дате
proposition: The English sentence carries a working cross-reference to the Time series and outbreak detection page (time_series.qmd); the Russian sentence points at the bare same-page anchor #timeseries_moving, which does not exist in moving_average.ru.qmd.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader who wants the promised slide_dbl() demonstration clicks a link that goes nowhere on the current page, and never reaches the Time series and outbreak detection chapter where the example lives.

heading: Rolling by group / Скользящее по группе
proposition: The English points the reader to the Grouping data page with a link target (grouping.qmd); the Russian gives only the bracketed text [Группирование данных] with no target, so no link is produced.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader is told to see the Grouping data page for the grouping details this section depends on, but gets literal bracketed text instead of a link and must hunt for the chapter by hand.

heading: Calculate with tidyquant within ggplot() / Расчет с помощью tidyquant внутри ggplot()
proposition: The Russian states the daily counts are plotted as a grey line ('в виде серой линии'), while the English says only that the line is faded (alpha < 1) and the chunk beside it sets no colour, only alpha = 0.2 on the default black line.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader looking for the argument that makes the raw-count line grey finds none in the chunk, and may add a colour = "grey" argument that the English example never used.

heading: Calculate with **slider** / **slider** ile hesaplama
proposition: The R function that computes a mean is named `ortalama` (`Ortalama`), so a slider formula is written `~ .x - ortalama(.x)`.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader copies `~ .x - ortalama(.x)` into `.f = ` and gets 'could not find function "ortalama"'. The English names the real base R function `mean`, which is what slider needs.

heading: Calculate with **slider** / **slider** ile hesaplama
proposition: The value to give `.complete = ` so that only complete windows are calculated is written `DOĞRU`.
reader_consequence: A reader writes `.complete = DOĞRU` and the call fails, because R has no `DOĞRU` value. The same paragraph writes `FALSE` untranslated, so the reader cannot tell which spelling is the real R literal.

heading: Indexed data / İndekslenmiş veri
proposition: The window extent for `.before = ` / `.after = ` may be given in units of the lubridate function `month()`.
reader_consequence: A reader wanting a one-month rolling window writes `.before = month(1)`, which is the lubridate month-extraction function, not a period. The English names `months()`, the period constructor that actually sets a month-wide window.

heading: Calculate with **slider** / **slider** ile hesaplama
proposition: The `.i = ` argument creates a column with which to index the window progression.
reader_consequence: A reader understands slider as generating the index column itself, and does not realise that `.i = ` requires an existing column (here `date_hospitalisation`) to be supplied. The English says 'provide a column'.

heading: Indexed data / İndekslenmiş veri
proposition: The days absent from `daily_counts` are days on which no cases were detected.
reader_consequence: A reader takes the gaps to be gaps in case detection, when `daily_counts` counts `date_hospitalisation` and the English says no cases were admitted on those days. That mis-attributes the gaps to surveillance rather than to hospital admission.

heading: Rolling by group / Biến động theo nhóm
proposition: The English section heading carries the anchor id {#roll_slider_group}, which the Vietnamese heading omits, while the Vietnamese text at line 116 still links to (#roll_slider_group).
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader who follows the 'cuộn theo nhóm' link at line 116, offered as the pointer to the rolling-average example, lands nowhere: the target id does not exist in the translated page, so the reader never reaches the grouped rolling-average example the sentence promises.

heading: Troubleshooting common errors / Solución de errores comunes
proposition: The English says the fix (lettered-drive library listed first) worked when knitting on a LOCAL drive while on a networked internet connection; the Spanish says it works on a local NETWORK drive ("una unidad de red local") if the internet connection is established over the network.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader concludes the reordering fix is verified for files sitting on a network drive, so they keep knitting from the network drive and expect the Pandoc 1 error to clear. The English advice is the opposite: the file was on a local drive and only the internet connection was networked.

heading: Troubleshooting common errors / Dépannage des erreurs courantes
proposition: The English quotes the literal LaTeX error text a reader will see, '! Package pdftex.def Error: File '...' not found: using draft setting.'; the French presents it as half-translated output, '! Paquet pdftex.def Erreur : File '...' non trouvé : utilisation de la fonction brouillon.', which pdftex never emits (it is English-only, and 'draft setting' is an option, not a 'fonction brouillon').
reader_consequence: A French reader matching the error in their console or .log file against the handbook string finds no match, and a web search for 'Paquet pdftex.def Erreur' returns nothing, so they cannot confirm they have this error.

heading: Troubleshooting common errors / Dépannage des erreurs courantes
proposition: The English says the Pandoc Error 83 message looks like `can't find file...rmarkdown...lua...`; the French says it looks like `Impossible de trouver le fichier...rmarkdown...lua...`, but Pandoc emits this message only in English.
reader_consequence: A French reader will not recognise the English message Pandoc actually prints as the error described here, so they skip the correct diagnosis section for error 83.

heading: Troubleshooting common errors / Dépannage des erreurs courantes
proposition: The English quotes the literal Pandoc failure text `Error: pandoc document conversion failed with error 61`; the French quotes `Erreur : la conversion du document pandoc a échoué avec l'erreur 61`, a message Pandoc/rmarkdown does not produce.
reader_consequence: A French reader cannot match the console output to this section, and searching the quoted French string online returns nothing, so the fix for error 61 is harder to reach.

heading: Useful commands / Commandes utiles
proposition: In English 'Useful commands' is a level-2 section, a sibling of 'Overview', 'RStudio as administrator' and 'Troubleshooting common errors'; in French 'Commandes utiles' is level 3, so it becomes a subsection of 'RStudio en tant qu'administrateur'.
reader_consequence: The French table of contents nests the diagnostic commands under the run-as-administrator topic, so a reader scanning the chapter outline for library-path and Pandoc commands does not see them as a top-level topic.

heading: Troubleshooting common errors / よくあるエラー
proposition: The English tells the reader to select the 32-bit version of R from inside RStudio via Tools/Global Options (confirmed by the next bullet, which says to re-install R with a different bit version). The Japanese says to try 32-bit RStudio and that Tools/Global Options lets you switch to 32-bit RStudio ('32-bit 版の RStudio を試してみてください。RStudio の Tools/Global Options から 32-bit 版の R Studioに切り替えることができます。'), which is a different program and is contradicted by the Japanese line 94 itself, which places the setting under R Sessions / R version.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader searches Tools/Global Options for a way to switch RStudio's own bitness, finds none (RStudio has no such setting), and may go looking for a 32-bit RStudio download instead of switching the R version, so the documented fix for 'internet routines cannot be loaded' is never applied.

heading: Troubleshooting common errors / よくあるエラー
proposition: The English places 'This PC' in the right hand pane of the Windows file manager ('right click on "This PC" on the right hand pane'). The Japanese places it in the left pane ('左パネルにある「PC」を右クリックし').
reader_consequence: The two versions of the handbook give opposite locations for the same click target, so a reader comparing them, or an editor reconciling them, cannot tell which pane is meant; only one of the two step descriptions can match the interface the reader sees.

heading: Troubleshooting common errors / よくあるエラー
proposition: The Japanese names a specific menu path for where the 32-bit option appears, 'Tools/Global Options の R Sessions/R version'. The English says only 'if 32-bit version does not appear in menu', naming no submenu.
reader_consequence: The reader is sent to a named submenu that the English source never states, so if that submenu name is wrong or has changed in the reader's RStudio version, the reader concludes the option is absent and wrongly diagnoses their RStudio as v1.2.

heading: Troubleshooting common errors
proposition: The English sub-heading says the C: LIBRARY does not appear as an option in the manual package-install dialogue; the Portuguese says the PACKAGE ("o pacote") does not appear.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader scanning the troubleshooting list for the symptom "my C: library is missing from the install drop-down" will not recognise this entry, and may instead believe the problem is a missing package, so they never apply the administrator-mode fix that follows.

heading: Troubleshooting common errors
proposition: The English says to right-click "This PC" in the RIGHT hand pane of the Windows file manager; the Portuguese says the LEFT pane ("no painel a esquerda").
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader following the mapped-drive procedure looks in the wrong pane of Windows Explorer for "This PC" and may conclude the entry is absent.

heading: Troubleshooting common errors
proposition: The Portuguese adds the hedge "(ou direita, dependendo da sua configuracao)" - that the pane position depends on the reader's configuration - which the English does not state.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader is told the interface location is configuration-dependent, which makes the step less definite than the English and gives no way to tell which case applies.

heading: Troubleshooting common errors
proposition: Setting RStudio to always run as administrator is advantageous when working from an Rproject, because you then open the project file rather than clicking the RStudio icon.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader is told to right-click the icon but is never told WHY a permanent administrator setting is needed. An Rproject user, who never clicks the RStudio icon, will right-click once, get an elevated session that day, and not understand why the C: library option disappears again the next time they open the project from the .Rproj file.

heading: Troubleshooting common errors
proposition: The instructions for installing TinyTex are on the R basics page, linked at basics.qmd.
reader_consequence: The Turkish text writes the reference as a bare bracketed label with no link target, so it renders as literal text '[R temelleri]' rather than a hyperlink. A reader who needs the TinyTex installation instructions has no way to reach the page from here and must search the handbook manually.

heading: Troubleshooting common errors
proposition: The literal R error text is 'Error in tools::startDynamicHelp() : internet routines cannot be loaded'.
reader_consequence: The Turkish version renders the quoted error literal as 'internet rutinleri yuklenemiyor', a string R never emits. A reader matching the message in their console against the handbook, or pasting it into a search engine to find the same fix, will not match this section.

heading: RStudio as administrator / RStudio với tư cách quản trị viên
proposition: English: the click that opens RStudio must itself be a right-click ('When you click the RStudio icon to open RStudio, do so with a right-click'). Vietnamese: click the icon to open RStudio, and then right-click ('Bạn cần nhấp vào biểu tượng RStudio để mở RStudio, sau đó bấm chuột phải').
reader_consequence: The Vietnamese reader launches RStudio normally as a non-administrator, then right-clicks with nothing useful to right-click on. The 'Run as Administrator' context menu never appears, so the reader cannot carry out the very first overarching principle of the chapter (principle 1, get administrator access).

heading: Troubleshooting common errors / Khắc phục các lỗi thường gặp (Pandoc Error 83)
proposition: English: R may be unable to find the file of the **rmarkdown** package itself, so check which library the **rmarkdown** package lives in. Vietnamese: R may be unable to find 'các package sử dụng trong file **rmarkdown**' (the packages used inside the rmarkdown file), so check which library 'package trong **rmarkdown**' (the package inside rmarkdown) is stored in.
reader_consequence: The Vietnamese reader diagnoses Pandoc Error 83 by auditing the packages their .Rmd document loads, instead of locating the rmarkdown package itself with find.package('rmarkdown'). They never find the inaccessible '\\\' library holding rmarkdown, so they never apply the fix the same paragraph goes on to describe (moving rmarkdown to a C: library).

heading: Overview / Tổng quan
proposition: English: save packages to a library on a 'lettered drive' (any drive addressed by a letter). Vietnamese: save packages to a library on an 'ổ cứng vật lý' (a physical hard drive).
reader_consequence: A mapped network drive is lettered but not physical. The Vietnamese overarching principle therefore excludes exactly the workaround the chapter recommends later under 'Định vị các ổ đĩa mạng' (map the network location to a lettered drive and use the drive-letter path), so a reader with no local disk available concludes the principle cannot be satisfied.

heading: Troubleshooting common errors / Khắc phục các lỗi thường gặp (Pandoc 1 error)
proposition: English states the fix is one of ORDERING: of the multiple library locations, have the lettered-drive one 'listed first'. The Vietnamese omits 'listed first' and instructs the reader only to 'chọn' (choose/pick) a location beginning with a letter.
reader_consequence: The Vietnamese reader does not learn that the remedy is to reorder .libPaths() so the lettered library comes first, which is precisely what the 'Switch order of libraries' chunk the bullet cross-references does. They treat it as a one-off choice of install target and leave the '\\\' library still ahead in the search order, so pandoc error 1 recurs.

heading: Packages from CRAN / Paquets disponibles sur le CRAN
proposition: The French p_load() call ends with a trailing comma after treeio, so the argument list contains one empty argument that the English call does not have.
reader_consequence: A French reader who copies the chapter's headline code block, as the surrounding prose instructs, gets 'Failed with error: invalid package name' and a 'Failed to install/load' warning from pacman. The chapter's single actionable deliverable does not run.

heading: Packages from CRAN / Paquets disponibles sur le CRAN
proposition: The French block installs and loads patchwork as an active argument, while the English block lists it only as a commented-out alternative to cowplot.
reader_consequence: A French reader installs a package the English reader does not, and loses the English signal that cowplot and patchwork are alternatives from which one is chosen, not two packages both required.

heading: Suggested packages / 推奨パッケージ
proposition: The Japanese states that the pacman and masking material is in numbered section '3.7 Packages' of the R basics chapter; the English only says 'the [R basics] section on packages' and gives no section number.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader navigates to a hard-coded section number instead of the named section. The number is a stale-prone hard reference: R basics currently has Packages as its seventh numbered section, but any added or removed section, or a change in chapter order, silently sends the reader to the wrong place, and the English text carries no such number to keep it in sync.

heading: Suggested packages / Pacotes sugeridos
proposition: The English says sub-packages are marked in the code by an INDENT plus a hash; the Portuguese says they are marked by a 'travessao' (a dash) plus a hashtag, and no dash marker exists in the code chunk.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader scans the pacman::p_load() block for a dash character to identify packages bundled inside another package. No dash is present, so the reader cannot apply the rule and may fail to see that the indented commented lines (#dplyr, #ggplot2, ...) are the bundled packages.

heading: Packages from Github / Пакеты с Github
proposition: The English states the chunk below installs exactly TWO packages from Github ('commands to install two packages'); the Russian drops the cardinality and says only 'commands to install packages from Github repositories'.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader loses the explicit count that tells them the following chunk is complete at two install calls, so they cannot tell from the sentence alone whether the two bullets below enumerate the whole set or only examples of a longer Github list.

heading: Packages from Github
proposition: The English says the development version of epicontacts can draw transmission trees on a temporal (time-based) x-axis; the Vietnamese says 'truc x tam thoi', which means a temporary or provisional x-axis, not a time axis. The code comment in the chunk immediately below (line 162, identical in both files) states 'for transmission chains with a time x-axis', which the Vietnamese prose contradicts.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader learns the wrong reason to install the development version of epicontacts. They understand the feature as some kind of provisional or placeholder axis rather than as plotting transmission chains against calendar time, so they will not reach for this package when they need a time-scaled transmission tree.

heading: ### Rotating nodes in a tree
proposition: English says rotating node 37 moves the samples of node 38 to the top; the Spanish says they move to the bottom ("se muevan hacia abajo").
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader compares the printed 'Rotated Node 37' plot with the text, sees node 38 at the top, and concludes either that ggtree::rotate() failed or that they picked the wrong node.

heading: ### Import data
proposition: English says read.tree() returns a list object OF CLASS "phylo"; the Spanish says the object is NAMED "phylo" ("un objeto tipo lista llamado \"phylo\""), which the adjacent chunk contradicts because the object is named tree.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader looks for an object called phylo, does not find one, and loses the class name that later functions (tree_subset, ggtree) actually dispatch on.

heading: ### Import data
