proposition: The example Newick string is given with decimal points in English ("((t2:0.04,t1:0.34):0.89,...)") but with decimal commas in Spanish ("((t2:0,04,t1:0,34):0,89,...)"), so the Spanish example is not a valid Newick string.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader takes the shown string as the Newick standard and writes or edits a .nwk file with decimal commas, which ape::read.tree() cannot parse because the comma is the Newick node separator.

heading: ## More complex trees: adding heatmaps of sample data
proposition: The Spanish states that the extra colour layer represents the genes conferring antimicrobial resistance ("otra capa de colores representando los genes que confieren resistencia antimicrobiana"); the English says only "another color scheme layer".
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader may expect the new colour scale itself to encode resistance genes, when new_scale_fill() only frees the fill aesthetic and the gene variable is supplied by the following gheatmap() call.

heading: Overview / Aperçu
proposition: The English names the second family of tree-building methods 'character-based methods'; the French renames that family 'les methodes probabiliste' (probabilistic methods).
reader_consequence: A French reader learns the wrong name for the standard opposing category to distance-based methods, and will not find 'methodes fondees sur les caracteres' in the phylogenetics literature. It also wrongly implies the defining property of that family is being probabilistic, when maximum parsimony is character-based and not probabilistic.

heading: Rotating nodes in a tree / Rotation des noeuds dans un arbre
proposition: The English chunk comment says the second geom_hilight() highlights node 37 in yellow; the French comment says it highlights node 39 in yellow, while the argument on the next line is node = 37.
reader_consequence: A French reader is told nodes 39 and 37 are both highlighted as node 39, so the two highlighted clades cannot be told apart. The following text rotates node 37 and flips nodes 39 and 37, and the reader cannot map either operation onto the coloured blocks in the figure.

heading: Subsetting a tree / 系統樹の分割（サブセット）
proposition: The English states that we first inspect the tree's nodes and tip labels in order to decide what to subset; the Japanese has no counterpart sentence and leaves the position blank.
reader_consequence: The Japanese reader meets the large node-labelled circular tree chunk with no stated purpose. They are not told it exists so they can read off a node number, so the node 528 used in the very next chunk appears to come from nowhere and they cannot repeat the step on their own tree.

heading: Clean and inspect
proposition: The Portuguese prose names the data frame "Sample_data" (capital S), while the code chunk immediately below it, and the English prose, name it `sample_data`.
reader_consequence: R is case-sensitive, so a Portuguese reader who follows the prose and types colnames(Sample_data) gets "object 'Sample_data' not found" and may believe the import step failed.

heading: More complex trees: adding heatmaps of sample data
proposition: The English says the data preparation step SUBSETS the sample_data data frame down to the one desired variable; the Russian says the desired variable is SUBSTITUTED INTO the data frame (мы подставляем в наш датафрейм нужную переменную), which reverses the direction of the operation and contradicts the code chunk beside it.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader is told to add a column to the existing sample_data frame, so the following chunks (which build separate one-column frames such as gender, cipR and MIC_Cip, each with Sample_ID as row names) read as unexplained. The reader can then pass the full sample_data to gheatmap() and get a heatmap of every column instead of the single variable, and the immediately following sentence about setting Sample_ID as row names loses its reason to exist.

heading: Example subtree with sample data annotation
proposition: The English says the annotation adds the YEAR of strain isolation to the tips; the Turkish says only 'suş izolasyonunun yani sira' (besides strain isolation) and drops the year.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader is not told that the blue tip labels produced by geom_tiplab(aes(label = Year)) in the chunk beside this text are isolation years, so they cannot read that column of the figure or reproduce the annotation on their own data.

heading: Clean and inspect
proposition: The English states the membership check runs in both directions ('and vice versa'): samples present in the tree file, and tree tip labels present in sample_data. The Turkish states only that all samples are present in the tree file.
reader_consequence: The chunk beside the text contains two lines, one per direction. A Turkish reader has no description for the second line, tree$tip.label %in% sample_data$Sample_ID, and may not check that every tip on the tree has sample data.

heading: Overview
proposition: The English hedges: portable sequencing devices 'hold promises to' make data available in real time. The Turkish asserts they do make it available ('kullanilabilir hale getirir'), with no hedge.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader takes real-time sequencing support for outbreak investigation as established practice rather than a stated prospect, which overstates what portable devices deliver today.

heading: Example subtree with sample data annotation
proposition: English says the cluster of cases at node 39 shows clonal expansion (growth of a single lineage); the Vietnamese says the cluster involves 'nhan ban vo tinh', which is the Vietnamese term for cloning / asexual reproduction, not clonal expansion.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader takes the node-39 cluster to be about cloning as a laboratory or reproductive process, and misses that the subtree is being read as one bacterial lineage expanding across 2017 and 2018, which is the reason the subsequent travel-history and country annotation is informative.

heading: ### Pivoting data of multiple classes
proposition: The English says the shared column-name structure ends in either "status" or "date"; the Spanish says it ends in either "estado" or "fecha", but the columns in the adjacent chunk are obs1_date/obs1_status/obs2_date/... and contain no Spanish suffix.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader inspecting df or its output looks for name parts "estado" and "fecha", finds neither, and cannot verify how names_sep = "_" plus ".value" produces the date and status columns that the next chunk creates.

heading: fill()
proposition: The French prose names the function to apply as `pivot_larger()`, while the chunk immediately below calls `pivot_wider()` and the English names no function at all.
reader_consequence: A French reader looks for a function called pivot_larger(), which does not exist in tidyr; typing it returns 'could not find function "pivot_larger"' and the reader cannot connect the sentence to the pivot_wider() call in the chunk.

heading: Pivoting data of multiple classes
proposition: The English says the special term ".value" makes the pivoted columns split on a CHARACTER in their name; the French says they are split on the basis of a WORD ("un mot") in the column name.
reader_consequence: A French reader concludes names_sep takes a word rather than a single separator character, and may pass "date"/"status" or a multi-character token to names_sep = instead of the underscore, producing a failed or wrongly-named pivot.

heading: Pivoting data of multiple classes
proposition: The English states that after the naive pivot the utility of the dates is lost; the French states only that the function converts the whole column to character and omits the consequence for the dates.
reader_consequence: A French reader sees the class coercion as a cosmetic type change and misses the reason the whole section exists: date arithmetic, sorting and date-scaled plotting no longer work on that column.

heading: Wide format
proposition: The French adds that the count columns comprise one column per age class plus one column for the day's total in that facility, and concludes that the case-count information therefore sits across several columns rather than one, 'hence the so-called wide structure'; the English segment states none of this.
reader_consequence: None harmful: the added definition is correct for this dataset, but the French reader meets the totals column and the definition of 'wide' one paragraph earlier than the English reader, so the two texts diverge in what has been established at this point.

heading: Wide format
proposition: The English hedges that wide format 'may be useful for presentation' and 'is not ideal for SOME TYPES of analysis'; the French asserts that it is useful for data entry and presentation and is not appropriate for MANY analyses ('de nombreuses analyses').
reader_consequence: A French reader takes a stronger prohibition on wide data than the English gives, and may pivot data that would have been fine to analyse as-is.

heading: Standard pivoting
proposition: The English says the resulting plot is a STACKED bar chart; the French says only 'un diagramme en batons' (a bar chart) and drops 'stacked'.
reader_consequence: A French reader is not told that fill = age_group stacks the age groups within each bar, which is the exact property that makes the doubled bar height in the next paragraph visible and explicable.

heading: Standard pivoting
proposition: The English says the totals are filtered OUT of the dataset before it is passed to ggplot(); the Japanese says the totals are 抽出する (extracted/selected) from the dataset, which describes keeping them, the opposite of the adjacent chunk's filter(age_group != "malaria_tot").
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader reads the code as selecting only the malaria_tot rows and so cannot reconcile the prose with the resulting plot, and may write filter(age_group == "malaria_tot") when applying the pattern to their own surveillance data, reproducing the double-counting the section exists to fix.

heading: Pivoting data of multiple classes
proposition: The English says various approaches exist to separate out the mess AFTER mixed classes have been merged into one column; the Japanese says various approaches exist to AVOID such a mess (このような混乱を回避するためには様々なアプローチがあります).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader is told prevention has many routes and is not told that remedies exist once a mixed-class column has already been produced, so on inheriting data that is already merged they do not know that recovery is possible; the sentence also becomes redundant with the clause that follows it about avoiding the situation with pivot_longer().

heading: Formato "Largo" (wide) / "Wide" format
proposition: The English says that in wide format the information for every age group on a given facility-day is stored in a single ROW; the Portuguese says it is stored in a single COLUMN ("estao armazenadas em apenas uma coluna").
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader is told the defining property of wide format backwards at the exact point the chapter defines it. Wide format means one row per facility-day spread across several count columns, so a reader who takes 'apenas uma coluna' at face value cannot see why pivot_longer() is needed, and the sentence also contradicts the same paragraph's earlier statement that each row represents a facility-day and that the counts occupy the right-most columns (plural).

heading: Formato "Largo" (wide) / "Wide" format
proposition: The English says the dataset provides age-specific counts in each of THREE age groups; the Portuguese says FOUR ("em cada um dos quatro grupos") while listing only the same three (<4 anos, 5-14 anos, 15 anos ou mais).
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader is given a count that contradicts the list beside it and the data itself: count_data has three age columns (malaria_rdt_0-4, malaria_rdt_5-14, malaria_rdt_15) plus a separate total column. A reader who believes there are four age groups will mistake malaria_tot for a fourth age group, which is precisely the error the later 'what has gone wrong?' section teaches them to avoid, and will expect four age categories in the pivoted age_group column.

heading: Wide format / "Широкий" формат
proposition: The English says the actual case counts are held in the right-most columnS (plural, the four malaria_ columns); the Russian says they are held in "в самом правом столбце", the single right-most column.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader looks for one column of counts and misses that four separate count columns are exactly what makes this table "wide", which is the fact the whole pivot_longer() example is built on.

heading: Data / Данные (Long-to-wide)
proposition: The sentence introducing the linelist preview, "Here are the first 50 rows:", is never rendered in Russian; line 374 of the translation is the untranslated English string.
reader_consequence: A Russian-only reader gets no Russian caption for the table that follows and can miss that the display is truncated to the first 50 rows, so they may read the widget as the whole linelist.

heading: Wide format / "Geniş" format
proposition: English: the column headers represent VALUES of a hypothetical "age group" variable. Turkish: the column headers represent the hypothetical "age group" VARIABLE itself ("bunlar hipotetik bir 'yaş grubu' *değişkenini* temsil eder").
reader_consequence: The Turkish sentence contradicts itself: it first says the headers do not represent variables, then says they represent a variable. The reader loses the central tidy-data argument for why this table must be pivoted, and may conclude the wide layout is already tidy.

heading: Wide format / "Geniş" format
proposition: English: the DATES of the observations range from count_data$data_date min() to max(). Turkish: "bu sayı" (this number/count) varies between count_data$data_date min() and max(), attaching the range to the malaria counts rather than to the dates.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader takes the min/max of the date column as the range of the case counts, and so misreads what the 3,038 rows span. They lose the fact that the dataset covers a fixed date window across the 65 facilities.

heading: Pivot wider / Daha geniş olarak pivotlama
proposition: The Turkish prose names the argument `name_from`; the chunk beside it (pivoting.tr.qmd:394-401) uses `names_from = gender`. There is no `name_from` argument in pivot_wider().
reader_consequence: A reader who types `name_from` gets an error, or silently passes an unmatched argument, and cannot reproduce table_wide.

heading: Pivoting data of multiple classes / Birden çok sınıfa ait verinin pivotlanması
proposition: The Turkish prose names the argument `name_sep`; the chunk beside it (pivoting.tr.qmd:295-307) uses `names_sep = "_"`. There is no `name_sep` argument in pivot_longer().
reader_consequence: A reader following the two-bullet instruction writes `name_sep = "_"`, the split on the underscore never happens, and the ".value" mechanism the whole section teaches fails.

heading: Standard pivoting
proposition: The Turkish prose names the tidyselect helper `start_with()`; the chunk beside it (pivoting.tr.qmd:164-170) uses `starts_with("malaria_")`. There is no `start_with()` function in tidyselect.
reader_consequence: A reader who copies `start_with("malaria_")` from the prose gets "could not find function" and cannot select the four malaria columns by prefix.

heading: Pivot wider / Daha geniş olarak pivotlama
proposition: English states that the columns given to `id_cols = ` "will thus identify each row". The Turkish sentence ends without this purpose clause, and instead garbles it into "döndürülmemesi gereken satırları içeren sütun adları vektörü" (a vector of column names containing the rows that should not be pivoted).
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader is not told what id_cols is FOR, namely that the named columns become the row identifiers of the wide table. They cannot decide which columns to pass, which is exactly the choice the N.B. at the end of the Fill section asks them to make.

heading: Standard pivoting
proposition: English says mapping age_group to `fill = ` produces a STACKED bar chart ("a stacked bar chart, by age group"). The Turkish says only "çubuk grafikte" (in a bar chart), dropping "stacked".
reader_consequence: The reader is not told that the bars stack, so the double-height artefact discussed two segments later (malaria_tot added on top of the three age groups) is harder to connect to the mapping just made.

heading: Fill > `fill()`
proposition: The translation calls the filled dataset a 'clean/tidy' dataset ('một bộ dữ liệu sạch để vẽ biểu đồ'); the English says only that it is a 'useful dataset for plotting' and, two paragraphs later, calls the same object 'this long, untidy dataframe'.
reader_consequence: The Vietnamese reader is told at line 476 that the data are already tidy ('sạch'), then at line 484 that the same object is 'dọc-chưa làm sạch' (long, not cleaned). The contradiction obscures the point of the following `pivot_wider()` exercise, which exists precisely because the data are not yet in the tidy/presentable shape.

heading: Wide-to-long > Pivoting data of multiple classes
proposition: The English quotation opens with the simile 'Like families,' ('Like families, tidy datasets are all alike but every messy dataset is messy in its own way'); the translation drops the simile and starts the quotation at 'Các bộ dữ liệu sạch đều giống nhau...'.
reader_consequence: The same sentence still credits the line to Tolstoy ('trích dẫn từ Tolstoy'), but the family analogy that makes the Anna Karenina allusion recognisable is gone, so the attribution has nothing to attach to and the reader cannot see why Tolstoy is named.

heading: Wide-to-long > Pivoting data of multiple classes
proposition: The English states that mixing variable types in a single column is 'a very big no-no when it comes to data management and tidy data', i.e. a strongly discouraged practice; the translation renders this as 'một sự ngỡ ngàng vô định' ('a boundless bewilderment'), which carries no prohibition.
reader_consequence: The Vietnamese reader loses the explicit normative warning that a mixed-class column violates data-management and tidy-data practice, and may treat the mixed `value` column produced by the plain pivot as merely surprising rather than as an error to avoid.

heading: R projects
proposition: An R project folder is portable.
reader_consequence: The Spanish reader learns only that the folder gathers all related files and is easier to manage. The reader misses that the whole project folder can be moved or shared to another machine and still run, which is the main practical reason to use a project with relative filepaths.

heading: Version control
proposition: The 'Find in Files' tool searches and replaces strings, not whole script lines.
reader_consequence: The Spanish text says the tool replaces 'lineas de script' across files. A reader expects a line-level replacement tool and may not use it for the common task of renaming a variable or a string fragment across a project.

heading: Examples
proposition: ggsave() with no plot argument saves the most recently PRINTED (displayed) plot, not the most recently created one.
reader_consequence: A reader who builds a plot object without printing it, then calls ggsave(here(...)), expects that object to be written. Instead the previously displayed plot is written, or an error occurs, and the reader cannot see why from the surrounding text.

heading: Organization / プロジェクト内の整理
proposition: The English suggests a "presentations" subfolder as one of the example project subfolders; the Japanese folder list (データ / スクリプト / 図や出力結果) omits it.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader setting up a project structure never sees the suggestion to keep a dedicated folder for presentations, so their recommended folder layout is narrower than the English one.

heading: Settings / 初期設定
proposition: The Japanese instructs the reader to set the "Restore .RData into workspace at startup" and "Save workspace to .RData on exit" controls to the value "No"; the English only says to set RStudio to not restore and not save, naming no control value.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader is told a specific UI value that the English never states. If the RStudio version in front of them offers checkboxes or a different option set rather than a Yes/No dropdown, the instruction does not match what they see.

heading: Examples / Exemplos
proposition: The Portuguese caption names the outer folder "saidas", but the ggsave() call in the chunk beside it writes to here("outputs", "epicurves", ...), so the folder the prose names does not exist in the code.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader following the caption creates or looks for a folder named "saidas" and the ggsave() call fails, or the reader cannot find the saved PNG. The mismatch is sharper because the same sentence and the two preceding examples leave the other path components ("epicurves", "data", "clean") untranslated to match the code.

heading: Suggested use / Önerilen kullanım
proposition: The English says the here package is for RELATIVE filepaths; the Turkish says it is for ALTERNATIVE filepaths ("Alternatif dosya yolakları için here paketi"), which the English does not support.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader meets the here package labelled as providing some unspecified 'alternative' kind of path rather than a path relative to the project root, so the one-line summary of what here is for no longer names its defining property, and the reader must recover it from the sub-bullet.

heading: Examples / Các ví dụ
proposition: The Vietnamese sentence carries the untranslated English fragment "from within an R projct." immediately before its Vietnamese rendering "bên trong một dự án R", so the same clause appears twice, once in raw English including the source typo "projct".
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader meets a broken sentence with an English fragment and a duplicated clause, and may read "projct" as a distinct technical term rather than a typo for "project".

heading: R projects / Dự án R
proposition: The English says the project folder is portable; the Vietnamese says only that it is self-contained ("khép kín") and drops portability.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader misses one of the two stated motivations for R projects, that the whole folder can be moved or shared between machines, and may not expect the project to run elsewhere unchanged.

heading: Creating an R project / Tạo một dự án R
proposition: The English states the .Rproj file is likely the primary way you will open your project; the Vietnamese states only that the file can act as a shortcut for opening it.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader does not learn that double-clicking the .Rproj file is the recommended default route into a project, and may keep using the File menu route instead.

heading: Cargar paquetes / Paquetes easystats
proposition: The package loaded for the alternative forest-plot output is named `see`; the Spanish package-loading chunk loads `ver` instead, while the Spanish prose in the easystats section (chapters/regression.es.qmd:664) still names the **see** package.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader who runs the setup chunk gets an installation/loading failure, because no CRAN package is called `ver`. If they skip past the error, the easystats forest plot at the end of the chapter has no `see` package loaded and its printed prose refers to a package the chapter never loads.

heading: Drop rows with missing values / Supprimer les lignes avec des valeurs manquantes
proposition: The English instructs the reader to make sure the explanatory_vars vector INCLUDES the age column; the French says the vector EXCLUDES ('exlu') the age column.
reader_consequence: A French reader is told to keep age out of explanatory_vars, which is the opposite of what the code chunk immediately below does (it appends 'age_cat' to explanatory_vars). The reader either omits the step or drops the age category from every later univariate and multivariable model, so the age results and the counts table never appear.

heading: Logistic regression / Régression logistique
proposition: The English gives the glm() argument as family = "binomial" (and family = "poisson"); the French prose gives it as famille = "binomiale" (and famille = "poisson"), an argument name and value that do not exist in R and appear nowhere in the surrounding code chunks, which all use family = "binomial".
reader_consequence: A French reader who copies the argument from the prose writes famille = "binomiale" and glm() fails with an unused-argument error, or silently fits the wrong family. The prose also contradicts every code chunk on the page.

heading: Logistic regression / Régression logistique
proposition: The English family/link table names the link argument as link = (for example `(link = "logit")`); the French table renames it to lien = in seven of the eight rows, although the paragraph just above it (French line 218) still gives the correct syntax family = familytype(link = "linkfunction")).
reader_consequence: A French reader who copies a link specification from the table writes lien = "logit", which R rejects, and the table also contradicts the syntax given two lines earlier in the same section.

heading: Univariate and multivariable regression
proposition: The linked editorial on multivariable versus multivariate is attributed to the journal of the American Public Health Association; the English names no journal.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader takes a source attribution as coming from the handbook when the English never states which journal published the editorial.

heading: Linear regression
proposition: The Japanese prose names the broom function as `argument()`; the code chunk beside it calls `augment(lm_results)`, as the English prose states.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader who types `argument()` gets 'could not find function' and cannot reproduce the fitted-line data frame.

heading: Logistic regression
proposition: The family table gives the default link for `"binomial"` as `(link = "logit` (unterminated); the English gives `(link = "logit")`.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader copying the binomial link syntax writes an unterminated string, and the malformed cell also breaks the rendered table row.

heading: Univariate `glm()`
proposition: The Japanese says the estimates printed by `summary(model)` are log odds RATIOS; the English says they are log odds.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader reads the intercept row as a log odds ratio, when it is the log odds of the outcome in the baseline age category.

heading: Printing results
proposition: The Japanese states that `bind_cols()` requires the two data frames to have the same NUMBER of rows; the English states the rows must be aligned (in matching order).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader checks only that row counts match and column-binds counts to model estimates that are in a different order, producing a silently wrong results table.

heading: **ggplot2** package
proposition: The English illustrates alpha-numeric ordering with the concrete case that "30" would appear before "5"; the Japanese drops this example.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader is told the default order is unsuitable but not why, so cannot recognise the same problem in other categorical axes.

heading: Univariate and multivariable regression
proposition: The English lists odds ratios as one of the association measures the chapter produces; the Portuguese list names only relative risks, risk relations and hazard ratios, and never mentions odds ratios.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader starts the chapter expecting relative risks, when every worked example in it estimates odds ratios from logistic regression, and so misreads the exponentiated coefficients as risk ratios.

heading: Logistic regression
proposition: The English says glm() is used to get odds ratios; the Portuguese says it is used to obtain probabilities ('para obter probabilidades').
reader_consequence: The reader takes the exponentiated glm() output as a probability, which it is not, and reports values above 1 as probabilities.

heading: Univariate glm()
proposition: The English says the estimates glm() prints are log odds; the Portuguese says they are log probabilities ('probabilidades em log').
reader_consequence: The reader exponentiates the summary() coefficients and believes the result is a probability rather than an odds ratio.

heading: Printing results
proposition: The English step 1 says tidy(exponentiate = TRUE) returns exponentiated log odds ratio estimates; the Portuguese says it returns log probabilities in exponential form.
reader_consequence: The reader labels the estimate column of the printed table as a probability, so the combined counts-plus-model table is captioned with the wrong measure.

heading: Looping multiple univariate models
proposition: The English says the loop produces univariate odds ratios; the Portuguese says it produces univariate probabilities ('probabilidades univariadas').
reader_consequence: The reader misnames every estimate in the looped univariate results table as a probability instead of an odds ratio.

heading: Building the model
proposition: The English says lrtest() from lmtest compares models with likelihood-ratio tests; the Portuguese calls them 'testes de probabilidade' (probability tests), not likelihood-ratio tests.
reader_consequence: The reader cannot connect lrtest() to the likelihood-ratio test named in the note about anova(model1, model2, test = 'Chisq'), nor look the method up under its real name.

heading: Building the model
proposition: The English says tidy() exponentiates the log odds and the confidence intervals; the Portuguese says it exponentiates log probabilities ('probabilidades em log').
reader_consequence: The reader interprets the final multivariable table mv_tab_base as holding probabilities, so the forest plot built from it is read against a probability scale rather than an odds-ratio scale.

heading: Logistic regression
proposition: The Portuguese calls the poisson family a log-linear model ('o modelo log-linear de poisson'); the English says only 'for poisson use family = "poisson"'.
reader_consequence: The reader is given a model characterisation the English text does not make and the chapter never supports or uses.

heading: Logistic regression
proposition: The English table lists the literal R values accepted by the glm() argument family = ("binomial", "gaussian", "Gamma", "inverse.gaussian", "poisson", "quasi", "quasibinomial", "quasipoisson"); the Russian table replaces every one of them with a Russian word inside the same quoted code span ("биномиальное", "гауссово", "гамма", "обратное гауссово", "пуассона", "квази", "квазибиномиальное", "квазипуассона"), which are not values glm() accepts.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader who copies a value out of this table writes family = "биномиальное" and glm() fails; the table also contradicts the bullet three lines above it (line 210), which correctly keeps family = "binomial" and family = "poisson", so the reader has no way to tell which spelling is real.

heading: Linear regression
proposition: English glosses the coefficient column of summary() output as "(Estimates)"; the Russian text glosses it as "(возможные значения)" ("possible values"), which is not what the Estimate column of summary(lm_results) reports.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader is told the summary() table shows possible values rather than estimated coefficients, and cannot map the sentence onto the Estimate column that the chunk on the next line actually prints.

heading: Looping multiple univariate models
proposition: English says the iteration applies one user-defined function ("We iterate through a user-defined function"); the Russian says the iteration runs over several different user-defined functions ("Мы проводим итерацию по разным определенным пользователям функциям"), while the chunk beside it passes a single anonymous function to map(.f = ~{...}).
reader_consequence: A Russian reader expects map() to cycle over a set of different functions and looks for them in the code, when the loop varies the explanatory variable and applies one function throughout.

heading: Univariate and multivariable regression
proposition: The English note contrasts two different terms, *multivariable* (several explanatory variables) with *multivariate* (several outcomes); the Turkish renders both as the single term *cok degiskenli*, so it asserts that a *cok degiskenli* model is a regression with several outcomes immediately after defining *cok degiskenli* as a regression with several explanatory variables.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader gets a self-contradictory definition and cannot learn the terminological distinction the note exists to teach; they may conclude the whole chapter is about models with several outcomes.

heading: Convert to 1's and 0's
proposition: The English names the recoding function `case_when()` (which is what the adjacent chunk calls); the Turkish names it `case_while()` twice, a function that does not exist in dplyr.
reader_consequence: A reader who types `case_while()` gets 'could not find function' and cannot map the prose onto the code chunk directly below it; searching dplyr documentation for case_while returns nothing.

heading: Convert to 1's and 0's
proposition: The English note says the '.' represents the column being processed by `across()`; the Turkish says it is processed by `cross()`, which is not the function in the chunk beside it.
reader_consequence: The reader cannot connect the '.' placeholder to `across()` in the chunk, and looking up `cross()` leads nowhere in dplyr.

heading: Drop rows with missing values
proposition: The English explains that `age` would have produced an error in the previous `case_when()` operation; the Turkish attributes the error to a previous `case_while()` operation, a function that appears nowhere in the chapter's code.
reader_consequence: The reader cannot identify which earlier step would have failed, so the reason `age` was excluded from the dichotomous recoding is lost.

heading: Logistic regression
proposition: The English states the outcome goes on the left of the tilde `~` and the explanatory variables on the right; the Turkish states the outcome is on the right of the tilde and the explanatory variables on the left, reversing the formula syntax.
reader_consequence: A reader following the Turkish writes the formula backwards (e.g. `age_cat ~ outcome`), fits the wrong model, and gets estimates that answer the opposite question, with no error message to warn them.

heading: Logistic regression
proposition: The English instructs the reader to use `family = "binomial"` for logistic regression; the Turkish instructs `family = "binom"`, which contradicts both the family table seven lines below in the same segment and every `glm()` chunk in the chapter.
reader_consequence: A reader who copies `family = "binom"` gets an error from `glm()` ('"binom" is not a valid family') and has no cue that the correct string is "binomial".

heading: Printing results
proposition: The English describes exponentiating the *log* odds ratio estimates; the Turkish describes exponentiated *gunluk* (daily) odds ratio estimates, introducing a time dimension the estimates do not have.
reader_consequence: The reader is told the estimates are daily odds ratios and may interpret or report them as a per-day rate, when they are exponentiated log odds from a single cross-sectional model.

heading: Looping multiple univariate models
proposition: The English states that the approach runs the `glm()` regression on each of the formulas created by `str_c()`; the Turkish sentence is truncated and omits this step entirely.
reader_consequence: The reader loses the middle of the pipeline description and cannot tell from the prose that each string formula is fitted with `glm()` before anything else happens.

heading: Looping multiple univariate models
proposition: The English states that each `glm()` output is passed to `tidy()`; the Turkish omits this step, jumping from `str_c()` straight to collapsing the outputs with `bind_rows()`.
reader_consequence: The reader does not learn that `tidy()` is what converts each model into a data frame, so the second `map()` in the chunk below has no explanation in the surrounding prose.

heading: Stratified
proposition: The English says stratified analysis is still being worked on FOR gtsummary, i.e. it is not yet available; the Turkish says stratified analysis is currently working ON gtsummary, which reads as the feature being operational.
reader_consequence: The reader may believe gtsummary already supports stratified analysis and waste time looking for a function that does not exist, instead of understanding that the section is a placeholder.

heading: Combine with gtsummary
proposition: The English says the `tbl_regression()` FUNCTION takes the regression output and produces a summary table; the Turkish reattaches the clause and states that the gtsummary PACKAGE is a summary table which takes the regression output.
reader_consequence: The reader is told the package itself is the table object, which blurs what `tbl_regression()` does and what it returns.

heading: Univariate `glm()`
proposition: The English instructs the reader to ensure the column is of class Factor before moving a level to the first position with fct_relevel(); the Vietnamese states only that fct_relevel() is used on 'a Factor variable' and gives no instruction to ensure or convert the column class.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader applying fct_relevel() to a character column gets an error or no re-levelling, and has not been told that converting the column to a factor is a prerequisite step.

heading: Printing results
proposition: The English says the demonstration combines model outputs WITH A TABLE OF COUNTS; the Vietnamese says only that model outputs are combined 'into a table'.
reader_consequence: The Vietnamese reader loses the stated purpose of the whole subsection, so the counts_table created two steps later arrives without motivation and the bind_cols() step reads as arbitrary formatting rather than as joining counts to estimates.

heading: Logistic regression
proposition: The Vietnamese adds a parenthetical gloss defining 'fit' as 'choosing the optimal predictive model based on observed data' (chon mo hinh du doan toi uu dua tren so lieu quan sat); the English defines nothing and says only that glm() is used to fit Generalized Linear Models.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader is told that glm() performs model selection, which it does not; model selection is introduced separately later via step() and lrtest(), so the reader may expect glm() alone to pick the best model.

heading: Univariate
proposition: The English states that YOUR USE CASE determines which R package you use; the Vietnamese states only that we need to decide which R package we want to use, dropping the use case as the deciding criterion.
reader_consequence: The Vietnamese reader is given a choice with no stated basis for making it, so the base R vs gtsummary decision reads as arbitrary preference rather than as driven by whether output goes to the console or to publication.

heading: Printing results
proposition: The English says round() is applied across all NUMERIC columns; the Vietnamese says it is applied to all columns.
reader_consequence: The prose contradicts the adjacent chunk, which uses across(where(is.numeric), ...); a Vietnamese reader adapting the code may drop the where(is.numeric) selector and hit an error on the character 'term' column.

heading: Combine with **dplyr**
proposition: The English bullet says round() is applied to all columns THAT ARE CLASS DOUBLE; the Vietnamese bullet says it is applied to all columns.

heading: Correlations / Correlaciones

heading: Simple statistical tests / Tests estadisticos sencillos

heading: gtsummary package > T-tests
proposition: English says the t-test compares the mean of ONE continuous variable BETWEEN two groups; the French says it compares means 'entre deux groupes de variables continues' (between two groups OF continuous variables), which makes the two groups groups of variables rather than groups of observations.
reader_consequence: A French reader is told the comparison unit is a set of continuous variables, so they may look for two collections of numeric columns instead of one numeric column split by a two-level grouping variable. The chunk beside it does the opposite: select(age_years, outcome) then tbl_summary(by = outcome), one continuous variable split by outcome. The parallel Wilcoxon section at line 287 states it correctly, so the two sections contradict each other.

heading: rstatix package > Summary statistics
proposition: English lists the default output of get_summary_stats() as n, max, min, MEDIAN, 25%ile, 75%ile, IQR, mad, mean, sd, se, CI; the Japanese renders the fourth item as 平均 (mean), so its list names 平均 twice and never names 中央値 (median).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader is told get_summary_stats() returns the mean in a position where it returns the median, and is never told the median is among the defaults; comparing the list against the printed table beside it, the reader cannot map the 'median' column to any documented statistic and may mistake it for a second mean.

heading: Correlations
proposition: English says the corrr package 'has a function to automatically plot the values'; the Japanese says it has a function to automatically 記入する (write in / fill in) the values, which is not plotting, and the chunk beside it calls rplot(correlation_tab), which draws a plot.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader does not learn that corrr can plot a correlation matrix, and misreads rplot() as a function that fills values into the table rather than one that produces a figure, so they may skip the one graphical feature the section exists to demonstrate.

heading: gtsummary package > Chi-squared test
proposition: English says add_p() switches to Fisher's exact test if any expected count is BELOW 5 (strictly less than 5); the Japanese says 5以下, which means 5 or fewer and therefore includes an expected count of exactly 5.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader applying the stated rule by hand predicts Fisher's exact test for a table whose smallest expected count is exactly 5, where gtsummary in fact reports a chi-squared test, so the reader cannot reconcile the printed p-value footnote with the documented rule.

heading: rstatix package > Wilcoxon rank sum test
proposition: The Japanese rstatix Wilcoxon section carries a prose sentence, 'Also known as the Mann-Whitney U test', where the corresponding English section has no prose at all between the heading and the code chunk.
reader_consequence: The Japanese reader gets a naming equivalence at this point that the English reader does not; the sentence is the one relocated out of the Kruskal-Wallis section below, so a reader comparing the two editions finds the sections do not correspond one to one.

heading: rstatix package > Kruskal-Wallis test
proposition: English states under the rstatix Kruskal-Wallis heading that the test is 'Also known as the Mann-Whitney U test'; the Japanese Kruskal-Wallis section has no prose between the heading and the code chunk.
reader_consequence: The Japanese reader never sees the English claim at this position. The claim is itself wrong in the English (Kruskal-Wallis is the extension of the Wilcoxon rank sum test, not the Mann-Whitney U test), so the omission removes an error rather than information, but the two editions no longer align section for section.

heading: Shapiro-Wilk test
proposition: The English says a quantile-quantile plot 'may be helpful' for samples larger than 5000; the Portuguese states it 'e recomendado' (is recommended).
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader takes a Q-Q plot as the handbook's prescribed procedure for large samples rather than one optional aid, and may treat other normality diagnostics as disallowed.

heading: T-test (rstatix)

reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader is not told that the two columns must be given as a formula (numeric ~ categorical) rather than as two arguments, so the tilde notation in the chunk below is unexplained.

heading: Chi-squared test (gtsummary)
proposition: The English conditions the switch to Fisher's exact test on any EXPECTED cell count below 5; the Portuguese says only 'caso alguma contagem seja abaixo de 5', omitting 'expected'.

heading: **base** R

reader_consequence: The Turkish sentence states only when the test is used (non-normal populations, unequal variance) and never states what it tests. A reader learns the precondition but not the hypothesis, so cannot say what the p-value beside the wilcox.test() chunk refers to.

proposition: `svymean()` is used to extract an appropriate DESIGN EFFECT; the Portuguese says it extracts an appropriate DESIGN ('Um delineamento apropriado pode ser extraido utilizando o `svymean()`').
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader is told that svymean() produces a survey design, which it does not. The reader loses the reason to call svymean() with deff = TRUE and may not realise the design effect is the quantity being obtained.

heading: Weighted proportions
proposition: The tables carry confidence intervals and the DESIGN EFFECT; the Portuguese lists only 'intervalos de confianca associados e delineamento' (design), omitting 'effect'.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader does not learn that the tables in this section report a design effect, so does not look for or interpret that column, even though the code beside it computes deff.

reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader loses the criterion for choosing srvyr over survey, which is that srvyr suits tidyverse pipelines, and reads it as a vague claim that srvyr fits workflows better in general.

heading: Survey design objects

reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader does not learn that srvyr exists to give tidyverse-compatible objects, so cannot connect this package choice to the dplyr piping used throughout the rest of the chapter.

proposition: English says the 'method' argument determines how TIES are handled (efron, breslow, exact); the French says it determines 'comment les liens sont traites', i.e. how links are handled.
reader_consequence: The French reader does not learn that efron/breslow/exact are tie-handling rules for coincident event times, so they cannot judge when the default matters in data with many equal follow-up times.

heading: Resources
proposition: English lists an eighth resource, 'Paper on different survival measures for cancer registry data with Rcode provided as supplementary materials' (PMC6322561); the French Resources list stops at seven entries and omits it.
reader_consequence: The French reader loses the only pointer to worked R code for alternative cancer-registry survival measures, which is the follow-up reference for the RMST note earlier in the chapter.

heading: Log rank test
proposition: The English states the log-rank test gives enough evidence of a survival difference by source of infection at alpha = 0.005; the Japanese states alpha = 0.05.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader takes the significance threshold used in this example to be 0.05 and copies the looser level into their own interpretation, so they judge the same result against a criterion ten times weaker than the one the English text applies.

heading: Data management and transformation
proposition: The English says the new columns are checked with summary() on futime AND a cross-tabulation of event against outcome; the Japanese says the check is a cross-tabulation of futime, event and outcome, which the chunk at lines 143-151 does not do (it runs summary(linelist_surv$futime) and tabyl(outcome, event)).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader looks for a cross-tabulation involving futime in the code below, does not find one, and does not learn that a continuous follow-up time is checked with summary() rather than with a table.

proposition: The English CAUTION states that survminer functions in general require the data argument to be given again alongside the survival object; the Japanese restricts the requirement to ggsurvplot().
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader applies the rule only to ggsurvplot(), then hits the same non-specific error with another survminer function such as ggforest() or ggcoxzph() and does not know the cause.

heading: Time-dependent covariate setup
proposition: The English says the BMT dataset is loaded from the survival package; the Japanese says it is loaded from the SemiCompRisks package.
reader_consequence: The two editions disagree about which package supplies BMT. The Japanese matches the chunk data(BMT, package = "SemiCompRisks"), so a reader who cross-checks against the English text, or who reads the English first, installs or searches the wrong package.

heading: Time-dependent covariate setup
proposition: The English states that TA is the time in days to acute graft-versus-host disease; the Japanese variable list drops the unit 'days' for TA, although it keeps it for T1.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader does not learn the time unit of TA, so they cannot read the interval boundaries in the reshaped data (for example patient 1 changing agvhd at time 67) as days.

heading: Fitting a Cox model
proposition: The English defines the printed p-value as the probability that the estimated coefficient could be 0; the Japanese says only that it is the p-value of the test of whether the coefficient is 0, and gives no definition.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader gets a circular gloss and no statement of what the printed p-value measures, so the bullet list of Cox output columns explains every column except that one.

heading: Load packages
proposition: The Japanese opens the paragraph with a sentence stating that running the code below loads the packages needed for the analysis. The English has no such sentence.
reader_consequence: Minor: the Japanese reader is told the following chunk loads the packages, a claim the English leaves implicit. The Japanese chunk at line 49 also drops echo=F, so the chunk is shown, which makes the added sentence consistent with the Japanese page but not with the English one.

heading: Import dataset
proposition: The English carries a level-3 section heading '### Import dataset {.unnumbered}'; in Portuguese the same words appear as an ordinary paragraph line ('Importar conjunto de dados'), so no heading exists and the import content is absorbed into the 'Carregar Pacotes' section.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader gets no entry for the data-import step in the table of contents or the section numbering, and cannot navigate or link to it; the import instructions read as a stray sentence inside the package-loading section.

heading: Overview
proposition: The English says the chapter focuses on 'right censoring' (a named censoring type); the Portuguese says it focuses on 'censura correta' ('correct censoring'), which is not a censoring type and is not supported by the English.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader does not learn that only right censoring is treated, so they may assume the chapter's methods cover left and interval censoring too, and they cannot connect the text to the standard term 'censura à direita' used in other sources.

heading: Building a surv-type object
proposition: The English says the '+' in the printed Surv object marks an observation that was right-censored; the Portuguese says it marks an observation that was 'bem censurada' ('well censored'), which the English does not support.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader misreads the '+' symbol as a quality flag on the censoring rather than as the marker of right-censoring, and so cannot correctly interpret the printed Surv vector.

heading: Plotting Kaplan-Meir curves
proposition: The English states that the proportion of participants surviving BEYOND 60 days of follow-up is around 40%; the Portuguese states that the proportion surviving 'nos ultimos 60 dias de seguimento' ('in the last 60 days of follow-up') is around 40%.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader reads the 40% as applying to a trailing 60-day window instead of to survival past day 60, and therefore reads the Kaplan-Meier curve at the wrong point.

heading: Cox regression analysis
proposition: The English says the hazard ratio is analogous to an ODDS RATIO in multiple logistic regression; the Portuguese says it is analogous to a 'taxa de probabilidade' (a probability rate), which is a different quantity from an odds ratio.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader is given a false analogy and may interpret the hazard ratio as a ratio of probabilities, losing the link to the odds ratio they already know from logistic regression.

proposition: The English third bullet says that if the HR (hazard ratio) is greater than 1 the predictor is associated with increased risk; the Portuguese third bullet makes the claim about 'a FC', an abbreviation the English does not use and which in Portuguese medical writing denotes heart rate ('frequencia cardiaca').

heading: Fitting a Cox model
proposition: The English says a continuous predictor's parameter estimate is the increase in the expected LOG of the relative hazard per one-unit increase; the Portuguese says it is the increase in the expected 'registo' (record/register) of the relative hazard, dropping the logarithm.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader does not learn that the coefficient is on the log-hazard scale, so they may read coef directly as a hazard ratio and skip the exponentiation needed to interpret it.

heading: Fitting a Cox model
proposition: The English names the comparison group for the 1.21x increased risk of death: patients whose source of infection was OTHER THAN FUNERALS. The Portuguese says only 'pacientes que tem outra fonte de infeccao' without stating what it is other than.

proposition: The English states that rowid_to_column() comes from the tidyverse package TIBBLE; the Portuguese attributes it only to 'o pacote tidyverse' and names no member package.

reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader is told the row count but not the rule that produces it, so they cannot generalise tmerge() to a covariate with more than two states and do not know that rows are split at changes in the time-dependent covariate.

heading: Time-dependent covariates in survival models
proposition: The English says the previous Cox analyses rely on the COVARIATE being measured at baseline; the Portuguese says they rely on 'a covariancia' (the covariance) being measured at baseline.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader is pointed at the wrong object: the stated limitation of standard Cox regression becomes a claim about a covariance rather than about when each predictor is measured, which is the whole motivation for the time-dependent setup that follows.

heading: ### Plotting Kaplan-Meir curves

heading: ### Fitting a Cox model
proposition: The English attributes the negative association with all-cause mortality to the onset-to-admission duration (the days_onset_hosp covariate); the Russian attributes it twice to 'продолжительность госпитализации', the duration of the hospital stay.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader concludes that a longer hospital stay reduces the risk of death by 10.7% per day, an entirely different and unsupported claim. The covariate in the fitted model at line 554 is days_onset_hosp, days from symptom onset to admission, and the Russian text at line 546 defines it correctly, so the reader also gets two contradictory definitions of the same variable within one section.

heading: ### Data management and transformation

proposition: The English gives a working cross-reference to the R basics chapter, [R basics](basics.qmd); the Turkish writes the label [R'ın temelleri] with no link target at all.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader who wants the background on R packages and p_load() sees plain bracketed text that does nothing when clicked, and is not told which chapter to open.

proposition: The English gives a working cross-reference to the descriptive tables chapter, [Descriptive tables](tables_descriptive.qmd), for the tabyl() and adorn functions; the Turkish writes the label [Açıklayıcı tablolar] with no link target.

reader_consequence: A reader following the Vietnamese writes a positional criterion such as i = ~ 7 >= 55 instead of i = ~ Pct_Death >= 55, which is what the chunk on lines 389-394 actually uses, and the call fails.

heading: Save single table
proposition: Saved images WILL have transparent backgrounds ("se co nen trong suot"); the English states only that they MAY come out with transparent backgrounds.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader treats a transparent background as guaranteed and either adds an unnecessary background-fill step, or reads an opaque exported PNG as a broken result.

heading: Load data
proposition: The translation instructs the reader to import this dataset with the `import()` function of the **rio** package; the English says nothing of the sort and the code chunk immediately below (es.qmd:67-75) loads the data with `appliedepidata::get_data(name = "campylobacter_germany")`.

heading: Interrupted timeseries
proposition: The translation says the two-part regression lets us calculate an incidence RATE ("una tasa de incidencia") comparing the two periods; the English says it lets us calculate an incidence rate RATIO comparing the two periods.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader expects the model to return an absolute incidence rate for each period and misreads the exponentiated beta_2 / beta_3 output (a ratio, null value 1) as a rate, which changes the interpretation of the intervention effect.

heading: Add rows
proposition: The translation glosses `end_date` as "(fecha de corte)", i.e. the cut-off date; the English gives no gloss, and the chunk at es.qmd:796-810 defines `cut_off <- yearweek("2010-12-31")` and `end_date <- yearweek("2011-12-31")` as two different dates one year apart.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader equates `end_date` with the baseline cut-off and expects rows to be added only up to the end of 2010, so the whole 2011 prediction period looks unexplained when the code fills rows to 2011-12-31.

heading: Lags and cross-correlation
proposition: The translation attributes `CCF()` to a package named **feats**; the English attributes it to the **feasts** package, which is also the name loaded in the setup chunk (es.qmd:41).
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader trying to install or look up the cross-correlation function searches for a package called "feats", which does not exist on CRAN, and cannot find `CCF()`.

heading: Autocorrelation
proposition: The translation defines the lag-2 line as the relation between each observation and "la observación anterior" (the immediately preceding observation), which is the wording it already used for lag 1; the English defines lag 2 as the relation between each observation and "the observation before last".
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader is given identical definitions for lag 1 and lag 2 and cannot work out what the x axis of the ACF plot counts, so the periodicity reading at lag 52 loses its basis.

heading: Prediction validation
proposition: The translation says the default behaviour of "la **tendencia**" (the trend) is to use **ciTools** for the prediction interval; the English attributes that default behaviour to the **trending** package, and the same sentence cites `?trending::predict.trending_model_fit`.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader cannot tell which component owns the default, and may look for a setting on the model trend rather than on the trending package, so the reason for `simulate_pi = FALSE` is lost.

heading: Interrupted timeseries
proposition: The translation again says the default behaviour of "la **tendencia**" (the trend) is to use **ciTools** for the prediction interval; the English attributes that default behaviour to the **trending** package.
reader_consequence: Same as the earlier occurrence: the Spanish reader attributes the ciTools default to the trend rather than to the trending package and cannot connect it to the `trending::predict.trending_model_fit` help page cited on the same line.

heading: Split data and fit regression
proposition: The translation carries a stray line "##hastaqui" ("up to here") in the body text; the English has no counterpart, and the string is untranslated working scaffolding rather than handbook content.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader sees an unexplained marker rendered in the middle of the outbreak-detection walkthrough and may read it as a section label or a code fragment that belongs to the following chunk.

reader_consequence: A French reader is given a definition of linear interpolation that has no second anchor point, so they cannot understand or reproduce what na_interpolation() does, and may believe imputation is anchored on missing values.

proposition: The French instructs the reader to import the counts data with the import() function of the rio package; the English has no such sentence and the adjacent chunk imports with appliedepidata::get_data(name = "campylobacter_germany").

proposition: The French says the second fourier() output predicts the year of interest "by defining the fourier() parameter"; the English says it is done by defining the `h` argument, which is what the adjacent chunk uses (h = num_weeks).

proposition: The English subsection heading "### Descriptive analysis" and its whole introductory paragraph have no counterpart in the French, where the basic_plot_bivar chunk follows the join chunk with no heading or prose.
reader_consequence: A French reader meets a bivariate plot with no introduction, no instruction to plot the data first, and no cross-reference to the pivoting-data chapter, and the section structure no longer matches the English table of contents.

proposition: The English states that the plot shows a clear relation in the seasonality of the two variables and that temperature might peak a few weeks before the case number; the French states neither.
reader_consequence: A French reader is not told what to look for in the plot, and loses the observation that motivates the four-week lagged temperature variable built two subsections later.

proposition: The French symbol glossary defines "Î'(x" as the indicator function while the French displayed equation writes that term as "Î´(t-t_0)"; the English uses one symbol, δ, in both places (β and δ are corrupted to Î² and Î´/Î' throughout the French).

heading: Time series data / Données de séries temporelles
proposition: The English states that cases drop in the last week of the year before increasing in the first week of the next year; the French states only that there is a reporting problem at the start of each year and that counts increase in the first week of the following year, with no statement that counts fall.
reader_consequence: A French reader learns only half of the year-boundary artefact and may not understand why weeks W51-W02 are later set to missing and interpolated.

heading: Autocorrelation / Autocorrélation
proposition: The English explains that the ACF value at lag 0 is always 1 because it is the relation between an observation and itself; the French says only that it shows "the relation between the two", without naming what the two are.
reader_consequence: A French reader is given no reason why the lag-0 autocorrelation equals 1 and may mistake it for a property of the data rather than an identity.

heading: Autocorrelation / Autocorrélation
proposition: The English notes that the lag-0 line is not shown in the plot produced by ACF(); the French omits this note.
reader_consequence: A French reader looks for the x = 0 line described in the text, cannot find it in the output, and may think the code or the plot is wrong.

heading: Prediction validation / Validation de la prédiction
proposition: The English gives the reason for validating on the latest year before the present one as "because you don't yet know the counts for the current year"; the French replaces this with the circular "because you cannot predict the current year" and never states that current-year counts are unknown.
reader_consequence: A French reader is not told why the current year is excluded from validation, so cannot judge when the same approach applies to their own surveillance data.

proposition: The Japanese adds a sentence stating the campylobacter data are imported with `import()` from the **rio** package (which reads .xlsx, .csv, .rds and many other file types); the English has no such sentence, and the code chunk immediately below on both sides loads the data with `counts <- appliedepidata::get_data(name = "campylobacter_germany")`, calling neither **rio** nor `import()`.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader looks for a **rio** `import()` call and a data file on disk that do not exist, may install and load **rio** needlessly, and may conclude the printed code chunk is incomplete or that they must supply a local .csv/.rds path before the chapter will run.

heading: Cut-off date / 日付のカットオフ
proposition: The English states that `num_weeks` is the number of weeks between the baseline cut-off and the end date being predicted for, having explicitly struck through the earlier description of it as the number of weeks in the year of interest; the Japanese keeps only the struck-through description ('we also define how many weeks are in the year of interest') and omits the corrected one.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader takes `num_weeks <- as.numeric(end_date - cut_off)` to be a fixed count of weeks in a calendar year rather than the span from the cut-off to the end date, so when they move `cut_off` or `end_date` away from a one-year gap they will misjudge how many forecast weeks the later `add_rows` and `fourier(h = num_weeks)` steps produce.

heading: Load data / Carregue os dados no R
proposition: The translation instructs the reader to import the campylobacter data with rio's import() function; the English has no such instruction and the adjacent chunk loads the data with appliedepidata::get_data(name = "campylobacter_germany").
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader looks for an import() call that does not exist in the chunk, and may try to point rio::import() at a local .xlsx/.csv/.rds file that the handbook never ships, so the load step fails.

heading: Add rows / Adicione linhas
proposition: The translation says the sequence of weeks runs between the first and the last week currently available in the data and the end week; the English and the adjacent chunk (seq(max(.$epiweek) + 1, end_date, by = 1)) say it starts one week AFTER the maximum week currently available.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader believes the added rows re-cover the whole observed period, so cannot reconcile the prose with max(.$epiweek) + 1 and may rewrite the seq() start, duplicating existing weeks and breaking the tsibble.

heading: Residuals / Resíduos
proposition: The translation asserts that the model will probably underestimate the observed counts, and presents this as a consequence of the poor fit at peaks and troughs ("Sendo assim, ele provavelmente ira subestimar"); the English only says it "might be more likely to underestimate", as a separate hedged observation.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader treats a directional bias as established and caused by the peak/trough misfit, and may correct or discount the fitted values for an underestimation the residual plots do not demonstrate.

heading: Load data
proposition: The Russian text instructs the reader to import the campylobacter data with rio::import(), but the adjacent code chunk (ru 71-79) loads it with appliedepidata::get_data(name = "campylobacter_germany"), and the English has no such sentence at all.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader follows an import route that does not exist in the chapter's code: they look for a data file to pass to import(), find none, and may conclude the chapter's data are unavailable, when the shown chunk already loads them from the appliedepidata package.

heading: Add rows
proposition: The Russian says end_date is defined below ("определенной ниже"); the English says it is defined above, and end_date is in fact set in the preceding Cut-off date chunk (ru 916).
reader_consequence: A Russian reader scrolls forward looking for the definition of end_date, does not find one, and may think the add_rows chunk depends on a value that has not been created yet.

heading: Load data
proposition: The translation instructs the reader to import the campylobacter data with rio::import(), handling file types such as .xlsx, .csv and .rds; the English gives no such instruction and the adjacent chunk (tr 65-73) loads the data with appliedepidata::get_data(name = "campylobacter_germany").
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader looks for a data file to feed to import() and for an Import/Export page link that is not rendered, instead of running the get_data() call that the chunk immediately below actually uses; the described function never appears in the chapter.

heading: Fourier terms
proposition: The translation's opening definition sentence has the code-chunk comment "epi hafta ve case_int degiskenlerini kullanarak fourier terimleri ekleyin" ("add fourier terms using the epiweek and case_int variables") spliced into the middle of it; the English sentence contains only the definition that Fourier terms are the equivalent of sin and cosine curves.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader meets an ungrammatical sentence in place of the definition of a Fourier term, so the one line that explains what the section is about cannot be parsed, and an instruction about specific variables appears before those variables have been introduced.

heading: Farrington method
proposition: The English heading "#### Farrington method" has no counterpart in the translation; the Farrington paragraph, its code chunk and its plot run on inside the parent "surveillance paketi" section with no heading of their own.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader gets no table-of-contents entry or visual break for the Farrington method, so the Farrington and GLRNB methods read as one block and only GLRNB appears as a named sub-section, making the first of the two announced algorithms hard to find or link to.

heading: Overview
proposition: The English states the example dataset comes from the **surveillance** package; the translation says only that it is a Campylobacter dataset from Germany and drops the package attribution.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader is not told at the outset where the demonstration data originates, so the later appearance of the surveillance package as both data source and outbreak-detection tool is unmotivated.

heading: Autocorrelation
proposition: The English states the null hypothesis tested by the Ljung-Box test is independence, that is, that the series is NOT autocorrelated; the translation names "the null hypothesis" but glosses it as "whether or not it is autocorrelated", never stating what the null asserts.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader cannot tell which direction the test runs and may read a non-significant p-value as evidence of autocorrelation, inverting the conclusion drawn from the chunk output below.

heading: Load data / Nhập dữ liệu
proposition: The translation states that this dataset is imported with the import() function from the rio package, while the code chunk immediately below (and the English text) imports it with appliedepidata::get_data(name = "campylobacter_germany").
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader tries to load the campylobacter data with rio::import() and a file path that does not exist in the handbook download, so the chapter's first data step fails; they also learn a stale workflow that the surrounding chunks no longer use.

heading: Autocorrelation / Tự tương quan
proposition: The translation names ACF() as the function for partial autocorrelation, whereas the English names PACF() and the adjacent code chunk uses PACF(case_int, lag_max = 52) for the partial autocorrelation plot.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader believes ACF() returns partial autocorrelation, so they run ACF() twice, get two identical plots, and cannot distinguish autocorrelation from partial autocorrelation when judging periodicity.

heading: From Stata / Desde Stata
proposition: The English says the dplyr call is rename(new_name = old_name); the Spanish says rename(nombre_antiguo = nombre_nuevo), i.e. rename(old_name = new_name), which reverses the argument order.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader copying the pattern writes rename(old = new), which either errors with 'Column `new` doesn't exist' or renames the wrong column. The same table in the SAS section of the same Spanish file (line 234) gives the correct order, so the reader also gets two contradictory rules.

heading: From Stata / Desde Stata
proposition: The English gives the Stata help syntax as `help [command]`; the Spanish gives it as `[comando] help`, reversing command and keyword.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader who trusts the Stata column types `[comando] help` in Stata and gets an error instead of the help page. The Spanish SAS table (line 205) prints `help [comando]` correctly, so the two tables disagree.

heading: From Stata / Desde Stata
proposition: The English says user-written functions are installed with `ssc install [package]`; the Spanish says they are installed 'utilizando el [paquete] ssc install', placing the package name before the command.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader takes the installation syntax to be '[paquete] ssc install' and issues an invalid Stata command when trying to install an ado file.

heading: From SAS / Desde SAS
proposition: The English states that the Label statement, the Where/If record selection and the Merge statement are all used in the SAS Data Step; the Spanish drops 'in the Data Step' from all three rows (line 237 leaves the truncated fragment 'etiquetarse en el mediante la sentencia Label').
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader is not told where these SAS statements belong, so the mapping from SAS to the R equivalents loses the context that these are Data Step operations; line 237 additionally reads as a broken sentence.

heading: From SAS
proposition: In SAS, multiple record-selection conditions in a Where or If statement are separated using the "and" command.
reader_consequence: A French reader consulting the SAS-to-R table sees the R side explain that filter() separates multiple conditions with & or a comma, but has no SAS counterpart to map it from, so the translation of multi-condition record selection from SAS to R is left unexplained.

heading: From SAS / Descriptive analysis table
proposition: The translation attributes summary() to the skimr package; the English attributes only skim() to skimr and treats summary() as separate.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader concludes summary() requires installing and loading skimr, and may install a package to run a base R function, or fail to call summary() when skimr is absent.

heading: From Excel / Benefits
proposition: The English says Excel workflows rely on the user's own memory of the steps; the translation says they depend on メモリ (computer memory).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader takes the stated source of Excel error risk to be machine memory rather than the analyst having to remember manual steps, and so misses the argument that scripted, written-down steps remove that risk.

heading: From Excel / R-Excel interaction
proposition: The English lists 'sideways text' as an Excel formatting feature lost in translation; the translation lists 補足のためのテキスト ('text for supplementary notes') instead.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader gets the wrong example of what R loses, and may expect rotated/vertical cell text to survive a round trip while expecting annotation text to be dropped.

proposition: The English says R has grown dramatically in scope (capability); the translation says R has dramatically expanded its user base (利用者を飛躍的に拡大).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader receives an adoption statistic claim that the handbook does not make and does not support, instead of the capability claim that motivates the following sentence about commercial competitors reacting to R's development.

proposition: The English states that getwd() and here() are called with empty parentheses; the translation omits that instruction.

heading: From SAS / Working directory table
proposition: The English states that getwd() and here() are called with empty parentheses; the translation omits that instruction.

proposition: The cross-reference for merging datasets with dplyr points to the Grouping data page ("Agrupando Dados", #grouping); the English points to the Joining Data page (joining_matching.qmd).

proposition: The SAS statement that shows the current working directory is `% de produção %sysfunc(getoption(work));`; the English gives `%put %sysfunc(getoption(work));`.

heading: From SAS
proposition: R help is obtained by typing `?função`; the English states it is obtained by typing [function]?, with the question mark after the function name.

proposition: The English R-side says that converting a column to Factor class and specifying levels labels the VALUES; the Russian says it labels the variables ("Подпись переменных").

proposition: The translation opens the SAS row with "Veri kümesini özellikle belirtmenize gerek yoktur" (you do not need to specify the dataset), a claim the English SAS table never makes; the English row instead states that no special procedure is needed to create a variable.

proposition: The English R column states that working directories in R can be EITHER absolute OR relative to a project root folder via the **here** package. proposition: The English sends the reader to the Import and export page through a working cross-reference, [Import and export](importing.qmd). The translation writes the bracketed label "[İçe ve dışa aktar]" with no link target, so the cross-reference does not exist.
