heading: From SAS / Basic data manipulation
proposition: The English row names the handbook page that documents dplyr joins and points at it (Joining Data, joining_matching.qmd); the Vietnamese row carries the bare label [Nối dữ liệu] with no link target, so the cross-reference to that page is absent.
reader_consequence: A SAS user told that dplyr offers merging functions has no way to reach the Joining Data chapter: the text renders as literal bracketed words, not a link, so the reader never learns which page explains left_join, inner_join and the rest.

heading: Calculating degrees / Cálculo de grados
proposition: The question introducing the chunk asks which individuals have the ten most contacts (top 10 by degree); the Spanish asks which individuals have more than 10 contacts, a threshold filter the adjacent code head(sort(deg_both, decreasing = TRUE), 10) does not perform.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader reads the printed output as the set of cases whose degree exceeds 10, and will conclude that exactly those cases cross that threshold. The output is simply the ten highest degrees, which may include values at or below 10 and excludes further cases above 10. The reader also learns the wrong idiom for a threshold query.

heading: Overview
proposition: The reader can drag the nodes of the interactive network to move them.
reader_consequence: A French reader is told only to hover and click, so they do not learn that the layout can be rearranged by dragging, and may conclude that an overlapping or cluttered network cannot be untangled.

heading: Creating an epicontacts object
proposition: Because the links are directional, the user must supply the `from` and `to` arguments accordingly.
reader_consequence: The French sentence loses its verb ('les arguments `from` et `to` en consequence'), so the instruction to set `from` and `to` is no longer stated; a reader may treat those two arguments as optional and call `make_epicontacts()` without them.

heading: Visualising edge attributes
proposition: The worked example sets `edge_col_pal` to give Community and Nosocomial links their own colours.
reader_consequence: The French prose introduces `edge_col_pal` and then says 'Voici un exemple', but the line is commented out in the French chunk, so the rendered figure shows default edge colours and the reader cannot see what `edge_col_pal` does.

heading: Specifying transmission tree shape
proposition: The first transmission-tree shape is selected with the value `branching`.
reader_consequence: The French text names the shape `branchee`, which epicontacts does not accept; a reader who writes `network_shape = "branchee"` gets an error instead of the branching layout.

heading: Specifying transmission tree shape
proposition: The `position_dodge` example plot is drawn 700 pixels high via the `height` argument.
reader_consequence: The French chunk misspells the argument as `hieght = 700`; a reader copying this block gets an 'unused argument' error rather than the dodged network shown in the English handbook.

heading: Timelines
proposition: Because 15 is not a character string, `tl_end_node_size` is interpreted as the actual node size rather than being mapped to a column.
reader_consequence: The French comment keeps only the negative half and adds a stray reference to the outcome column, so the reader never learns the rule that a numeric value is taken as a literal size; they cannot generalise it to the other `tl_*` arguments.

heading: Timelines
proposition: Because 2 is not a character string, `tl_edge_width` is interpreted as the actual edge width rather than being mapped to a column.
reader_consequence: The French comment states only that the argument is not tied to the hospital column, so the reader does not learn that the number is the literal edge width and may expect a width scale to be derived from the data.

heading: Handling > Subsetting
proposition: English: setting what = "contacts" filters the contacts to keep cases that are found in THE LINELIST. Japanese says it filters the contacts to keep cases found in the CONTACTS ("contact で見つかった症例を含むように contacts をフィルタリング"), which is circular and contradicts what thin() does.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader learns a self-referential, meaningless definition of thin(what = "contacts") and cannot tell the two thin() modes apart. They will not understand that thin(x, what = "contacts") drops transmission links whose cases are absent from the linelist, which is exactly the operation used in the very next code chunk and in the plotting section.

heading: Handling > Subsetting
proposition: English states two independent filters applied by the example: node filtering keeps male linelist cases infected April-July 2014, and edge filtering keeps transmission links that occurred in hospital. Japanese states a single conjunctive node filter: only male cases with an April-July 2014 infection date AND a hospital-acquired transmission link are kept in the linelist.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader concludes that edge_attribute further restricts which CASES survive in the linelist. It does not: node_attribute and edge_attribute filter the linelist and the contacts separately, which is why the following thin() step is needed at all. The reader will mispredict the contents of sub_attributes$linelist.

heading: Preparation > Creating an epicontacts object
proposition: English specifies that the case_id and infector columns being renamed to from and to are the columns IN THE CONTACTS data frame. The Japanese sentence drops the "in the contacts" qualifier, leaving "`case_id` と `infector` の列名が `from` と `to` に変更" attached to the same clause that began with "linelist の".
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader can read the whole sentence as describing the linelist, and so expect from/to columns in epic$linelist. They then cannot locate the renamed columns when inspecting the object, and will misread later code such as nrow(sub_attributes$contacts).

heading: Creating an epicontacts object
proposition: In a linelist, rows correspond to unique cases; the Portuguese says columns correspond to unique cases ("colunas sao variaveis e colunas correspondem a casos unicos").
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader is told a linelist has columns that are variables and columns that are cases, which is self-contradictory and hides the row-per-case structure the whole epicontacts object depends on.

heading: Visualising edge attributes
proposition: The Portuguese file carries the untranslated English sentence about edge_color/edge_width/edge_linetype as a separate line immediately before its Portuguese translation, so the paragraph is stated twice.
reader_consequence: The reader meets the same instruction twice, once in a language the page is not written in, and may believe the two lines describe two different steps.

heading: Identifying clusters
proposition: The Portuguese file carries the untranslated English sentence "Let us look at the largest clusters..." as a separate line immediately before its Portuguese translation, so the paragraph is stated twice.
reader_consequence: The reader meets the same instruction twice, once in English, and may read the two lines as two separate operations on the epicontacts object.

heading: Saving plots and figures
proposition: The English says visSave saves a plot; the Portuguese says it saves "um mapa" (a map).
reader_consequence: A reader looking for how to save the transmission-network figure may not connect this section to it, because the chapter produces no map.

heading: Overview
proposition: Clicking a node highlights downstream cases; the Portuguese says it highlights "casos subjacentes" (underlying cases), which reverses or removes the direction of transmission.
reader_consequence: The reader loses the fact that the highlight follows transmission forward from the clicked case, and may read the highlighted set as the sources of the case instead.

heading: Overview
proposition: Clicking a node in the interactive plot highlights the cases DOWNSTREAM of it in the transmission chain.
reader_consequence: The Russian reader is told only that clicking highlights 'cases of the disease', so they do not learn that the highlight traces onward transmission from the clicked case, and cannot interpret what the demonstration plot (which sets highlight_downstream = TRUE) is showing them.

heading: Load packages
proposition: The version of epicontacts required is the DEVELOPMENT version, not the released one.
reader_consequence: The Russian reader sees only 'you will need the epicontacts version', so a reader who already has the CRAN release installed may skip the p_install_gh() step and then fail on the timeline features of this chapter, which exist only in the development branch.

heading: Load packages
proposition: The install command needs to be run only ONCE, not every time the package is used.
reader_consequence: The Russian text says the command must be run 'only below' ('только ниже'), which states nothing about frequency, so the reader does not learn that the GitHub install is a one-off step and may re-run a slow install on every session.

heading: Subsetting
proposition: The two case IDs whose clusters are examined are 2ae019 and 71577a.
reader_consequence: The Russian prose names 2ae019 twice and never mentions 71577a, while the chunk immediately below it runs subset(epic, cluster_id = c("2ae019","71577a")). The reader thinks the count of 13 comes from one ID's cluster and cannot reproduce or reason about the second cluster.

heading: Subsetting
proposition: The number 13 counts linelist CASES involved in the clusters.
reader_consequence: The Russian says '13 line lists' ('13 построчных списков') rather than 13 cases from the line list, so the reader misreads what nrow(sub_id$linelist) counts and mistakes the unit of the result.

heading: Visualization > Basic plotting
proposition: The reader can drag the nodes, hover over them for more information, and click them to highlight connected cases.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader is not told the plot just produced is interactive at this point, so they do not try dragging, hovering or clicking on their own network and miss the connected-case highlighting.

heading: Visualization > Visualising node attributes
proposition: The English '#### Visualising node attributes' heading exists as a heading; the Turkish line has no space after '####', so it is not a heading at all and renders as literal body text.
reader_consequence: The Turkish page shows the literal string '####Nod ozelliklerinin gorsellestirilmesi {.unnumbered}' inside the previous section, the subsection is absent from the table of contents, and a reader cannot navigate to the node-attribute material.

heading: Handling > Accessing IDs
proposition: The ten IDs asked for in the example are the first ten IDs of the CONTACTS dataset specifically.
reader_consequence: The Turkish question says only 'the dataset', so a reader who has just read the six-way list of get_id() options cannot tell which option the following get_id(epic, "contacts") call demonstrates.

heading: Analysis > Calculating degrees
proposition: type = "both" counts the in-degree AND the out-degree.
reader_consequence: The Turkish text says the type argument means 'both the degree and the degree', so a reader never learns what the two counted quantities are and cannot choose between type = "in", "out" and "both".

heading: Analysis > Calculating degrees
proposition: A high degree indicates an individual who was in contact with MANY others.
reader_consequence: The Turkish sentence reduces to 'a high degree indicates a person in contact with others', which is true of any degree above zero, so the reader loses the epidemiological point that degree measures how many contacts a case had.

heading: Visualization > Saving plots and figures
proposition: The prose says this chunk saves the plot as a self-contained interactive html file, but the Turkish chunk carries a stray '""' before 'label = FALSE' that the English chunk does not have, so the code cannot parse.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader who copies the save example gets an R parse error at the label argument instead of a network.html file, and has no way to tell from the prose that the chunk itself is corrupt.

heading: Visualization > Timelines
proposition: Any number of further columns may be added to the timeline data frame and mapped to node and edge properties.
reader_consequence: The Turkish text says 'another column' (singular), so a reader may believe the timeline data frame accepts only one extra column beyond id, start and end, and will not add both outcome and hospital as the following code does.

heading: Calculating degrees
proposition: English asks which individuals have the ten MOST contacts; the Vietnamese asks which individuals have 10 contacts, dropping the superlative, while the chunk beside it runs head(sort(deg_both, decreasing = TRUE), 10), which returns the ten highest degrees rather than cases with exactly 10 contacts.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader reads the printed output as a list of cases whose degree equals 10, and concludes the code filters on a degree of 10 instead of ranking cases by degree and taking the top ten.

heading: Calculating degrees
proposition: English asks for the mean number of CONTACTS (the mean node degree computed by mean(deg_both)); the Vietnamese asks for the mean number of infections/transmissions ('So luong lay nhiem trung binh'), which is a different quantity from the degree the code averages.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader takes the printed number as an average number of onward infections per case, a reproduction-number-like quantity, when it is the average number of contacts (in-degree plus out-degree) per case in the linelist.

heading: Pairwise characteristics
proposition: English states there is a statistically SIGNIFICANT association between transmission links and gender, which is what the fisher.test() output beside it supports; the Vietnamese states there is a LARGE association ('mot moi lien he lon'), a claim about effect size that the Fisher test result does not make.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader reads the Fisher test as evidence that the gender association is strong in magnitude, rather than as evidence that it is unlikely under the null hypothesis, and may over-state the practical importance of the association.

heading: Iteratively produce tables for different levels of a variable
proposition: The third indicator is the MEDIAN age of cases; the Spanish says "la edad media de los casos", which is the mean age, while the code beside it computes median(as.numeric(age), na.rm = TRUE) and names the column median_age_cases.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader believes the table column reports an arithmetic mean age and interprets or reuses the indicator as a mean, when the code returns a median. On the skewed age distribution of an outbreak line list the two differ, so the reader reports the wrong summary statistic.

heading: Basic syntax and structure
proposition: The base-R equivalent of the every-second-row filter is written `function (x) (x%%2 == 0)` with the double-percent modulo operator; the Spanish prose writes `function (x) (x%2 == 0)` with a single percent, which is not the R modulo operator and does not match the `x%%2 == 0` used in the chunks at es.qmd:214 and es.qmd:221.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader who copies the operator from the prose writes `x%2`, which R parses as an incomplete special operator and fails with a syntax error, and the reader has no working reference in that segment to correct it from.

heading: Basic syntax and structure
proposition: The alternative code shown next is base R code ("A possible base R code for the same task"); the Spanish says only "Un posible código para la misma tarea" and drops the identification of the approach as base R.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader loses the point of the segment, which is that the same selection can be done in base R with `base::Filter()` instead of the dplyr pipeline above, and reads the chunk as just another variant rather than as the base-R contrast the section is teaching.

heading: How does R build functions?
proposition: The third component of a function is inspected with the R function `environment()`; the French text renames it to `environnement()`, which is not an R function and is not the call used in the code chunk immediately below (`environment(contain_covid19)`, English lines 130-136, French lines 131-137).
reader_consequence: A French reader who follows the prose and types `environnement(ma_fonction)` gets 'could not find function', and cannot tell whether the third component is inspectable at all.

heading: Testing and Error handling
proposition: The English says the `missing(argument)` check returns a "TRUE" or "FALSE" value; the French says it returns the value "VRAI" or "FAUX", which are not R logical values and are not what the chunk at French lines 506-525 produces.
reader_consequence: A French reader may expect or write `VRAI`/`FAUX` in a condition, or fail to recognise R's `TRUE`/`FALSE` output as the value the text described.

heading: How does R build functions?
proposition: The English says `body()` is the code within the brackets (curly braces) or following the parenthesis; the French says it is 'entre les parenthèses ou à la suite des parenthèses', naming parentheses for both alternatives, so it states the body sits inside `( )` rather than inside `{ }` as the example function at French lines 117-124 shows.
reader_consequence: A French reader is told the function body lives between parentheses, loses the brace-versus-parenthesis distinction the English draws, and reads a sentence whose two alternatives are identical.

heading: Column names and tidy evaluation
proposition: The prose on both sides presents the chunk as the skeleton template code taken from the tidyverse programming tutorial, but the French chunk adds a third closing parenthesis on the `summarise()` line (`max = max({{ var }})))`), so the French code is not valid R and is not the template it is described as.
reader_consequence: A French reader copying the advertised template gets a syntax error and no working demonstration of the `{{ }}` embrace operator, the one point the section exists to teach.

heading: Using purrr: writing functions that can be iteratively applied
proposition: The purrr section is a top-level chapter section (`##`) in English but a third-level heading (`###`) in French, so in French it renders as a subsection of 'Exemples' instead of as a sibling of it.
reader_consequence: A French reader sees the purrr material nested under 'Exemples' in the table of contents and section numbering, and its three subsections appear as siblings of the purrr heading rather than as its children.

heading: Return proportion tables for several columns
proposition: The English names the base R "apply" family as the simpler alternative to the for loop; the French translates the function name itself to "appliquer", a name that does not exist in base R, while the chunk beside it calls `base::lapply()`.
reader_consequence: A French reader looking up an "appliquer" function in base R finds nothing, and does not connect the sentence to the `lapply()` call printed directly below it.

heading: Testing and Error handling / テストとエラー処理
proposition: The translation states that the following code runs mean() on each ROW of linelist (linelise 各行に対し mean() を実行し); the chunk beside it runs map(linelist, mean), which applies mean() to each COLUMN of linelist, and the English says only 'first running the mean() as function'.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader believes purrr::map() iterates over rows of a data frame. They will then expect map(linelist, mean) to return one value per patient record, and will misread the printed output (one entry per variable, with NA/warnings for character columns) and misuse map() on data frames elsewhere.

heading: Iteratively produce graphs for different levels of a variable / 異なる変数で繰り返しグラフを作成する
proposition: The translated heading says the graphs are produced for different VARIABLES (異なる変数で); the English says they are produced for different LEVELS OF A VARIABLE, and the code loops over the levels of the single variable `province`.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader scanning headings looks for a recipe that iterates over several columns, and does not find the section that actually solves 'one plot per category of one variable'. They may also expect chart_outcome_province() to take a variable name rather than a province value.

heading: Iteratively produce tables for different levels of a variable / 異なる変数で繰り返し表を作成する
proposition: The translated heading says the tables are produced for different VARIABLES (異なる変数で); the English says for different LEVELS OF A VARIABLE, and print_indic_prov() is called once per level of `province`.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader misidentifies what the section demonstrates and may look elsewhere for the 'one table per group level' pattern, or expect the second argument of print_indic_prov() to be a column name rather than a province value.

heading: Functions / 関数
proposition: The translation asserts that you do not need to think about the program's connections from start to finish (私たちはプログラムの繋がりを最初から最後まで考える必要はなく); the English asserts only that functions should not be thought of as fixed at the top or at the end of the programming chain.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader takes away general permission to skip reasoning about program flow, instead of the intended narrower point that a function can appear anywhere in a pipeline, including inside another function or a list.

heading: Basic syntax and structure / 基本的な構文と構造
proposition: The translation states the error occurs when you supply an argument that is not defined in the function definition (関数定義に定義されていない引数を与えると); the English says only that the argument is 'not recognized', and the call beside it passes barrier_gest, wear_mask and get_vaccine, all of which ARE defined in contain_covid19().
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader concludes the failure is caused by an unknown argument NAME, when the example is about an unhandled argument VALUE ('sometimes'). They will look for the wrong cause when their own function returns nothing useful for an unanticipated value.

heading: Return proportion tables for several columns / それぞれの列の割合を返す
proposition: The translation attributes the F2 shortcut to RStudio specifically (そのための RStudio のショートカットは); the English says only 'The shortcut to do so'.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader using another editor concludes the technique is unavailable to them, and does not try the equivalent 'view source' action in their own environment.

heading: Basic syntax and structure / Sintaxe e estrutura básicas
proposition: The English says the anonymous function selects every second observation of the dataset; the Portuguese says it selects the second record of the dataset ("selecionar o segundo registro"), a single row rather than every even-numbered row, which the adjacent chunk `filter(row_number() %%2 == 0)` contradicts.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader believes the modulo filter returns one row (the second observation) and will misread the 10-row output of the chunk, and may reuse `%%2 == 0` expecting a single-record selection.

heading: Testing and Error handling / Teste e tratamento de erros
proposition: The English says to run `mean()` and then run it with `safely()`; the Portuguese names the wrapper `secure ()`, a function that does not exist and that does not appear in the adjacent chunk, which calls `safely(mean)`.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader looks for or types `secure()`, gets "could not find function", and cannot connect the sentence to the `safe_mean <- safely(mean)` line directly below it.

heading: Modify class of multiple columns in a dataset / Modificar a classe de várias colunas em um conjunto de dados
proposition: The English attributes `map_if()` to the **purrr** package; the Portuguese attributes it to the **purr** package, which is not the package used in the adjacent chunk (`purrr::map_if`).
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader tries to install or namespace `purr`, which is a different (unrelated) name, instead of `purrr`.

heading: Iteratively produce tables for different levels of a variable
proposition: The third indicator is the MEDIAN age of cases; the Russian text names it the mean/average age ("средний возраст больных"), while the chunk beside it computes median(as.numeric(age)) and labels the row "Median age of the cases".
reader_consequence: A Russian reader believes the table reports an arithmetic mean age, misreads the printed indicator, and may reproduce the code expecting mean() where the chapter deliberately uses median().

heading: How does R build functions?
proposition: The Russian text states the function body sits inside SQUARE brackets ("внутри квадратных скобок"); the English says only "brackets", and in R a function body is delimited by curly braces { }, never square brackets.
reader_consequence: A Russian beginner looks for or writes square brackets when defining a function body and produces syntactically invalid R, and misidentifies which part of a definition body() returns.

heading: Why would you use a function?
proposition: The English cross-reference carries a link target to the Iteration, loops, and lists page (iteration.qmd); the Russian keeps only the bracketed label with no target, so no link exists.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader sees literal text "[Итерации, циклы и списки]" instead of a link and cannot navigate to the prerequisite chapter that this paragraph tells them they have already covered.

heading: Testing and Error handling
proposition: The English says the list returned by safely() holds two objects, the result AND the error it skipped; the Russian says the two objects "are the results" and separately that the error "is skipped", dropping the claim that the second element is the error itself.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader does not learn that the second list element is the captured error object, so they do not know to inspect $error after mapping a safely()-wrapped function.

heading: Testing and Error handling
proposition: The English recommends stop() to make errors MORE detectable; the Russian says to use stop() "for OTHER detectable errors" ("Для других обнаружимых ошибок"), asserting a distinct class of errors that the English does not describe.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader takes stop() to apply to some separate category of errors rather than as the tool that makes a function's own failures visible, and may not use it in the checks the section is teaching.

heading: Testing and Error handling
proposition: The English names the base R function `missing(argument)` as the way to check whether an argument was supplied; the Turkish names `eksik(değişken)`, which is not an R function and does not appear in the code chunk beside it (line 479-491 uses `missing(barrier_gest)`).
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader who follows the prose and types `eksik(...)` gets 'could not find function "eksik"' and cannot reproduce the missing-argument check the very next chunk demonstrates.

heading: Testing and Error handling
proposition: The English states the check returns the value "TRUE" or "FALSE"; the Turkish states it returns "DOĞRU" or "YANLIŞ", which are not values R produces.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader expects R to print DOĞRU/YANLIŞ and may not recognise the actual TRUE/FALSE output, or may write comparisons against the Turkish words.

heading: Basic syntax and structure
proposition: The English says the test is what happens when a value is "no" or not "yes", matching the literal strings the function compares against; the Turkish writes the literals as "hayır" and "evet", which the adjacent chunk (tr line 149, `get_vaccine = "no"`) and the function body (tr lines 107-114, comparing to `"yes"`) do not use.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader who passes "evet"/"hayır" as argument values gets the failure branch for every call, because the function tests equality with the English literal "yes".

heading: Tips and best Practices for well functioning functions
proposition: The English adds the caution "It should produce the contrary.", warning that functional programming must not end up making code harder to read; the Turkish omits this sentence entirely.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader loses the warning that badly written functions can make code harder rather than easier to read, which is the premise the whole tips section rests on.

heading: Naming and syntax
proposition: The English warns against names already taken by other functions existing in your environment; the Vietnamese warns against names already used by other functions 'trong hàm của chúng ta' (inside our own function).
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader checks only the names used inside the function they are writing, and still collides with names of loaded package or base R functions in the global environment, which is the collision the advice exists to prevent.

heading: Basic syntax and structure
proposition: The English says selecting every second observation is relevant 'after having ordered by date or visit'; the Vietnamese drops the ordering step and renders it as 'ví dụ như ngày đặt lịch khám hoặc lần khám' (for example appointment date or visit), an example of records rather than a sorting prerequisite.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader applies the every-second-row selection to unsorted longitudinal data and gets an arbitrary subset instead of the intended date- or visit-ordered one, without knowing that sorting first is required.

heading: Functions
proposition: The English makes the reduced error rate conditional ('given there were no errors in the function itself'); the Vietnamese states it as an established cause ('vì không có lỗi trong chính hàm này', because there is no error in the function itself).
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader takes it as given that a function contains no errors, and loses the warning that a bug inside a function is silently reproduced at every call site.

heading: How does R build functions?
proposition: The English states that you CAN verify each component by calling the associated function; the Vietnamese states that we NEED to ('chúng ta cần kiểm tra') check each component.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader treats calling formals(), body() and environment() as a required step after writing every function, rather than as an available inspection tool.

heading: Tips and best Practices for well functioning functions
proposition: The English sentence reads 'It should produce the contrary'; the Vietnamese reads 'Tuy nhiên, điều ngược lại có thể xảy ra' (However, the opposite can happen), turning a statement about what functional programming should do into a caution about what may happen.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader receives a warning that functional programming may make code harder to read, a caution the English text as written does not state; the two versions set different expectations for the tips that follow.
